member of the commission. mr president, thank you for the opportunity to discuss the results of the successful montreal conference on climate change held in december. in montreal, in addition to the 11th conference of the parties to the united nations framework convention on climate change, we also had the first meeting of the states that have ratified the kyoto protocol. i am particularly pleased with the presence and positive activity of the ten members of the european parliament at the montreal conference. it underlines the importance that both our institutions attach to tackling the challenge of climate change and the role of the multilateral process in this process. our frequent contacts and cooperation in montreal have borne fruit. it is therefore important that we continue this practice in future sessions. the outcome of the montreal conference is an important step forward for the multilateral climate negotiations. the kyoto protocol is now fully implemented, and the agreement on the montreal action plan paves the way for future international cooperation on climate change. this will, inter alia, provide greater certainty for the european carbon market and the private sector. the list of montreal's political accomplishments is indeed impressive. firstly, we agreed to launch two rounds of formal dialogue on the future climate change response system. the convention dialogue circle includes all parties to the convention, including the united states and australia, which have not ratified the kyoto protocol. and of course all the big developing countries. a long-term, in-depth dialogue will be held under the convention, organised in four working meetings over the next two years. the results of this dialogue will be presented to the conference of the parties in 2007. the kyoto round will discuss further emission reductions by developing countries under the kyoto protocol for the period after 2012. a special ad hoc united nations working group was set up under the kyoto protocol. the group will complete its work as soon as possible and in a timely manner so that there is no gap between the first and second commitment periods of the protocol. secondly, in montreal all the decisions necessary for the full operation of the kyoto protocol were taken as follows: the kyoto protocol's operational rules, known as the marrakesh agreements, were adopted in their entirety. the decision on compliance shall make the protocol binding on all contracting parties and provide for the establishment of a relevant compliance committee. the five-year work programme on adaptation includes a full range of activities, including work aimed at complementing our knowledge of the impacts of climate change and the problems it creates. it also includes specific actions for the design of adaptation and the implementation of the relevant measures. the adjustment fund will finance adjustment activities. its resources will be a contribution to the clean growth mechanism which will probably start to be paid in 2008. thirdly, the montreal conference went further by making the kyoto protocol a stronger and more effective system. the clean growth mechanism has been strengthened. the executive and supervisory role of the clean development mechanism governing board has been clarified and strengthened. the secretariat will be staffed with more staff in order to improve the services it provides to the governing board and its committees. the parties also committed to provide a financial contribution to the operation of the clean development mechanism. the majority of this money will be a contribution from the european union. the operational bodies for common implementation were also set up. the preparatory work on the clean development mechanism may also be used for the approval of joint implementation projects. this means that it is possible to speed up the approval of projects of common application for which plans have already been drawn up. the european union also pledged to provide financial support to the joint implementation monitoring committee. finally, the european union used the montreal conference to demonstrate its significant progress in implementing the kyoto protocol. the many positive reactions i have received strengthen my conviction that the european union's response to the climate challenge can not only be the most efficient and economically viable, but also provide a competitive advantage for european businesses. the strong interest in the emissions trading system we have put in place makes it clear that we are an example to be followed. the european union has taken a leading role internationally in the fight against climate change. it continued to support the kyoto protocol when serious doubts were cast on its entry into force. however, we must always be aware that greater efforts are needed within the union. most member states need to implement additional measures to achieve the kyoto targets. new joint measures at european union level will also be required. the current second phase of the european climate change programme will help identify the best measures. i would also like to mention the debate within the european union on climate change. i believe that the agreement to open an international dialogue reached in montreal is an important stimulus for the european union. the european union's strategy of seeking to complement the process at the united nations with bilateral commitments and focusing on confidence-building and taking into account the views of other contracting parties has proved successful. the montreal conference endorsed this approach. the european union should now engage with all parties, in particular those with large emissions such as the united states and emerging economies, in a constructive dialogue to explore participation in the future international climate change regime. i believe that montreal marks a new phase in international cooperation to tackle climate change. the search period is over. we now have an international system with all the necessary mechanisms. the commission's proposals are aimed at improving the quality of life of the citizens of the union, and at improving the quality of life of the citizens of the union. but we cannot rest on our laurels. climate change is an urgent need and affects us all. we will need drastic cuts in greenhouse gas emissions in order to stabilize, and then reduce, the concentrations of these gases in our planet's atmosphere. that is why this year, in the second phase of the european climate change programme, we will be discussing new initiatives to strengthen our climate policy. this second european climate change programme will include a comprehensive review of the first phase of climate policies, including the european union's emissions trading system, action on carbon capture and storage, aviation and other transport and other issues. on the basis of this review, i will propose new initiatives to strengthen our climate policy depending on the outcome of this stakeholder consultation process. i know that i can count on the support of the european parliament for this project.

level. the users of port services, i.e. shipowners, businesses, shippers and producers, believe - and i think they are right - that we need a european regulation on market access. let me give you just five brief reasons for a european-style market access regime: first, market access should be made possible for new service providers through regular public tenders for public leased land. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted through state resources. secondly, in favour of existing port handling companies, the present transitional provisions are intended to ensure the continuation of public leases for a period of up to 46 years. the commission's proposals do not therefore endanger any single establishment or job, but allow existing establishments to continue their activities thanks to the long transitional periods. in the interests of the dockers our proposals are correct, because we want to remove self-manufacturing from the directive. we believe that there is no need for a european regulation on self-handling, especially since self-handling is not possible in the area which characterizes the typical activity of a modern port, namely container traffic. because no container ship has a loading dock that could be used by the ship's crew to take the containers on or off board. we are also still safeguarding the jobs of the dock workers by means of the long transitional provisions which i have just explained. finally, there is no danger of social dumping or of worsening working conditions, because the directive explicitly states that it does not interfere with the social legislation of the member states and with collective bargaining. fourthly, in the interests of shipowners and the shipping industry, our proposals are correct. in future, when new companies enter the market, they will be able to choose between the most efficient and cost-effective suppliers and will not be in a monopoly situation, as is the case in some ports, where they will have to accept whatever is offered to them. fifthly, from the point of view of the economy and the consumer, the amended directive is the right one, because it is important for imports and exports that all ports regulate imports and exports even more efficiently and at a lower cost to our consumers. in this respect, i believe that fair market access while protecting the interests of existing businesses and jobs is the best solution. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he has not already made a statement on this matter. i would ask involving all actors. we need everyone's contribution if europe is to unlock its full potential. mr president, growth and jobs are the core preoccupation of our citizens. we must show them that europe can deliver a credible response to their concerns. the spring european council in march is the first real test of the determination of all actors to move forward towards economic reform and modernisation. member states have drawn up their national reform programmes. the commission is finalising its assessment of those programmes and will report to the spring european council. i would like to thank the european parliament for its support and look forward to continuing to work closely with you on the growth and jobs agenda. the parliamentary dimension of the lisbon agenda is not window dressing but an essential element in promoting and ensuring support for the implementation of the necessary reforms. in that sense, we can say that the revised lisbon agenda has already been successful. it has managed to create a common vision and a strong consensus. no one seriously continues to dispute that the priority should be on growth for jobs. it is now time to turn words into deeds, vision into action. the message we need from the spring european council is that europe has made a credible commitment to structural reforms and is determined to exploit fully all its potential for growth and more and better jobs. we therefore welcome the austrian presidency's willingness to inject new dynamism into the discussion of some pending proposals that are key to the success of the lisbon strategy, including the services directive. the establishment of a well-functioning internal market in the area of services is a key opportunity to free up the potential of europe. the commission will cooperate fully with the presidency and parliament to seek political agreement on directives between the council and parliament. i welcome the fact that parliament is actively preparing the ground for a balanced approach, that is to say, an approach which will apply the treaty provisions on trade in services while, at the same time, ensuring compliance with the working and employment conditions for posted workers and recognising the specific nature of services of general interest. to this end, i believe the role of the european social partners can be a crucial one. we will be calling on our social partners for a joint contribution to a balanced and ambitious solution for the services sector. let us be frank about this: the services sector and small and mediumsized enterprises are the most important drivers for the creation of jobs in europe. they should receive the support they deserve from political leaders. progress on the revised lisbon agenda will have to factor in the work undertaken as a follow-up to the hampton court meeting. this covers key areas like research and development, universities, demographic change, energy, migration, security and the role of europe in the world. the commission will propose new initiatives in the fields of research and education, preparing the establishment of a european institute of technology and furthering work on the mutual comparability and recognition of qualifications. we will provide a focus for debate on demographic change and on its implications for a fairer work/life balance. we shall also present a roadmap for gender equality which will look at different european union policies and see how they can contribute to reducing gender gaps in employment or unemployment conditions and to addressing the phenomenon of violence against women and trafficking. we will seek to strengthen the effectiveness of the european union in pursuing its external objectives and interests by increasing the coherence of our action. energy issues mark the debut of this presidency, and i want to thank the austrian presidency for its excellent cooperation in dealing with the recent gas dispute between russia and ukraine. energy issues will remain a dominant theme of our future agenda. the recent crisis and persistently high oil prices teach a lesson to those who normally resist and obstruct the provision of a european dimension for energy policy and to all those who always resist a european dimension in politics and policy-making. europe must have an improved, more coordinated energy policy based on the principles of diversification of sources, security of supply and sustainability. well before hampton court, when leaders clearly stressed the need for a new approach, the commission announced a green paper on secure, competitive and sustainable energy policy. we are also preparing a series of new initiatives on energy efficiency and clean technologies. we will take up the debate initiated with the biomass action plan and complement it with a communication on biofuels. finally, we will put forward ideas for developing a real pan-european energy market, enhancing cooperation with our neighbouring countries. this is an example of common sense driving a common approach, where no option should be excluded. national leaders and citizens see the sense of a common, coherent european policy. now is the time for the european institutions to play their role with ambition and rigour. i look forward to working with you over the coming months to give shape to european energy policy. this brings me to another important point. the commission has presented sustainable development as an overarching objective and, last december, presented a communication on the review of the sustainable development strategy. we welcome the fact that the austrian presidency has chosen to put that at the top of its priorities. this will provide the momentum needed to complete the preparation of a new european union sustainable development strategy. the commission document is an ambitious and concrete one. it offers a long-term vision for addressing issues such as climate change, preservation of natural resources, social exclusion and world poverty. it sets clear objectives, realistic targets and procedures for monitoring and measuring progress. it identifies involving all stakeholders not only institutions, but business too in a real partnership as a priority. regional authorities and citizens should work together to deliver concrete results. another issue that will remain high up on the european agenda in the coming months is security. i am pleased to see that the austrian presidency's priorities in the area of freedom, justice and security are in line with those of the commission. the translation of the aid programme into practical measures remains our common priority. in the area of migration, we will continue the debate launched by the policy plan on legal migration, adopted in december 2005, and come forward with proposals on the long-term resident status of persons in need of international protection. during this semester we shall also table a green paper on drugs and civil society, a proposal on the applicable law in divorce matters, and a green paper on conflict of law in the area of matrimonial property regimes. the commission will present the first implementation report on the hague action plan. we look forward to achieving significant progress on those important issues during the austrian presidency. one last priority that i want to comment on is our relations with our neighbors. the year 2006 will be a decisive period. in the spring, the commission will review the progress made by bulgaria and romania in preparing for accession and assess the level of their readiness to join the union. on the western balkans, we welcome the priority set by the austrian presidency. since 2003 the countries of the western balkans have had a clear european perspective. that process is critical for ensuring peace and stability in europe. the commission attaches great importance to the careful monitoring of the situation in the region and the region's relationship with the union. that is why i have decided to personally visit the region in the coming weeks. europe also needs to prepare to take greater responsibility in kosovo. as discussions on kosovo's future status reach a critical stage, the european union has to show that it is able to bring a concrete contribution to a complex and delicate issue. last year, heads of state and government launched a period of reflection on the future of europe. citizens, civil society and political actors are expressing and debating their views, expectations and ideas. the commission is playing its part fully, implementing plan d for democracy, dialogue and debate. i am pleased to report that members of the commission made a total of 68 visits to national parliaments during 2005, explaining our policies and their added value to european citizens, and listening, because a process of dialogue is not just about explaining; it is also, and above all, about listening to the message citizens give us. the european parliament, with its counterparts in the national parliaments, is putting its weight behind this debate. the commission is ready to cooperate fully with its initiatives. european leaders before us were prepared to dream of what could be. they had the courage of their european convictions. they opened a pathway to reconciliation and progress for europe which none had walked before. today we are the beneficiaries of that legacy and of their foresight. however, at a time when past achievements and current freedoms are so easily discounted, we cannot take future public consent for granted. it must be earned. my vision is of a stronger europe which provides a solid political, economic and social framework for our citizens, a europe based on culture, a europe based on common values. it is of a europe of democracy, accountability and transparency. in our troubled world today, we more than ever need a strong european union, a european union which promotes security, human rights and respect for the rule of law. following the june european council, the commission will take stock of the preliminary results of the public debate and of the discussions under plan d. we also intend, at the request of the austrian presidency, to propose an agenda for further debate and action at european level. this will provide a basis for the heads of state and government to determine the way forward for the union with a renewed commitment to translate our common objectives into actions. the union's main asset is a core of common values and a rich culture which should inspire our reflection on the future of europe. institutions are important, of course they are, but institutions are instruments for achieving our goals and we should not forget the main goals of our project. we need to provide determined leadership and reinforced consensus to bring europe forward together. we need to concentrate on the essentials. we need to focus on delivery. we need to communicate our public purpose in plain and meaningful terms. i will conclude by saying, as i told chancellor schüssel when i and other commissioners visited him in vienna, that i think it was a great decision by the austrian presidency to choose all the beautiful and bright colours of europe as its logo. i believe it is now time for us to do away with grey and black colours, to insist on the possibilities of such diversity of europe and to use these very important six months of the austrian presidency to show our renewed commitment to a europe that belongs to the future and believes in in writing. the european parliament's joint resolution on afghanistan is particularly appalling in that it contains no criticism of western military operations. instead, it supports the nato operation (international security assistance force) isaf and the so-called war on terror - operation enduring freedom (oef). the greens' demand that the command structures of isaf and oef should be separated is completely inadequate. the isaf and oef are closely integrated on the ground. the expansion of the isaf mission in southern afghanistan into a more open combat zone will further exacerbate the war effort. the strong presence of european troops in afghanistan will relieve the us troops and thus the occupying forces in iraq. the closure of military bases which are the only means of ensuring the presence of troops in afghanistan is also necessary. in particular, the termez military base of the german bundeswehr in uzbekistan must be closed. termez is the main supply route for all troops stationed in afghanistan. cooperation with uzbekistan is a scandal. uzbekistan is ruled by an authoritarian regime, which is responsible in particular for the andischan massacre. the dismantling of the military bases in afghanistan is also overdue in view of the recent bombing of a pakistani village by cia units, which is contrary to international law.
the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament! it is a great pleasure to speak to you today for the first time in this chamber and to meet you. i am particularly pleased that the interinstitutional dialogue which must be conducted between the various institutions is a subject where cooperation is particularly important. it is true - as the two rapporteurs have already said - that 2005 was a difficult year. mr voggenhuber even used the word crisis. we are in fact facing a crisis of confidence with the european citizens. we must answer the legitimate questions of the citizens. i also agree with mr duff that this crisis of confidence, this doubt about the european project, is an opportunity for us all. we must all together - the commission, parliament and the council - seize this opportunity. i should like to thank parliament in particular for having dealt with this question at a time when governments were not yet ready to start a serious debate. the duff/voggenhuber report has been the subject of a debate in this parliament which will help us. the austrian presidency has made every effort from day one to take up this debate, to continue it and to intensify it. you've all noticed that this debate has been very heated from the beginning. the whole range of opinions was expressed, as is also reflected in the report adopted by the committee on constitutional affairs. one thing is clear: there are no easy solutions, no tricks or shortcuts to bridge this gap of trust between europe and its citizens in a hurry. the only way to have a serious and long-term impact is to deal with the problems in a real and serious way. we believe that this debate must be broad, as is also reflected in your report which is being debated today. it is not just a question of the constitutional treaty and a legal debate. it is a matter of a wide-ranging debate: what kind of europe do we want? vice-president of the commission. mr president, honourable members, in this first plenary part-session of the year i should like to wish all of you an excellent 2006. from the constitutional point of view, i believe it can only be better than last year. i hope, as the person responsible both for constitutional issues and for interinstitutional affairs, that we can continue our fruitful, effective and close cooperation. i wish to thank the rapporteurs for this report on the period of reflection and the motion for a resolution. i have already discussed it on several occasions with the two members of the european parliament who were members of the european convention. i would like to underline the considerable progress made since the initial considerations and congratulate the co-rapporteurs for the job they have done and also for their ability to take on board the many views expressed during the intense discussions in committee. i will limit my remarks to four points. the first is that we all wish to achieve a constitutional settlement, to make europe more transparent, more democratic and more effective. the question is how to achieve that settlement after the french and dutch ‘no’ votes. i was happy to see that all options regarding the constitution remain open in your resolution. during the reflection period it is essential to listen to citizens, social partners, political parties, and national and regional parliaments without prejudging the result of the wider dialogue and debate. if we do not, this exercise will lose all its value. i also took note of your favourite option. maintaining the constitution, however, will not be possible without french and dutch support with, if necessary, additional clarifications and measures. recent eurobarometer surveys have shown that european citizens’ support for the concept of a constitution for the eu has increased by two percentage points over the past five months to 63%. therefore, as has been said many times in the committee on constitutional affairs, it is important to change the context rather than the text. that is why the dialogue has to focus on the european project in connection with constitutional reform, and on the ultimate objective linked to the instruments to deliver it. it is only after the listening exercise based on the results of national debates is complete, that we will be able to draw conclusions on the best constitutional settlement for europe. that is also why the commission wants to focus on policy priorities addressing citizens’ concerns on growth, jobs, employment and security. secondly, i fully share your resistance to proposals for core groups of certain member states. what we want is a europe for everyone, not just for some. the union is in the process of consolidating the most recent accession process. we still have to work hard to ensure the smooth integration of the new member states. my view is that any enhanced cooperation must, in all circumstances, be undertaken within the existing treaties and remain open to all member states. you can rest assured that the commission and myself will not support any proposal for enhanced cooperation outside the european union institutional framework. (applause) thirdly, it seems reasonable to me to draft final conclusions on the reflection period in 2007, under the german or portuguese presidency. the june 2006 european council is clearly a major milestone in this process, but it should not be the end of it. it will, of course, be up to the european council to decide on any potential extension of the reflection period beyond the june 2006 extension already suggested by the austrian presidency. in any case, as announced in plan d, the commission will prepare a communication for the june european council setting out its thinking on the initial feedback received during the period of reflection, and this will be based on the national visits currently being undertaken by the president, myself and fellow commissioners, a special eurobarometer report, discussion forums and the 9 may conferences. this synthesis report should explain the background and approach taken by the commission over the last year, outline the initial results of the listening exercise and provide a series of conclusions for the austrian presidency on the next steps to be taken. this will complement the factual report that will be prepared by the austrian presidency on the basis of contributions from the member states. fourthly, i support your rejection of piecemeal implementation of the constitution. the reason for that is simple - it has to do with respect. respect for those who said ‘no’ and for those who have already ratified, and respect for the institutional balance. cherry-picking could give the impression that the union is trying to circumvent the results of national referenda and is liable to impair the overall institutional balance. we should respect the difference between our institutions and those in the member states and, most of all, when we embark on various praiseworthy initiatives and projects we should always respect each country’s democratic traditions. all of us play important, but different, roles. in conclusion, i would stress that we cannot discuss these issues without entering into political debate and discussing political priorities. european citizens will see that there are political differences in europe. this is another forum for discussing political priorities, but without it and without any discussion on constitutional matters nothing will work. we have to combine this process with creating legitimacy for our institutions by delivering the political results that european citizens want, so we have to consider their daily concerns as well as the constitutional issues. (applause)
draft opinion of the consultative committee on foreign affairs. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the draft constitutional treaty produced a balance in the convention and the intergovernmental conference, which was essentially supported by the national parliaments, which formed the strongest group in the constitutional convention. fourteen countries have ratified it, two by referendum and two by a vote against. this failure, which is also linked to national issues, but also to the mood in europe as a whole, is a failure of national politics, but also of european politics, because we have not succeeded in establishing europe. we must take the concerns of the citizens seriously; we must take them seriously in france and in the netherlands too and we cannot just ignore them, but we should make it clear why we need this europe. the reflection phase must be used for this. this is not a period of debate on the details of the constitution, but one in which europe must be returned to the people in its foundations. we must also see and make it clear that the constitutional treaty contains precisely those things which the citizens criticise as being lacking, such as greater capacity to act in the field of foreign and security policy, which is the focus of my opinion. all the polls show that this is exactly what the citizens want: the representation of europe abroad. and for that, the constitution provides regulations that only it provides and that we cannot create on the side under the current conditions. it creates a new way of subsidiarity, with the involvement of the national parliaments, to prevent centralism and to link this idea of subsidiarity with solidarity. the civil rights and the charter of fundamental rights play a major role. the citizens are the decisive actors of this constitution and they are also protected. it is also necessary to see that in future, for example, the president of the commission, as the head of the european executive, emerges directly as a result of the elections to the european parliament and that citizens play a role in this. we should therefore also focus on the fact that parts i and ii are the actual constitutional treaty, while part iii is the treaty of nice. we have not been able to clear up this misunderstanding. i am therefore grateful that the austrian presidency will be presenting a road map and that germany will be taking new initiatives during its presidency. we should now concentrate on the dialogue, evaluate the reflection phase and present the proposals in 2007. this means that we should not take action now, as duff and voggenhuber suggest in their motion. this is premature and does not meet the wishes of the citizens.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on agriculture and rural development. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. first of all, i would like to congratulate mr duff and mr voggenhuber on their balanced report. i am very pleased to be able to briefly present the opinion of the committee on agriculture and rural development on this report. the european parliament has had to fight for a long time for the right to vote in agriculture. the draft constitution has welcomed the adoption of the codecision rules in the fields of environmental protection, food safety and consumer protection, which have been established since the amsterdam treaties. in the field of agricultural policy, the council of agriculture ministers can still override the opinion of the european parliament, since the co-decision procedure under the present treaty does not apply to the common agricultural policy. in this context, the draft constitution did indeed offer the prospect of gaining democratic legitimacy in that all fundamental decisions on agricultural policy should be subject to co-determination. the committee on agriculture, fisheries and rural development has already adopted the proposal for a directive on the common organization of the market in fishery products. the objectives of the common agricultural policy referred to in article iii-227 are incompatible with the objectives of the european union as set out in article i-3 and are no longer negotiable. they urgently need to be updated to take account of the multifunctionality of our modern agriculture. agriculture in the eu today provides jobs for 10 million people. it is the only guarantee of sustainable rural development and is inextricably linked to it. the present draft constitution is not sufficient to achieve a socially acceptable cap. on the contrary, a future treaty should extend the codecision procedure as a matter of priority to the common agricultural policy, in particular by filling the remaining gaps in the agricultural field in articles iii-230 (2) and iii-231 (2) of this text. given the importance of the cap and its prominent position in the eu budget, european citizens deserve the highest level of transparency and, above all, participation in this sensitive area. i believe that this can only mean that the european parliament has full co-determination in all matters of agricultural policy, consumer protection and food safety.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. one sentence in the report cannot be underlined enough: 'the treaty of nice does not provide a viable basis for the continuation of the european integration process'. i 'll add: this treaty marks the beginning of the end of an enlarged union of citizens. what's nice? the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european parliament's budget for the financial year 2000 is a very important one, and it is a very important one. the list of all that europe has to lose without a constitution is very long. there can be no march back to the past! is nice really going to be poured into concrete? i do not want the european union to become a free trade area with limited social responsibility. a nuclear europe which creates new divisions in europe is unacceptable. that's why the constitutional process must continue. europe needs a new treaty. only one thing is absolutely clear: a simple 'continue like this' will not do it. the concerns and problems of the people must finally be taken seriously. this is the clear message of the constitutional referendum in france and the netherlands. what we need is a change of policy in the european union towards a social europe. only then will we have the active support of the citizens for the enlarged union and for a peaceful united europe.

we're coming to the question period. question no 1 by mr liam aylward (h-1119/05) subject: the use of the european parliament in the european parliament subject: climate changethe european council is asked to make a statement on the success or failure of the united nations conference on climate change held in montreal, canada, during the week beginning 5 december 2005.
the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, as the honourable member is aware, the european council recently welcomed the positive results of the united nations conference on climate change, held in montreal from 28 november to 10 december 2005. the montreal plan of action now calls for future climate talks to be conducted on two fronts. first, the parties to the kyoto protocol will enter into negotiations on binding emission targets for developed countries during a second commitment period. second, all parties to the unfccc, including the united states and major developing countries, have agreed to engage in a global discussion on long-term coordinated action on climate change. all in all, the kyoto protocol is now fully operational and we believe that the way forward within the united nations framework has been paved.
my dear colleague! i have now been very generous in welcoming the presidency of the council. but i would like to remind all colleagues once again that they have only 30 seconds to respond to demand. if we all go overboard, we can only deal with a very few issues. so please be so kind as to adhere to the demand time.
the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, it is clear - and the montreal negotiations have shown this - that the major greenhouse gas producers are now increasingly involved in the dialogue on a future climate regime, and it is important that there is no single entry. the future regime may well involve structural changes, which should make the efforts made so far significantly easier for europe to further reduce greenhouse gas emissions. there are also quite remarkable developments outside the international climate process, and different regions have taken different initiatives. the gleneagles action plan, if i may mention it at this point, sets out the priorities of the eu's main trading partners for technology transfer and tackling the effects of climate change, and it provides for dialogue and technological cooperation with india, china and russia. it is in the european union's interest to ensure with all countries inside and outside the international climate dialogue that our common targets for reducing emissions are not undermined by the actions of groups or states.
the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, the eu emissions trading system is one of the cornerstones in the fight against climate change. it is the world's first international trading system for co2 emissions, and it tracks some 12 000 installations, or just under half of all european co2 emissions. it helps eu member states to meet their emissions targets. no other system allows such cost-effective reductions in emissions. the council is well aware of the difficulties in implementing the eu emissions trading system during the pilot phase you have mentioned. this first period has brought valuable experience which should be incorporated into the future development of the system. on the basis of these initial findings, the directive already provides for a full review in 2006. this review will allow all possible areas for improvement to be examined and incorporated for the period after 2012.
the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, the european union has always been committed to global cooperation on climate protection. the european union and its representatives have also made this clear in all international forums and in the council conclusions. the european implementation of the kyoto protocol gives credibility to the eu's efforts and shows that climate action is feasible and compatible with economic growth. we do not consider that economic and climate concerns are opposites. for example, the eu's path to an emissions trading system is the most cost-effective way to achieve emissions reductions. furthermore, international studies have repeatedly shown that inaction would have far more severe consequential costs than funding climate action now and in the future. the earlier measures to protect the climate are taken, the lower the costs to the economy in the long run. it therefore makes economic sense for the european union to take climate action, which also creates new jobs, for reasons of energy efficiency.

the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, first of all, the questions by mr posselt, mr papadimoulis and mr karas on kosovo. according to the thessaloniki declaration, adopted by the eu and the western balkan states at their summit in june 2003, the future of the western balkan region, including kosovo, lies in the european union. the council's position on kosovo is based on a set of principles adopted by the european council in its declaration on kosovo at its meeting of 16 and 17 june 2005. any solution to the status of kosovo must be fully compatible with european values and standards, be consistent with international legal instruments and obligations and the charter of the united nations, and contribute to the realisation of the european perspective for kosovo and the region. the status must in any event ensure that the situation in kosovo does not return to that which existed before march 1999. the basis for determining status must be a multiethnic society and full respect for human rights, including the right of return for all. this status, and this is particularly important, must also provide for effective constitutional guarantees for the protection of minorities, including mechanisms to ensure minority participation in central and local government. it must also include specific safeguards for cultural heritage and religious sites and promote effective mechanisms to combat organised crime and terrorism. the status must lead to greater security and stability in the region. the european union is not prepared to accept any unilateral or forcibly imposed solution or any change in the present territory of kosovo, and there can be no partition of kosovo or merger with another country or part of another country. the territorial integrity of the neighbouring countries must be fully respected. the council also considers that the continued implementation of the standards is of crucial importance, both now and in the future, especially as regards the protection of minorities. in this context, the council has repeatedly stressed its appreciation and support for the work of the united nations special representative for kosovo, mr søren jessen-petersen. the council is determined to cooperate fully in the determination of the status of kosovo and to be involved in the relevant negotiation process under the auspices of the united nations. to this end, in november 2005, the high representative solana appointed mr stefan lehne as the european union's representative to work closely with the united nations high commissioner for status, president athisaari. the council approved this appointment. the european union delegate shall provide the un delegate with input for the negotiations, while helping the eu to prepare for its future role in kosovo in the post-resolution 1244 period. it also works closely with the member states and the commission. the european commission will also be represented in vienna, where the office of the united nations high commissioner for human rights has been set up. the european union will be particularly interested in areas such as the protection of human rights, minority issues, cultural and religious sites, the rule of law and economic development. the un envoy has indicated a willingness to work closely with the eu on these and other issues. at the same time, the eu has entered into informal consultations with unmik, together with other international organisations and partners, in the context of the restructuring of the united nations interim administration mission in kosovo (unmik). the aim is to explore options for a future international presence in kosovo without prejudging the outcome of the status talks. against this background, high representative solana and commissioner olli rehn also presented their second report to the council in december on how the eu could prepare for the challenges ahead. the new international formation for the post-resolution period would be inclusive and have a strong eu component. the eu is to play a central role in the rule of law, including a police mission, capacity building and the economy. the competent authority the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion is enshrined in international human rights instruments. i would refer in particular to the globally applicable article 18 of the international covenant on civil and political rights, which establishes freedom of thought, conscience and religion as an individual right. this right, it says, includes the freedom to have or to adopt a religion and belief of one's own choice and the freedom to manifest one's religion, alone or in community with others, publicly or privately, by worship, observance of religious customs, practice and teaching. the european union attaches great importance to this human right and therefore holds regular talks on this subject with third countries, most recently in new york, where the eu member states successfully introduced a resolution on the elimination of all forms of intolerance and discrimination based on religion or belief to the third committee of the united nations general assembly. the council has repeatedly condemned all forms of intolerance on the grounds of religion and is also closely following developments in the field of human rights. the council takes the opportunity offered by the dialogue with third countries to express clearly its concern about intolerance towards religious and other minorities.
president-in-office of the council. as i have said, the european union raises the question regularly in all dialogues as well as in international fora, which is very important. we have raised it at the united nations. we do not name and shame, but we are very clear when we speak to the countries concerned if we believe, or have reason to believe, that there is persecution or restriction of the right to religious freedom. to give you an example: we very much emphasise the question of religious freedom in our human rights discussions with china, because we believe this to be an issue that must be raised in the context of our dialogue with china. the same is true in other areas. the adoption of a resolution, which was adopted by a large majority of members of the united nations, is a step in the right direction. this will give us even more leverage in the future to raise this question in our relations with those countries. the fact that we do business with those countries does not prevent us from speaking out clearly when it comes to violations of human rights.

the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the spread of the disease. however, any violation of human rights is a cause for concern. the continuing internal armed conflict in colombia is also the cause of most human rights violations, which are committed mainly by illegal armed groups. the eu therefore continuously appeals to the parties to the conflict to respect human rights and international humanitarian law, and it also maintains regular contacts, in particular with the colombian authorities and the office of the united nations high commissioner for human rights in bogota. i can add that it was just before christmas that the colombian vice-president was in austria - i spoke to him and spoke to him very intensely, particularly on the question of human rights. in its conclusions of 3 october 2005, the council reaffirmed its full support for the government of colombia, in particular in its efforts to enforce the rule of law throughout the country and to combat terrorism and the production and trafficking of illicit drugs. the council also reaffirmed its long-standing policy of supporting the colombian government in its efforts to resolve the internal armed conflict by negotiation, including direct talks with the illegal armed groups willing to negotiate a peace agreement. we therefore welcome the recent contacts between the illegal armed groups and the colombian authorities and we also call on all parties to do their utmost to bring about a peaceful solution and thus to put an end to the internal armed conflict, which has now lasted well over a generation and is the main cause of human rights violations.
the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, madam president, you are asking a question that cannot be answered. is the european union doing enough in the face of the suffering in so many countries? this is a question that cannot really be answered in the abstract. we're doing the best we can. i would like to point out, however, that in the context of the council conclusions of last october, i have already mentioned concrete initiatives, and i would add that most of these initiatives fall within the commission's remit. however, i would point out, for example, that in december 2005 the commission decided to make available an amount of one and a half million euro under the rapid reaction mechanism. the question remains whether this is enough or whether we cannot do more.

in writing. why i continue to oppose the eu constitution treaty:1. the eu constitution treaty must finally be put to the test, so that a perspective for a social and civil europe can be opened. the eu constitution is intended to give a decisive boost to the militarisation of the eu. a number of militarization projects are laid down in the constitutional treaty (iii-311). the eu constitution is intended to equip the eu for global warfare. it opens the way for worldwide military interventions (i-41.1 and iii-309). the eu treaty contains an explicit obligation to arm (i-41.3). if ratified, the tendency to spend more money on armaments would increase. 5.the eu's foreign policy is bound by the eu's constitutional treaty only to the principles and not to the un charter as a whole (i-3,4). this leaves room for interpretation for the eu to wage war even without a un mandate. the eu constitution treaty serves as a programmatic blueprint to push the militarization of the eu beyond the current treaty situation. the eu arms agency (iii-311) is being expanded and the battle groups (iii-312) are being set up. the eu constitution is intended to give neoliberalism constitutional status (iii-177). the anti-social bolkestein policy is just a first taste. the proposal by german chancellor angela merkel to attach to the eu constitution a legally non-binding declaration on the 'social dimension' of europe, only to have it voted on again in france and the netherlands, is simply scandalous.
in writing. the report by british conservative mep charles tannock, voted on today in the european parliament, reaffirms the main features of the eu's neighbourhood policy: the eu's geopolitical interests are to be enforced by human rights rhetoric. 1.the eu's neighbourhood policy aims to create a geopolitical space of influence for the european union and its member states. a 'privileged partnership' is sought with neighbouring countries (including the south caucasus). the report explicitly identifies the geostrategic orientation of the neighbourhood policy towards the eu's resource security. energy policyis set to become an important topic in the eu's neighbourhood policy, as the eu is surrounded by the world's main oil and natural gas reserves (russia and the caspian basin, the middle east and north africa). the geostrategic importance of transit countries such as georgia and armenia is also underlined. the european union must also take action to ensure that the situation in belarus is not further destabilized. if one looks at the different treatment of belarus and uzbekistan, the toleration of military bases by eu member states, such as germany's in termez, it becomes clear that this is primarily about the expansion of the eu's sphere of influence. 5.neighbouring countries will also be bound to the eu militarily. the eu's military infrastructure and military interventions should be open to them.

member of the commission. mr president, the european commission welcomes the own-initiative report of the european parliament on the effects of globalisation on the internal market and thanks everyone involved, in particular the rapporteurs mrs herczog and mr markov, as well as the members of the imco and inta committees, for the good work undertaken in putting this report together. i know that it was not an easy task as the issue of globalisation is an extremely complex one. it was also very useful to organise a hearing on the matter. i appreciated the opportunity to speak about the way i see the challenges, and to hear directly what members of parliament and stakeholders had to say. the result is a very balanced and comprehensive report, one which addresses the key challenges in a succinct way. the report is a timely contribution to an important debate. europe needs to find appropriate responses to today’s key challenges: the steadily increasing forces of global competition, the impact of new technologies and our ageing population. as international integration accelerates, the concept of open markets and a globalising economy have come under attack. of course, there are legitimate concerns about globalisation. there have to be proper structures, which can help developing and emerging economies in particular. there is also a clear need for appropriate forms of governance. however, there are those who abuse these arguments to try to undermine the whole concept of economic freedom. i am not denying that many industries go through difficult and sometimes painful transitions. but it does no good to try to shift the balance elsewhere – foreign takeovers, cheap imports, and migrant workers. protectionism is not the answer. it never was historically – it only ever led to great tensions between nations – and it is not now. comparing the degree of openness of economic systems with economic growth and development will show that openness pays. it always has done and it always will. for people first. with jobs. with thriving businesses. by releasing human energies, not capping or constraining them. i am very glad that in its report the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, as well as the committee on international trade, which has given an opinion, takes a constructive and balanced approach towards globalisation. as the report says, we can make globalisation a success if we provide the right conditions, and if we focus on our strengths. and we do not need to be modest about this. europe has a lot to offer. we must make sure that europe and the internal market remain an attractive place for consumers and businesses; an attractive place to invest, particularly for research and innovation activities in high-value products and services, where our businesses excel. this requires a strong, knowledge-based and properly regulated internal market, using the experience we have gained and the lessons we have learned. this is europe’s best response to its domestic problems of low economic growth and high unemployment, but also to the challenge of globalisation. priorities in this context are: an effective implementation of the new lisbon strategy for growth and jobs; the completion of the internal market, including for services, telecoms, energy, and financial services; ensuring simple and effective regulation, which frees businesses and citizens from unnecessary costs and red tape; and making better use of the existing internal market framework, which includes better administrative cooperation across borders. most of the relevant work is already under way, and it is important that all players, at the eu level and at member state level, do everything to make it happen. as the report quite rightly stresses, globalisation also has a strong external dimension for internal market policy-making. we need to be much more outward-looking than in the past and to be aware of the external aspects of our internal economic policies, such as our internal market rules. nothing is simply domestic any more. we need more international regulatory convergence and equivalence of rules. this is particularly important in the area of financial markets, which are leading the way in globalisation. furthermore, europe must use its scale to help deliver ambitious and balanced solutions to problems of market access or regulatory issues. a successful conclusion of the doha round, including on services, is a key element in this respect. everyone will benefit! last but not least, we need a new partnership of the eu and member states. neither can deliver on their own to ensure that europe remains the attractive place that it still is. i am confident that the report of the european parliament will contribute significantly to this important wider discussion on europe in the globalised world.

and i am referring specifically to services of general interest and services of general economic interest - should be covered and dealt with separately in a framework directive. they are not covered by this directive. instead of this clear limitation, we now have a catalogue of individual exceptions. there are a few missing: education is still lacking, social services are not yet settled, nor is the construction of social housing. some services are completely exempt. other services, such as the major network services, are only partially exempted. all of this creates a patchwork of individual regulations that make it difficult to keep track of. there is a lack of transparency and legal certainty. and legal certainty was the topic that everyone was talking about today. the small and mediumsized enterprises need legal certainty above all. otherwise, there will be no investment, and the consumer will not buy. the second is article 16, the controversial question of the principle of the country of origin. here too, there would have been a simple and clear alternative: opening up market access for home-country services to the whole of the eu, but with the clear requirement that local laws and standards be respected for the provision of services locally. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a regulation on the application of the principle of the free movement of goods, which would allow the free movement of goods within the community. but that also raises some unanswered questions. this also leads to a lack of legal clarity and legal certainty. the court of justice shall have the final say on this proposal. we cannot support this draft directive. it does not create confidence in european legislation and parliament is weakening itself with this directive. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. as we know, the free movement of persons, goods and capital, as laid down in the ec treaty, is established within the union, so that it is hardly possible to call for an absolute ban on the free choice of location, especially since such a ban would lead to a negative immobilisation of the european economy. but it is necessary - and the reform of the structural funds and the law on aid offers the opportunity - to introduce a complement to the principles of free movement, provided that this is done within the framework of cohesion policy. this means that it is essential that the commission, when it approves aid and also funds from the structural funds, ensures that the granting of such aid is linked to medium-term guarantees of location and employment. yes, europe must provide for this! this report by mr hutchinson - although it was the subject of intense discussions in the committee - makes it clear that the undertakings receiving aid are committed to implementing the policy of economic, social and territorial cohesion. this means, in plain language, that the commission's proposal under the structural funds will be enforced consistently in that companies which have received public aid but do not fulfil their obligations will have to repay it, but will in no case be allowed to receive public aid for the new sites and will be excluded from structural fund support or state aid for a period of at least five years - or better seven years - after the relocation. the report stresses the need to take all necessary measures to prevent european regional policy from providing incentives for relocation of enterprises, which would result in job losses. the report by mr hutchinson is balanced in its present form and should be supported.

question 48 was declared inadmissible (annex ii, part a, point 3 of the ra). question no 49 by mr mölzer (h-0102/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: turkish lira coin for a year now, turkey has been issuing a one-lira coin (worth 0.6 euro) which bears an uncanny resemblance to the two-euro coin. firstly, the head of kemal atatürk on the one-lira coin is liable to be confused with that of king albert ii. the technical similarities in weight and thickness caused a high level of damage to vending machine owners in the eu. the problem is also with the sorting machines of the banks, apart from the ordinary citizen who may not even be aware of the danger of confusion. how does the commission assess this latest turkish move? how is it possible for the currency of a country to bear such close resemblances to the euro? what does the commission intend to do to protect european citizens?
vice-president of the commission. the question concerns turkish coins issued from the beginning of 2005, which are quite similar to eu coins. of course the commission shares the concern of the honourable member of parliament about this issue. that sort of thing should not happen. the right to issue coins is one of the most fundamental sovereign rights of a country. however, informal consultations are recommended. there is a network called the coin registration office, established by the international mint directors conference. member mints are assumed to have consulted the coin registration office when preparing a new coin, so that similarities can be avoided. obviously that was not done properly in this case, so coins have appeared which are similar to euro coins. that was not the first time such a thing has occurred. in 2000, in some countries, some coins were very similar to euro coins. even in my own country, when i was in charge of that area, we issued coins which were similar to deutschmarks and we therefore had to change our production. the commission is working with the turkish authorities and they have promised to modify their coins slightly. the production of coins is very expensive and a large exercise. however, there is no panic and the risks are very limited. the vending machines – which are the main issue – can be adjusted. our estimation is that there are some old models of vending machines that are more difficult to adjust, but the majority of new ones can be properly adjusted so that they can take the correct coins. visibly they are quite different. if these coins are handled in the retail trade, they can easily be distinguished. so the risks are limited. the commission has also worked with manufacturers of the coin mechanisms to keep them informed that mechanisms must be adjusted to this problem. we are working with the turkish authorities to ensure that the new production of coins will be slightly modified so that they will not be so similar to euro coins.
vice-president of the commission. this must be negotiated in all frameworks, including the accession negotiation framework. there is some kind of gentleman’s agreement that this sort of thing should not happen. if it does, then the producers of smaller coins must make some adjustments so that the situation with the use of similar coins can be avoided. this will be negotiated. i will have an opportunity to meet the members of the turkish government soon, so i will definitely raise the issue within a certain time, because, as i say, the production of coins is a huge and very expensive exercise. in time we can solve this problem, but until then we will work with the producers of coin mechanisms to avoid possible damage.

member of the commission. i am deeply aware of the pending cases of international adoptions of romanian children and the understandable anxiety surrounding this issue among the families who would like to give these children a new home. as part of the legislative reforms in preparation for acceding to the union, and with the support of the european parliament over the years, romania recently adopted new legislation on child protection. according to this legislation, which entered into force on 1 january 2005, international adoption is a last resort, if a suitable in-country solution, ranging from smaller homes to foster care, cannot be found. through this law, romania has aligned itself with the legal provisions of the european union in this area, as also embodied in the un convention on the rights of the child. the application of these provisions must be seen within the context of former abusive practices relating to international adoptions in romania. as to the more precise legal aspects, it should furthermore be noted that there is currently no community legislation in the field of international adoption. in fact, council regulation (ec) no 2201/2003, which provides for mutual recognition of judgments on parental responsibility, explicitly excludes adoption from its scope. this means basically that the acquis communautaire in the area of child protection has been implemented in romania and bulgaria. the un convention on the rights of the child is taken as a foundation in both romania and bulgaria. the un convention on the rights of the child does not distinguish between the internal and external borders of the european union.

in writing. the enthusiasm of the hazan report, which was adopted by a large majority in the european parliament today, with regard to the european arrest warrant is totally incomprehensible. the council also expressly recommends that the judge executing the european arrest warrant should not be required to carry out a systematic review of compliance with fundamental rights. the main aim is to eliminate judicial controls. this decision continues the anti-fundamentalist course of europe. the principle of mutual recognition of judicial and extrajudicial decisions, and the absence of uniform standards, will leave fundamental rights in the european union in the lurch. the european union has a duty to ensure that the rights of the accused are respected. there is no indication in the report that national transpositions of the european arrest warrant have been rejected by the constitutional courts, as in germany, simply because they are contrary to fundamental rights. on the contrary, it also calls on the member states to 'take the necessary measures without delay to remove constitutional or legal obstacles to the application of the european arrest warrant to their nationals'. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
in writing. i voted in favour of the cottigny report after the epp-led motions received a sufficient majority, which contain my proposals to the employment committee. the restructuring of enterprises is differentiated. on the one hand, companies are being moved to cheap foreign locations, which is causing different business cultures to clash. the synergies often announced are lost and the employees, including those in management, are left behind. on the other hand, restructuring is necessary whenever there is a need to respond to new markets, customer proximity and improved competitiveness. to better prepare eu workers for the necessary mobility, they need adequate support for continuing training and retraining, as well as integration into live-long learning programmes. the restructuring aid, which must be consistent with the lisbon objectives, should primarily benefit smes. in order to assess the legality of support, it is necessary to facilitate the traceability of funds in order to recover funds wrongly withdrawn. the current structural funds are not enough, so i welcome the planned special fund of 500 million euro per year for retraining and professional re-entry, as a sign of our solidarity. however, its criteria must be discussed, since it is only available for transfers to non-eu countries and redundancies of more than 1,000 employees per company. its management must not lead to new bureaucracy at the eu commission and national authorities.
in writing. it is scandalous that exactly 20 years after the chernobyl accident, two thirds of the members of the european parliament voted in favour of the continued use of nuclear energy in the resolution on the lisbon strategy. nuclear power remains a risky technology with unpredictable consequences. the whole cycle of nuclear energy use violates fundamental rights and irreversibly degrades the living conditions of future generations: uranium mining is associated with massive depletion of natural resources and radioactive contamination of groundwater. enriched uranium can also be used to produce nuclear weapons-grade material. it is not really possible to separate the 'civilian' use of nuclear energy from the military use. the normal operation of nuclear reactors also involves a permanent danger (low-level radiation, the risk of contamination of the fluids used to cool nuclear reactors, etc.). large areas of land and seas are repeatedly contaminated by radioactive waste from reprocessing plants. the disposal and final storage of the daily accumulation of highly radioactive nuclear waste, which will remain radioactive for at least 10,000 years, is still unresolved. the €3.1 billion allocated to nuclear research under the eu's seventh framework programme for research (2007-2011) is double that of the previous framework programme. instead of investing in nuclear technologies, the eu should be expanding renewable energy even more. only decentralised supply from renewable energy sources can ensure energy security in the long term.

fundamental freedoms it establishes – in particular the free movement of capital – or to the right of establishment within it. fundamental to these rights is the freedom for companies to re-structure, including by change of ownership. to deny this possibility to companies as a matter of principle or by failing to implement correctly the provisions of the ec sectoral legislation introducing competition in the markets – such as energy, telecoms and financial services – would amount to a serious restriction of their ability to adapt to the challenges presented by the integration of markets in the eu, to the rapid advances in technology which many industries are experiencing, and generally to the evolving dynamics of doing business in the europe of today. european industry is rising to these challenges, including by the appearance of an increasing number of cross-border european businesses. whilst the effects of individual mergers must be assessed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the relevant competition rules, mergers between companies based in different member states are likely to increase competition in the member state concerned, thereby contributing to the realisation of concrete benefits for european consumers in the form of lower prices and wider choice. take the energy sector as an example. the green paper published by the commission last week was very clear. sustainable, competitive and secure energy will not be achieved without open and competitive energy markets, based on competition between companies looking to become europe-wide competitors rather than dominant national players. open markets will strengthen europe and allow it to tackle its problems. at the same time, the process of cross-border corporate restructuring enhances the competitiveness of european businesses by equipping it to succeed in global markets. any interference in this process by national governments which is not justified by legitimate interest as provided for in the treaties, secondary legislation or jurisprudence, risks being seriously damaging to europe’s prospects of benefiting from the opportunities presented by market integration and globalisation. the commission, as you know, has two principal legal instruments at its disposal – the single market rules in the ec treaty and article 21 of the ec merger regulation – for addressing undue interference by national authorities in relation to corporate restructuring. it has the duty to enforce these rules accordingly wherever appropriate. as guardian of the ec treaty, and as the institution responsible for merger control on competition grounds at the european level, the commission is determined to guarantee that companies can effectively benefit from the advantages of the eu’s internal market. that is why enforcement of these provisions is, and will remain, one of the commission’s central priorities.

documents - that the commission had not always drawn the right conclusions from these documents of the vienna report and had deliberately pursued a policy in which we had doubts on certain issues as to whether this was the right way to go. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the european union. they have a different origin, they have a different meaning for the functioning of society. the fact that we are now submitting a new oral question after the last interim report by commissioner kroes - and there will be an accompanying resolution next week - is a continuation of the tradition of the previous legislature. i want to make it very clear that it is, of course, perfectly clear from our point of view that old braids should be cut off. we are no longer in the middle ages, and the guild system is over. nevertheless, the specific features of the professions, and in particular the legal professions, which are the subject of the legal affairs committee, must of course be given special consideration. they're part of the justice system and they have to work. if this does not work, it is bad for the citizen. the citizens are not then afforded adequate legal protection, and an essential element of democracy, the rule of law, is also called into question. it is therefore necessary to examine very carefully and in great detail the regulations governing the professions and to consider carefully what is needed and what is necessary in order to ensure that legal protection and access to justice are as effective and as secure as possible for all citizens, and to do so in practice, taking of course into account in particular the case law of the european court of justice. i would like to come now to a specific problem which was of course raised in this question and which was the reason why we in the legal affairs committee wanted to deal with this issue again in the plenary today. this is the specific role of the fee system in the legal professions. these are of a very special and important nature in many member states of the european union, particularly when it comes to the question of reimbursement rules in court proceedings and when it comes to legal expenses insurance companies wanting to provide reimbursement for their clients on their own. this is not possible in practice without charging systems and is firmly and deeply rooted in the legal tradition of many member states, so that it should not be shaken without necessity, because this is also an essential aspect of consumer protection. this is something that should be made very clear at this point. the european court of justice has in the past dealt with these issues very carefully in its case law. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is very important to us that this crucial issue, which is of great importance for the functioning of the legal professions in many member states, should not be dealt with by the commission in the manner that has been suggested by the commission's documents. the commission cannot treat the professions as it treats supermarkets. they have a very special meaning and role. we now have member states in the european union which have abolished fee systems. the interesting thing is that the prices for lawyers and for the ordinary consumer have increased and are sometimes considerably higher on average than in the member states which still have such a system, although this system has ensured that legal protection has remained affordable and accessible to the consumer, especially in terms of price developments. we would now be pleased if commissioner kroes, who has already had the opportunity to speak to us in committee on this matter, would answer our oral question on behalf of the commission. we will then have the opportunity to react to this in the
