vice-president of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. i would like to begin by congratulating the european parliament and, of course, the rapporteur, david hammerstein mintz and michael cashman, on two very important reports. if i may begin by commenting on the openness of the council, the commission fully supports open council meetings. we already said in plan d in october that the council should be open when it legislates and we support the initiatives taken by the council. i am convinced that opening up the council meetings would increase the credibility of the eu and the interest of its citizens. i know that there is a consensus of principle between our institutions on this issue and it is now up to the member states to act and deliver. i also think that it would be an effective way of ending what we call the blame game, so this is an important issue. transparency also applies to public access to documents and regulation 1049/2001. formally, this legislation only applies to parliament, the council and the commission, but it has nevertheless come to cover many more. the various eu offices and agencies and most bodies have voluntarily adopted corresponding rules on access to documents. in this way, and thanks in large part to the european parliament, the eu institutions have, in a remarkably short time, as the rapporteur, mr michael cashman, said, reached a level of transparency that is very good compared to many member states. that's not to say it can't get better. it can, and it will. in 2003, the commission carried out a study on the way the implementation of the regulation has worked in the first years. in 2004, we published our evaluation report. at that time, the regulation had only been in force for two years but had worked well, and there was no immediate need to revise it, nor any legal obligation to do so. that is why the commission felt it was better to wait for the ratification of the constitutional treaty before we did anything further. the constitution requires new legislation in this area. but we all know the state of the constitutional treaty. in the meantime, the court of justice has also made several proposals to introduce the rules on access to documents. the commission has therefore considered that now is the right time to start a review of the regulation, and the decision to do so is part of the wider 'european transparency initiative' that we decided in the commission in november last year. the report by mr cashman is therefore very timely, at best, when we are looking at how we can improve the rules on public access to documents. the commission and i personally, i can promise you this will look very closely at the recommendations in the report. one of the conclusions drawn by the commission in its evaluation report in january 2004 was that the regulation has been used primarily by eu professionals, lobbyists, consultants and law firms rather than by the general public. that is something we want to change, and we need to do much more to reach the citizens. the first thing we are talking about is public access to documents, the right of the public to be informed, and this is another reason why we want to have a public consultation before we change the legislation. the commission intends to hold such a consultation from july to october this year, and after that we will present a concrete proposal at the end of this year or the beginning of next year. without going into detail on the various recommendations in the report, i can only make a few clarifications. recommendation no 2 calls for greater transparency in the legislative process and a clearer distinction between legislative and administrative documents. this is a very interesting proposal which we will look at carefully. the same recommendation also applies to the official journal and to electronic publication. here, our institutions decided jointly to look at the issue as early as 2004, and the publications office has already published a report on the future of the official journal. recommendation 3 deals with classified documents. here we must be careful not to confuse different things. confidentiality is not in itself a general exception to the right of access to documents. a refusal to disclose a classified document must be justified in the same way as any other document. the procedure is the same and the institution's obligations are the same. the same recommendation also addresses the issue of access to classified information by the european parliament. here, too, we risk mixing things up. parliament's rights in this area are not regulated by the regulation but by annex 1 to the framework agreement between our institutions. the framework agreement is working well, is our experience. in recommendation no 5 i have found several very interesting and useful suggestions for more user-friendly registers and databases. those proposals do not need legislation, because they are about practical details and measures, and the interinstitutional committee set up by this regulation met last november and decided to set up a working group to look at those issues, so a solution may be closer than we think. finally, the commission is very much involved in the issue of public access to documents. we have started a review of the regulation and have started to look at many of the issues raised in the report. we hope for continued support from the european parliament and we expect a lot from the general consultation we will be conducting between july and october. public access to documents is about transparency, about credibility and, basically, about democracy. it is therefore important that we continue to work well together and listen to the public. also want to make it clear that the pieces here, as in many other cases, are of course in the details and that you have to be careful not to spill the child with the bath. i would like to give an example: if i read in the commission document, for example, that it is intended to simplify all commercial and company law, then i know, as one of the permanent rapporteurs on this subject in the legal affairs committee, that many of the directives and regulations we have found there have been the result of highly complex compromise negotiations and that a simplification proposal always involves the risk of opening pandora's box and, in the end, of calling into question compromises reached after much effort. in this context, the instrument of simplification must be used with great care. i therefore believe that it is quite sensible to consider whether, as in the case of codification, an interinstitutional agreement between the three institutions, which would clearly define the procedure for simplification legislation, should not also be adopted for simplification. the second point i would ask the commission to consider is the question of the priority given to simplification proposals. directives are usually not addressed to citizens but to national legislators, and practitioners end up dealing with laws that are enacted at national level. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information it receives. the commission should give priority to regulations because regulations are directly applicable law and reach the law-seeking public directly. the second theme is impact assessment. i would like to emphasise once again that, from the point of view of the parliamentary majority, an independent element in the impact assessment of legislation is absolutely necessary. in a report in december, parliament called for an independent agency on the american model. i want to make it clear that this is not a conditio sine qua non for me. you can talk about that. however, it is essential for me that there is an independent external factor that must be involved in the impact assessment. it cannot be that the officials who make the proposals are also solely responsible for the evaluation of the legal effects, because the consequence is that this evaluation of the legal effects is nothing but part of the reasoning. that's not what we want. i think it is therefore necessary to reach a reasonable conclusion with the commission on this matter. we have had an interinstitutional agreement since december 2003. this agreement establishes that the commission is in principle responsible for the impact assessment. but this also means that it is essentially sharing responsibility with the legislator, that is to say, with parliament and the council, and that is why we believe that we as parliament also have and should have a say in how the impact assessment is carried out. this is also why we have suspended the decision on the follow-up administrative arrangements within the conference of presidents for the time being, because of course this will have to be renegotiated, also in the light of the decisions we will take on these four reports in may this year. let me refer to a very topical point. since 16 march, advocate general sharpston has delivered a lecture in spain v council, in which she explicitly refers to the impact assessment in her opinion. she said that if there was no adequate impact assessment, it would be an indication that the act was arbitrary. this is a proof that the court of justice is also increasingly concerned with this issue. i think it is crucial - as mr doorn has already pointed out - that comitology decisions also require an impact assessment of the law. there are a number of examples where the real bureaucratic madness was in the comitology decisions and not in the legislation. so here too, we need a reasonable legal impact check. let me come to one very last point. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the commission has relied heavily on the european umbrella organisations in its previous approach to legislative preparation. i am not against the european lobbying associations. but the decision-making processes in these umbrella bodies are sometimes more member of the commission. mr president, the commission's duty is to enforce the treaties and i take it for granted that on previous occasions, when the euro area was created, or when the twelfth member of the euro area was admitted, the commission and the council of that time, with the opinion of the european parliament, took account of the obligation to enforce the treaties. i am sure that i, as commissioner, and the commission, which is chaired by mr barroso, will not abdicate our obligation to apply the treaties and enforce them. the economic criteria, including inflation, are defined in a protocol annexed to the treaty, with an equivalent legal value, identical to that of the treaty provisions or articles. therefore, we cannot ignore it or transform it. it is true that there is academic discussion about the more or less accurate definition of the criteria, but the convening of an intergovernmental conference and a ratification process will be the procedure for changing the treaties when it is deemed appropriate and when there is a sufficient majority to do so. the commission is not the one to change the treaties and has an obligation to apply them. it is true that there is an asymmetry, because you are required to meet the criteria to enter the euro area and then, once inside, you can break the criteria; once you are a member of the euro area, you can have more inflation, or more debt, or more deficit. in the case of deficit and debt, there are the rules of budgetary discipline (article 104 of the treaty) and the stability and growth pact, and in the case of inflation, there are no such rules, but there are rules which are probably tougher than the legal rules implementing the treaty: the market rules. today, countries in the euro area are suffering considerably from their inability to moderate the evolution of inflation and unit labour costs. i think we also have to take into account the harsh reality of how markets judge those who do not comply with certain rules, apart from the commission's obligation to enforce the rules of the treaty.
member of the commission. mr crowley, the revised stability and growth pact was agreed by the ecofin council almost a year ago, in june 2005, following political agreement at the european council in march last year. the first experiences with the revised pact are positive and encouraging and point to renewed membership or renewed ownership of the framework by the member states. in all the recent cases we have dealt with, when the commission and the council have applied the rules of the excessive deficit procedure, in accordance with the spirit and the letter of the revised pact, there has been full consensus and there have been no difficulties or political disagreements, as on the previous occasion. on the preventive side of the pact, our review of the 2005 stability and convergence programmes in the first months of 2006 showed that the member states had set their medium-term budgetary objective in accordance with the agreed principles. some countries have decided to set even more ambitious targets, reflecting a national strategy to ensure better sustainability of their public finances. and as regards the adjustment path towards the medium-term objective, member states which are not yet in a balanced situation in the medium term generally meet the requirement of a budgetary effort equivalent to at least 0.5% of their gross domestic product in structural terms. to cite a few examples, i would remind you that since last year, when the new pact was adopted, the excessive deficit procedure has been applied to italy, portugal, hungary, the united kingdom and germany, with unanimity in the council and without the political appropriation problems that existed in the previous phase. in answer to your question, therefore, the commission is satisfied with the way the new pact is working.

member of the commission. mr president, the european capital of culture action is probably one of the most popular european initiatives. it has been appreciated by member states and the general public alike since its birth 20 years ago in 1985, thanks to melina mercouri. the main idea is still to highlight the richness and diversity of european cultures and the features they share, as well as to promote greater mutual acquaintance between european citizens. this is also a topic very close to the previous one. however, our experience has shown that some aspects of the current programme of cooperation need improvement, mainly in four areas: competition between cities, the role of the selection panel, the european dimension of the action, and the monitoring process. that is why last year the commission adopted the proposal that is intended to replace the decision of 1999. that was a parliamentary request voiced by mrs prets and i promised at that time personally to introduce a new proposal. the new system should encourage member states to organise competition at national level between interested cities. a mixed selection panel should evaluate the applications as part of the national competition. that mixed panel will be made up of seven experts appointed by the institutions, together with six experts to be nominated by the member state concerned. the member state will then propose one city to the european institutions. as in the past, the council will make the final decision concerning the designation of the city. in addition, the proposal lays down streamlined and clearer criteria compared to those in the current decision. following the designation of the european capitals, a monitoring process will be put in place to provide cities with support and advice in finalising the preparation of the programme and in particular with a view to ensuring that european added value is effectively reflected. a prize will be awarded to the european capitals of culture that meet the criteria and objectives of that initiative. at the same time, i will propose a substantial increase in the community contribution to such cities participating in the programme via the culture 2007 programme. i am very pleased that parliament, the council and commission have worked in close cooperation in order to find compromise amendments suitable for all. this report is in line dutch programme, which reduces administrative work by 25%. we want to make it easier for young entrepreneurs to start a business. the aim is to have a new plant in place within a week, and a single you know, raising awareness of this issue in all european countries is a particular concern of the austrian presidency, in order to lay another essential foundation for a common european road safety culture. the presidency therefore held the informal meeting in bregenz, austria, on 2 and 3 march, to focus on road safety at european level for two days. in the course of this meeting and in the context of numerous bilateral talks, we also succeeded in living up to the austrian presidency motto 'crossing borders in road safety - creating a trans-european road safety culture'. i am therefore very grateful to the commission for presenting the mid-term review of this european road safety action programme, which was discussed at the informal meeting of transport ministers in bregenz on 2 and 3 march, and most recently at the council of transport ministers in brussels on 27 march. i should like to mention at this point that the austrian presidency of the council also intends to adopt conclusions on road safety at the formal council of ministers meeting in luxembourg on 8 and 9 june 2006. the 2003 european road safety action programme halving the number of road deaths in the european union by 2010 sets eu-wide road safety targets for the period 2003 to 2010. it contains 60 measures to be implemented at eu level, most of them of a non-legislative nature. this was a consistent continuation of the priority given to road safety in the 2001 white paper on transport. the long-term goal behind all efforts in the field of road safety is to ensure that no eu citizen is killed or seriously injured in road accidents in the future. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the next meeting of the european council. the mid-term review of the eu road safety action programme, also presented by vice-president barrot at the above-mentioned meetings, clearly shows that europe is on the right track, but is still moving too slowly. i can only mention two or three striking figures. mr president, i would like to thank the commissioner for his report. the aim is to have a number of road deaths of around 25 000 in 2010. we could do that if we were better off. if we were to continue with the current result, we would come to 32,500. this means that we must intensify all our efforts to get as close as possible to this ambitious goal. the three essential pillars of a successful transport policy are people, vehicles and infrastructure. the commission has also been able to discuss all three pillars in detail at the meetings mentioned. the worrying thing - and i must emphasize this - is the development of the killed motorcyclists and mopeds. it is the only group of road users in which the number of road deaths is not decreasing but increasing. if this trend is not stopped, in 2010 there will be only half as many road deaths in europe, but one in three of those killed will be a motorcyclist, compared to one in six today. on the infrastructure front, europe must be aware of its responsibility to provide infrastructure operators with the appropriate tools. this is the only way to minimise the risk to road users on our european road networks. in the context of the vehicle, it should be stressed that modern e-safety technology can make a significant contribution to improving road safety. the e-safety technology is intended to provide an intelligent link between man and machine and to enable the driver to abandon routine activities. a major focus of the informal council in bregenz, austria, was on the issue of awareness-raising. in bregenz we had the opportunity to study and compare the awareness-raising activities of our european colleagues in a very compact and concentrated way. as the evaluation of individual campaign activities has shown, targeted awareness-raising can actually do a lot. we in austria have also done a great deal in this respect in recent years: to shake up, to think or to encourage thinking and finally, and this is the most important thing, to bring about a change in behaviour towards greater road safety, fewer road deaths, fewer injured and seriously injured people in road accidents. we also agreed on synergies and increased efficiency that could be achieved by a thematically joint european awareness-raising campaign. we have identified, after a survey, that the topics 'alcohol at the wheel' and 'fatigue at the wheel' should be addressed as a matter of urgency. the commission has gratefully promised to provide support, in particular in organisational terms, in accordance with the rules in force, and has indicated that the high level group on road safety will be asked to develop a proposal in this respect. the commission's intention to establish a 'european day of road safety' is also in the interests of our common objectives in the field of road safety. such an initiative will certainly also help to raise awareness throughout europe. i would like to thank mr barrot in particular for his special commitment. since 2001, significant efforts have been made to make europe's roads safer. a number of legislative measures have been adopted in the technical and regulatory fields, such as provisions on seat belts, digital tachograph, driving and rest periods, driving licences and provisions for professional drivers. the commission has also launched a number of initiatives, such as the cars 21 initiative and the european road safety charter, which are raising awareness among european municipalities, countries, companies, associations, european level. in conclusion, if in some member states with a high volume of transit traffic the problem is even greater than in the average european country, then we should start where the sink also appeared necessary to avoid any distortion of internal and external competition. finally, the three institutions took note of the commission's intention to commission a study on the distribution of security funding between public authorities and operators. the commission undertook to submit to the european parliament and the council the results of this study and the proposals which would result from it. a similar position was adopted in 2004 with the adoption of the regulation on the improvement of the safety of ships and port facilities. it was recognised that the effective and uniform application of security measures raised important issues, always related to funding. in this connection, the commission was also to undertake a study with a view to providing information to the european parliament and to consider possible proposals to be made. the commission has since 2004 put in place an inspection system which has contributed significantly to the enhancement of aviation safety. to date, the commission has carried out 69 inspections in all member states. in the light of these inspections, the commission proposed at the end of 2005 the revision of regulation 2320/2002, which is currently being examined by the committee on transport and tourism, for which you, mr president costa, are the rapporteur. with this proposal for revision, the commission presented the first annual report on the implementation of the regulation currently in force, together with the main results of the inspections. i would also point out that the regulatory committee set up by importance of the question of financing. as regards aviation, the study was completed in 2004. the results were published on the commission's website. the study on the financing of maritime security will be completed shortly. as soon as the results are available, they will be submitted to you. the study shows that civil aviation safety expenditure in the then 15 member states of the union was between eur 2.5 and 3.6 billion in 2002. this amount can be considered a significant figure, but it should be noted that for intra-community transport the combined airport and security charges and fees represented 1% to 2% of the average air ticket prices. the study also highlighted a certain diversity of funding methods. there are great differences in the role of the state. it also pointed out a certain lack of transparency as regards taxes and security charges. i should like to inform parliament that i have decided to hold a meeting of all air traffic operators tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. the main subject of this consultation will be airport charges, but it will certainly include these safety problems and their cost. as regards maritime security, the preliminary results of the study also confirm that the costs are significant, even if the expenditure in the maritime field is rather limited in relation to the total costs. the european union has more than 1200 seaports and some 3700 port facilities, for which the average investment in security is over 400 000 euro, according to this study, with running costs of over 200 000 euro per year. as far as ship safety is the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, with regard to these questions, and in particular to the question put by mr evans, the council can confirm that it has taken note of the judgment of the court of justice of the european communities of 10 january 2006 in the case of international air transport association, european low fares airline association v department for transport. the council welcomes the court's conclusion that the examination of the questions referred by the national court for a preliminary ruling has not revealed anything that would preclude the validity of articles 5, 6 and 7 of regulation (ec) no 261/2004 of the european parliament and of the council establishing a common system of compensation and assistance to passengers in the event of denied boarding and of cancellation or long delay of flights, in order to repeal the regulation. it should also be recalled that regulation (ec) no 261/2004 of the european parliament and of the council confers certain rights on passengers in the event of denied boarding and in the event of cancellation or delay of flights. article 16 'infringements' of the regulation provides that each member state is to designate a body responsible for the enforcement of this regulation on its territory. where appropriate, that body shall take the necessary measures to ensure that the rights of passengers are respected. there is also provision for passengers to lodge a complaint with a designated body concerning an alleged infringement of this regulation and, finally, article 16 (3) requires that the penalties to be imposed by the member states for infringements of the regulation must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. it is therefore primarily for the member states and the national enforcement bodies to ensure that air passengers actually enjoy the rights conferred on them by the regulation, also on the basis of complaints lodged by them. (the president cut the speaker off) article 211 of the ec treaty also requires the commission to ensure that the provisions of the regulation are effectively applied. the council will monitor the application of the regulation closely. in particular, it will carefully examine the report on the application and results of this regulation, which the commission is required to submit by 1 january 2007 pursuant to article 17 of the regulation. in particular, in connection with mr ryan's question, the council recalls that in 2004, in the context of the codecision procedure, it adopted, together with the european parliament, the above-mentioned regulation on assistance to passengers in the event of denied boarding. i would also like to mention that the council will shortly adopt, also under the codecision procedure, together with parliament, a regulation on the rights of disabled and reduced mobility air passengers. finally, it should be noted that the european commission has the right of initiative for proposing legislative acts on the strengthening of air passengers' rights and that no new proposals have been submitted. accordingly, the council does not intend to adopt any further legislative acts in this area in the near future.

member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by paying tribute to the lives lost and the communities hurt in the chernobyl devastation. we know from the latvian press that many people are still suffering the consequences, even now. latvia was not directly affected, but we have 6000 liquidators. today half of them are invalids and 500 are dead. my personal contact with chernobyl was very close. on the day of the accident i was kayaking in ukraine and i heard about it only two days later when one of the locals asked me whether i had heard about the accident at the nuclear power station nearby. my second contact with it was through my brother-in-law, an ordinary man who was called to liquidate the consequences of the chernobyl disaster. on the 20th anniversary of the chernobyl accident, the european commission joins the european parliament in a thorough reflection on the consequences of the accident and, in particular, on the lessons learned. firstly, since 1991, the european union has provided important financial assistance to improve nuclear safety in russia, ukraine, armenia and kazakhstan, including the consequences at the chernobyl site itself. to ukraine alone, the community has provided more than half a billion euros in assistance to projects relating to nuclear safety, including assistance to the chernobyl shelter fund. as a measure of continued eu commitment, the commission has also proposed an instrument for nuclear safety to reinforce it outside the european union borders for the period 2007-2013, with a proposed budget of eur 500 million. for the international community, the chernobyl accident represented a turning point, raising awareness of the need for rules and common standards to reduce the risk of an accident to a minimum, as well as preparation for immediate reaction in case of a radiological emergency. a number of international conventions signed under the auspices of the international atomic energy agency reflect the response of the international community in the wake of the accident: the convention on early notification of a nuclear accident; the convention on assistance in the case of a nuclear accident or radiological emergency; the convention on nuclear safety; the convention on the physical protection of nuclear material; and the joint convention on the safety of spent fuel management and on the safety of radioactive waste management. the european atomic energy community and the member states are contracting parties to all these conventions. at european level, i would recall that the chapter in the euratom treaty on health and safety provides both for the protection of the health of workers and of the general public against the dangers arising from radiation. the treaty also obliges member states and operators to supply the commission with regular information on installations and nuclear material in their possession. in addition, secondary legislation reflects the lessons learnt from the chernobyl tragedy. this includes foodstuffs legislation: soon after the accident, restrictions on certain agricultural imports were adopted and some border controls still apply today. if ever needed, a community mechanism will allow prompt fixing of the maximum permitted levels of contamination of foodstuffs and feedingstuffs. secondly, there is secondary legislation on emergency planning: there is an obligation that the necessary emergency plans must be drawn up at a national and local level, including inside the facilities, and emergency teams must be in place. member states must cooperate in emergency planning and in responding to an emergency. thirdly, there is secondary legislation on information in cases of radiological emergency: a community system is in place for the early exchange of information in the event of a radiological emergency. all member states, switzerland, bulgaria, romania and turkey participate in that mechanism. furthermore, all member states have established on their territory a network of facilities for monitoring the levels of radioactivity in the environment. it was such equipment in the nordic countries that detected the chernobyl accident well before it was revealed by the authorities of the soviet union. informing the population covers advance information to people living close to nuclear installations, as well as protection mechanisms to be provided to the population actually affected by such an emergency. the european union has provided financial support for the upgrading of the operating conditions of a number of nuclear installations within the european union. the reactors where sufficient upgrading could not be carried out will be or have been closed down. the staged closure of the remaining reactors in ignalina, bohunice and kozloduy was agreed in the negotiations for accession to the european union. they will be closed and we will provide financial support for the countries concerned. since 1986, the european union has made significant progress particularly in the fields of safety, radiation protection and emergency preparedness. the commission would like to thank parliament yet again for its support of the eu role in nuclear safeguards, as expressed in the resolution of 15 march 2006 on the lisbon strategy. this resolution recalls that the eu possesses globally acknowledged expertise in the area of nuclear energy and notes that this expertise relates, inter alia, to the efficiency and quality of production installations and to decommissioning processes. it is also worth recalling that the council in june 2004 set up a working party on nuclear safety, which is due to produce a final report at the end of this year. parliament is also aware that the commission has made specific legislative proposals intended to provide the union with common rules on nuclear safety, safe management of spent fuel and radioactive waste, and decommissioning funds. furthermore, the commission will make every effort in the area of research and development to help to find a sustainable solution to the issue of the radioactive waste. once again, i wish to thank parliament for its support and i thank you very much for your attention.

increasing global competition. the single market exists today, but it is not yet fully operational. this means that consumers do not have optimal access to comparable products and that industry cannot benefit from economies of scale in a large, single market. five areas need to be revised. first, the area of eligible assets. the eligibility criteria are interpreted differently by the national different scale and do not communicate sufficiently with each other. the result is uncertainty, loss of time and unnecessary additional costs for industry. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. thirdly, the area of simplified prospectuses. the commission's recommendation on this subject has been implemented in different ways by the member states. simplified prospectus of two to three pages must be developed as quickly as possible and introduced uniformly and compulsorily throughout europe. industry will also benefit from having to provide the same information in each country, always in the national language. fourthly, the issue of crossborder mergers and pooling. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the fifth point is the processing of funds. here the efforts of industry are promising. we should therefore trust industry to solve the problems on its own initiative. in-vehicle systems, which require reliability, robustness and functionality. i welcome parliament’s call to the stakeholders to look into the use of incentives. consumer studies indicate that, although they value safety very highly, consumers may not be willing to pay extra for safety features in cars. with the support of parliament we will continue to pursue two lines of discussion on the issue of incentives, namely the financial incentives with the member states and the possible reduction of insurance premiums with the insurance industry. regarding the issue of getting ecall to users in rural and isolated areas, i would like to point out that ecall is for all, including the more affordable car models. it is not a luxury car item but for all citizens and for all cars. how quickly its use will spread will of course depend on many things, for example, whether or not we manage to implement the incentive schemes. i believe that here there will be an after-market solution which will speed up the take-up of ecall. i can assure you that ecall is very high on the commission’s priority list and i am pleased that parliament has helped us by making it one of its priorities. we the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i thank the commission for its initiative and the rapporteur for his report. it is a welcome contribution to making our roads safer. the everyday madness: road accidents. even the most advanced technology cannot completely avoid it. we are still seeing more than 41 000 people die on our roads every year, and more than 1.6 million are seriously injured. in the future, vehicles will become lifesavers when equipped with ecall, the electronic emergency call system, to call for assistance autonomously in the event of a major accident. of course, the call for help will also be triggered manually, for example, if you witness an accident or find yourself in a life-threatening situation. this makes it much easier for emergency services to reach the scene of an accident, especially if it is in a remote, hard-to-reach area. this will save up to eur 26 billion in accident costs each year. the 4.5 billion investment costs are probably well spent money. up to 7 000 lives can be saved by ecall each year, and approximately 45 000 people can reduce the severity of their injuries. if this isn't worth fighting for, what are we fighting for? more than one third of all accidents involving personal injury occur at night. more than half of these are single accidents. it is still a coincidence today when the victim of such an accident is discovered in time. especially in winter, it is a regular occurrence that motorists succumb to their injuries after accidents on lonely roads. they die of hypothermia, not from the immediate consequences of their accident. after all, the decision about life or death after an accident often falls in what medical doctors call the first "golden hour". in order to ensure that the ecall electronic emergency call system is operational as soon as possible, the european union should make clear to the member states the importance of rapidly establishing a satellite-based system of emergency call points and infrastructures. such a system should be operational by the end of 2009. in addition to the implementation of these infrastructures, industry should be obliged to offer all new vehicles equipped with ecall technology from a certain date. as buyers of lower-priced vehicles in particular are reluctant to invest extra money in safety equipment, i would like the system to be introduced in series production by the automotive industry in order to reduce costs to a minimum as soon as possible. ecall is also vital, especially for motorcyclists who often cannot make their own emergency calls. the same applies to trucks and buses. it is taken for granted that ships and aircraft have long been equipped with a comparable system. emergency services, police and motoring associations, regional politicians, media representatives and even senior citizens' associations in my constituency are hoping for a mandatory introduction of ecall. we're not there yet. i ask you to approve the report.

member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by thanking both rapporteurs, mrs poli bortone and mrs scheele, for their excellent work and cooperation with my services in working out this compromise. i also wish to thank the shadow rapporteurs for their contribution. it is true that it was not an easy task. you will remember the great differences that separated the views of the three institutions on this issue. however, i believe – and the rapporteurs have rightly said – that we have managed to reach a good compromise. that is a fact. however, as with any compromise, it leaves a little to be desired by all sides, so each side would have preferred to go a bit further in one direction or another. nevertheless, these compromises on both documents have managed to balance the interests of all involved: consumers, industry and economic operators. but this is a delicate and sensitive balance and i believe that the two documents should be adopted as agreed in the compromise, because anything else would upset this balance and would definitely upset the compromise. these two regulations state that, if economic operators voluntarily use claims or other marketing tools to sell their products, they have to be truthful and accurate and the claims must be scientifically based. this means that it is the consumer’s choice – it is ultimately for the consumer to decide – but the consumer has to be presented with correct, accurate and scientifically-based information in order to make this informed choice. i agree with the rapporteur that this is a very important step in the long-term struggle that has just begun for the health and nutrition of european citizens. the health claims regulation will prevent consumers from being misled by unsubstantiated or misleading claims. at the same time, it will provide harmonised rules allowing products to circulate freely in the internal market. it will also create a clear legal environment, a level playing field for economic operators to ensure fair competition, and it will encourage investment in innovative food practices. for example, in addition to the list of permitted nutritional claims or the list of physiological function claims, it will now allow, through an authorisation procedure, claims related to the reduction of a disease risk, something that until now has been prohibited. so, these harmonised rules will be of great interest to the european food industry but, through the process we have adopted in the legislation, we also guarantee consumer protection. also, for health claims based on newly developed data, the compromise now provides for a simpler and faster procedure in order to boost innovation in the area of food. i am sure parliament recognises the effort that both the commission and the council have made on that point. on the nutrient profiles, which have already been described, these are products that, on the basis of the claims, are made to appear better to consumers, encouraging more consumption. we therefore need proper criteria in this respect. the nutrient profile is one good criterion that could be used and the proposed compromise introduces flexibility in order to facilitate the application and use of these claims. in the context of this compromise, i should like to make the following statement:‘in establishing the nutrient profiles referred to in article 4(1) through the regulatory committee procedure, the commission undertakes to accompany the proposed commission measures, submitted to the standing committee on the food chain and animal health, with an explanatory note outlining the criteria that will be taken into account for the establishment of the nutrient profiles.’ as i have said, i believe that this is a good compromise which covers the interests of all the key stakeholders. on the regulation concerning the addition of vitamins and minerals, again we have reached a good compromise. on the basis of this compromise, i should like to make the following statement: ‘further to its statement accompanying the adoption of the common position, the commission has the intention to present, as soon as possible and in any case within two years of the adoption of the regulation, a proposal for the revision of directive 90/496/eec on nutrition labelling for foodstuffs. in that context, the commission has the intention to consider the review of the rule concerning the meaning of ‘significant amount’ as mentioned in the annex to that directive.’ i very much hope that parliament will support this compromise package, which regulates the composition aspects of foods and ensures the safety of the product. it also introduces appropriate specific rules on labelling, presentation and advertising, and at the same time provides the basis for scrutinising and if necessary regulating the addition of certain other substances, as already mentioned by the rapporteur. that will ensure a very high level of protection for public health and consumer protection and at the same time allow the industry to have a stable, concise, clear regulatory environment that will allow for innovation and the need to remain competitive at community and international level. in conclusion, may i again thank the two rapporteurs and everyone else who has cooperated in achieving this compromise. i am looking forward to an interesting debate.

in writing. after long discussions and much persuasion, we have not been able to find reality again. the composition of a particular food is not the decisive factor, but the overall picture in the interaction between a healthy, balanced diet adapted to the person in his particular situation (activity, age, sex). all of this should go into a profile. but because these factors are constantly changing, we have to recognize that there are no nutritional profiles, only the path of education and upbringing. the rural women in germany call this "learning everyday skills". this is best communicated in the family and through school and general education. i also hope that the further consideration of a "lighthouse designation" is just a silly joke. but who knows what "so clever a man" might come up with? an example of the unrealistic approach is that beverages with an alcohol content of more than 1.2% by volume (wine) may not be labelled. on the one hand, scientific profiles are required, on the other hand, the dissemination of scientific findings is prohibited. moreover, wine is already regulated in eu regulations, which must also apply here. we have discussed a great deal, but as the compromise shows, not enough. i supported the amendments in the hope that this would make the lazy compromise tolerable.
in writing. i reject the regulation on nutrition and health claims as adopted by the member states. the regulation provides for the compulsory establishment of nutrition profiles for all foodstuffs. furthermore, food may only be advertised with health and nutrition claims if these claims have been recognised in advance in a uniform european procedure. these regulations, which are supposed to combat poor dietary habits, create a high technical and bureaucratic burden for food manufacturers without addressing the root of the problem: obesity cannot be effectively combated by regulatory interventions, but only by changing eating and living habits. less time in front of the tv or computer and more exercise would be needed. the whole regulation also deprives the consumer of his rights and ultimately of his right to exercise his own judgement. the single authorisation procedure for health claims at the european food authority is a matter of concern. this is an unnecessary bureaucratic monster, which is particularly burdensome for our mediumsized enterprises. large companies can more easily afford this additional effort for an application. the additional costs for smes, on the other hand, are of an existential nature. this law is a counter to all efforts to cut red tape and to the proposals for 'better regulation'.
president of the commission. mr president, i am delighted to have the opportunity to present to you today the results of our assessment of bulgaria’s and romania’s preparations for accession and i the result of an extensive process of review and dialogue with all the major stakeholders. the starting point of our approach is that the european union must honour existing commitments. at the same time, we need to be rigorous as regards the criteria to be met by acceding countries. i should like to make a few brief remarks before, with your permission, giving the floor to mr rehn, who will comment in more detail on the commission’s findings in the monitoring report. since october, the governments of bulgaria and romania have worked extremely hard to deliver on their outstanding commitments. they have continued to make progress in their preparation for membership. let us give credit where it is due. however, there are still some important issues which need to be addressed. i would highlight, in particular, the need for further progress in the area of justice and home affairs. the commission considers that romania and bulgaria should be ready for membership by 1 january 2007, provided that they address a number of outstanding issues in the course of the next month. let me first turn to the situation in judicial reforms and the fight against corruption. we expect any acceding country to have in place a fully functioning judicial system equipped to fight corruption and organised crime. this is of paramount importance, since it underpins the functioning of the whole society and the economy. both countries have shown determination to undertake the necessary remaining reforms and our reports give them full credit for the results already achieved. bulgaria still needs to demonstrate clear evidence of results in the fight against corruption, in particular high-level corruption, notably in terms of investigations and subsequent judicial proceedings. it also needs to further reform the judiciary and remove any ambiguity regarding its independence. we also expect bulgaria to step up efforts on the investigation of organised crime networks. romania needs to continue its efforts and demonstrate further results in the fight against corruption, notably in terms of further investigations and subsequent judicial proceedings. it needs to consolidate the implementation of the ongoing judicial reforms. turning to the level of alignment of bulgaria and romania with the acquis communautaire, we have registered further progress. however, we still have serious concerns about a few sectors: agriculture and food safety, justice and home affairs and public finance. any acceding country needs to be in a position to implement the european union policies properly upon accession. the rules of the club must be respected. we expect bulgaria and romania to take immediate corrective action in those problematic sectors. no later than early october, we will review the situation with those outstanding issues. on that basis, the commission will consider whether it is still possible to adhere to the accession date of 1 january 2007. it is practicable for the two countries to be ready in 2007, but they must take decisive action. at the same time, the european union needs to give a clear signal that it stands ready to honour its commitments. that is crucial, in order to keep up the momentum. practical preparations for accession need to continue. i count on the support of all governments and parliaments that still need to complete their procedures to ratify the accession treaty. our approach is based on strict conditionality and adherence to undertakings. that approach has allowed us to gain strength and confidence from each enlargement. like the previous enlargements, especially that in 2004, the forthcoming enlargement will be a success. enlargement has always been europe’s response to strategic challenges and history has shown that this response has been the proper one. time and again, it has been accompanied by a dynamism that has given the enlarged europe a greater capacity to make its mark in the world. in the situation in which we find ourselves today, it is more important than ever to preserve the spirit of openness and ambition that has always inspired us to press ahead with the construction of europe. that is precisely why commissioner rehn and i have decided to go to bucharest today and sofia tomorrow to explain these issues and give the two countries a clear message of encouragement. hydrocarbons. i would like to reiterate that in the long term there are only three countries that have a lot of natural gas resources: russia, iran and qatar. at the same time, the eu will import 70% of its energy in 2030, compared with 50% today. over time, the remaining fossil fuel resources will become more concentrated, as i said, in a rather small number of countries. as a consequence, energy interdependence is becoming a global issue, with major shared concerns, such as increased demand for limited resources in the world, the lack of investment in new production and the climate change issues. therefore, a broad range of actions at eu and member-state level are required to address these challenges. it has been highlighted in the green paper. i have just highlighted one of the actions in my answer to the honourable member’s previous question about biofuels. that is one of the actions that we indicate. the green paper emphasised opportunities, such as policies to improve first of all energy efficiency and energy savings, as well as enhancing the market penetration of renewable energy sources. it also highlighted external policy options, such as strengthening the framework for energy relations between the eu and russia in order to give more confidence to both sides, as well as policies and measures to diversification of the geographical sources and transportation routes of external energy supplies to the eu. in this context, it is important to underline that the eu is making continuous efforts to improve energy relations with other energy-producing organisations – such as opec, the gulf cooperation council, the countries of the caspian basin and north africa – as well as with the consuming regions in the framework of the international energy forum, the international energy agency, g8 and through bilateral agreements and dialogues. this policy of diversification is not directed against our current suppliers: it is a necessity dictated by the global energy security challenges and by the challenge posed by global warming and other environment-related issues. together with the austrian presidency of the european union, i recently sent a letter to the russian energy minister, mr khristenko, on the issue of energy cooperation and in particular gas interdependency. in this letter we reiterated the importance the eu attributes to deepening energy relations with russia, the eu’s most important energy supplier. furthermore, we stressed that the importance the eu attaches to diversifying sources of supply should not be interpreted as limiting deliveries of russian gas to the eu market, particularly as demand for gas in europe is forecast to rise. in this relationship with russia, the eu is promoting such principles as market reciprocity, fair transit conditions through russia and third-party access to infrastructure in russia. therefore, the short answer to the questions that have been asked is that we are looking for diversification, but it is extremely important to establish measures on the demand side, because only with demand-side measures, energy efficiency and savings can we actually establish our energy independence more strongly and, at the same time, look towards our goals of sustainability and competitiveness.

technical harmonisation, so that goods can be traded within the european union without restrictions. more than 20 directives have been adopted to follow this approach. the commission has already taken law-making. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's environmental legislation is properly implemented. in addition, standardization can also play an important role in strengthening the competitiveness of european industry. standardization allows the interoperability of different techniques. it paves the way for the introduction of new technologies and encourages innovation. at present, european standardization is financed by the commission on the basis of legislation dating back to the 1980s. in view of the development of budgetary law, it is urgent to establish a modern legal basis for the financing of standardisation. the budget for financing european standardisation must be approved annually in the budgetary procedure. the current amount is 19 million euros. beneficiaries of community funding are the european standards organisations cen, cenelec and etsi, listed in annex i to directive 98/34/ec of the european parliament and of the council on the state of public finances in economic and monetary union, enriching the much-needed debate on how to conduct economic policy and, in particular, budgetary policies, with the common objective of all of us to boost economic growth and promote job creation. i must begin my brief remarks with two comments which separate my view from the statements in mr rosati's report, probably because time has passed, and it has passed in a positive way, since since the commission's report on public finances was drawn up last year, the figures of which form the basis of mr rosati's report, until now we have received information, both on economic growth and on the situation of public budgets or deficits in the countries of the european union, which improves the picture. i would like to refer briefly to that. on 8 may i had the opportunity to present the commission's spring economic forecasts and in doing so i was able to state publicly that, in our view, based on the analysis of the commission services, growth in 2006 in the euro area and in the european union as a whole will be around our potential growth: it will exceed 2% in the euro area, in particular it will reach 2,1% compared with 1,3% in 2005, and in the european union as a whole it will be 2,3% which is also clearly above the growth recorded in 2005. we are therefore entering a phase of recovery that is much more pronounced than we could have foreseen when the commission presented the 2005 report on public finances, which is in itself a positive development, although i would be quick to say that it is not enough, because growing at the rate of our current growth potential is not enough to meet all the demands of citizens and, in the first place, to create enough jobs to achieve a sustained and clear reduction in unemployment, which is still above 8%. we must increase our growth potential - and i agree with the views expressed in mr rosati's report - we must persevere on the path set out in the review of the lisbon strategy, we must continue to implement the national reform plans within the framework of that strategy, we must continue to reform the product, service and labour markets, we must correct where budgetary imbalances persist, we must make our public finances more sustainable, of course, we must improve the quality of public spending and, in particular, we must make a greater effort in all policies aimed at the qualification of human resources, research and development, innovation and, in general, education. the second comment i wanted to make concerns the particular subject of public deficits. the report points to a worsening of the situation in 2005 and attributes this to a misapplication of the stability and growth pact. the end-of-year 2005 figures contradict this claim; the government deficit in 2005, both in the euro area and in the european union as a whole, has been much lower than we estimated a few months ago: it has been 2.3 per cent in the european union as a whole and 2.4 per cent in the euro area, thus several tenths of what we had forecast when the commission published its 2005 public finance report. our forecasts for 2006 and 2007 are that this situation will continue and, if additional measures are taken by the states, will clearly improve. i believe that we cannot speak, in my view, of a misapplication of the new stability and growth pact, but rather of the success of the implementation of the new stability and growth pact in correcting excessive deficits: there were seven countries in an excessive deficit, with an excess of 3%, at the end of 2005, compared with 12 countries in an excessive deficit under the current procedures, which will probably be withdrawn from the procedure once these improvements in government deficits are confirmed. and in the stability and convergence programmes, adopted for the first time in accordance with the guidelines and parameters of the new pact, there is a qualitatively clear improvement in the medium-term budgetary strategies of the member states, with greater attention to sustainability and greater effort to improve the quality of public finances and to link budgetary and fiscal policies with the growth strategies included in the lisbon strategy and in the national growth plans. in all other respects, apart from these two comments, there is a great deal of convergence between the proposals and statements in mr rosati's report and the commission's views and criteria. we agree on the need to avoid pro-cyclical policies, on the need to reorient public spending towards greater accumulation of physical, human and technological capital, on the need to make a greater effort to standardise budgetary procedures in the member states and in particular in the euro area; we obviously agree to put emphasis on how to meet the challenge of demographic ageing. and i believe that we have - and i agree with the report's view - a unique opportunity, now that the economic recovery is beginning, now that we have defined the lisbon strategy, now that the 25 member states have defined their priorities for structural reforms geared to growth and employment, to end an era of low growth, economic pessimism and lack of confidence among economic actors. we have a unique opportunity to use the institutions and the european dimension to serve the demands and aspirations of citizens.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission is not prepared to accept this. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr rosati, for his efforts to produce a report which is consistent with all the shadow rapporteurs and others. we have approved this concept in the economic committee by a large majority - i would say almost unanimously. the epp group has also agreed to this, of course. we will of course be critical in our assessment of the amendments tabled, and i am therefore very grateful that the commissioner has also expressed his criticism of two or three of the points contained in these amendments. sound public finances are the most important thing in the whole of the economic and monetary union and beyond. only sound public financing can help europe's economic recovery in the long term. unfortunately, this idea is not popular with all european governments. the political will to reform the public finances is often lacking. the criteria laid down in the stability and growth pact must be clearly respected. there should be no repeated attempts to circumvent or undermine these stability criteria. we called them 'stability criteria' in 1997 - and some of us did call them that - because they give stability to the financial area and the economy in europe. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the high budget deficits have a negative impact on the economic cycle. we just heard there's been some activity here. the increase in deficits is only a continuation of this spiral and must be stopped. of course we must increase our spending on the right things, on innovation and on future development. this does not change the fact that they are still expenditure which must be included in the general accounts. in this context, i welcome the independence of the european central bank - as has been made clear elsewhere today - in its interest rate policy, which must continue to pursue price stability as its primary objective. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. a long-term policy of balanced public finances is needed in the present euro area countries and as a prerequisite for all future euro area accessions. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the stability and growth pact and the monetary policy of the european central bank provide a reliable and sufficient framework which we need only to respect.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. i thank you very much for allowing me to speak again this evening. the debate is drawing to a close. the report by mr rosati on public finances in economic and monetary union is, in my view, a very important report because it rightly draws the public's attention to the fact that in the present situation the member states are responsible for the finances of the european union and also for the debt that is associated with them for future generations. the rapporteur's appeal is rightly directed to the member states. however, in my view, it goes beyond the mark in some areas. i would like to expressly endorse the rapporteur for the epp group, mr hoppenstedt. i would like to make one further point. in 2007, the german household deficit will be below 3%, thus meeting the criteria of the stability pact. commissioner almunia, you yourself have put it in the appropriate terms. the german economic development will thus give a new impetus to the whole of the european union - at least i hope so. the troubled children are known. we therefore need greater coordination of economic policies, but above all by the member states, so that individual countries cannot increase the costs of the whole economic area. i would like to refer again to the report by mr garcía-margallo y marfil, who in the last plenary session gave an account of the state of the european economy, with the european parliament's aim of developing a smart growth strategy for europe. i believe that we are not far enough along this road and that there is still a lot to be done. although the price of oil has risen, we still have a stable inflationary trend and consumption in the european union is also at a level that can be described as quite acceptable. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation in the community, and it is therefore not necessary to paint it black, but there is a need for action, particularly in terms of improving the economic climate and further integrating the internal market. i hope that mr rosati's report will also point the commission in the right direction.
member of the commission. madam president, i would like to thank all the members who have spoken in this debate, referring to initiatives or positions of the commission. i think there is a fairly broad degree of agreement and consensus on the diagnosis and on the main guidelines on what the response should be from the european institutions to ensure that public finances, good fiscal and budgetary policies, help to achieve more growth, more employment and more satisfaction of the demands of the citizens in europe. in fact, there has been a significant improvement in confidence and optimism among european economic operators and consumers in recent months. all the indicators bear witness to that. we are now in the process of trying to translate that confidence and optimism into concrete data on the evolution of the economic situation, of more consumption, more employment and more economic growth. i think that, in part, it is being achieved, which does not mean that the road is easy. there is, of course, a problem - and i agree with those who have pointed this out - of low potential growth in the european economy. the european economy, on its own, without further reforms, is not capable of growing beyond the figures we are estimating for 2006, i.e. slightly above 2%. there is evidence of extraordinarily dynamic competitors, both in other industrialized countries and in emerging countries; there is a risk - which some of the honourable members have mentioned - arising from the evolution of energy prices; there are global imbalances in other important areas of the world economy which may affect this phase of growth. and when we come to the answer to the question of what to do in this situation, we have a relatively strong degree of consensus: good fiscal and budgetary policies, which are not procyclical, which are countercyclical, which improve the quality of income and expenditure, which contribute better to growth and to the qualification of human resources; better functioning of the internal market; use of our enormous potential as a market of 450 million consumers; and - we all mentioned this - the need for better coordination. as a witness to the monthly functioning of the eurogroup and the ecofin, i cannot but agree with all the honourable members when they ask the council, and the eurogroup in particular, for more coordination, but i can also convey to them the will of the council and the eurogroup to improve that coordination and to improve the involvement of all sectors and all institutions - and of course this parliament - in the dialogue necessary for that coordination to be appropriate to the objectives and priorities and to be effective. i think we are facing a very good opportunity at that turning point, to which mr sánchez presedo referred a few minutes ago. we cannot pass up this opportunity, nor can we fail to learn from the mistakes that european economies and the euro area made in the previous period of economic recovery, by failing to use good periods of economic growth to consolidate public accounts to improve their sustainability and to use the dynamism of economies in the service of more and better jobs, which is what the citizens are asking us to do.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. after difficult negotiations, we are presenting to you today the text of an interinstitutional agreement on budgetary discipline and sound financial management. i would like to begin by thanking all those who have contributed to this outcome on behalf of parliament, in particular the negotiating team, which includes janusz lewandowski, ralf walter and jan mulder. i would like to express my gratitude to the coordinators and staff of the political groups and in particular to the staff of the secretariat, who have really done an excellent job in the past few months. this togetherness, despite all the contradictions, has been and is the strength of parliament, because we are committed to european added value and not to a one-sided debate on the net and the return of funds. the title of this agreement is also the programme. the commission, council and parliament commit themselves to the framework conditions for the annual budgetary procedure and the multiannual financial planning until 2013. they undertake to improve the current agreement and to make changes to the council decision of december 2005. this means that we now have more flexibility in budgetary procedures. we could respond better and faster to political, humanitarian and economic emergencies. we have introduced reform of budgetary law, simplification of the financial regulation, certification of eu programmes and reporting obligations by member states, more reliable financial planning and clear agreements on the creation of new agencies. the commission, council and parliament also undertake to modernise financial instruments by integrating the european investment bank's loan facilities. this is important for research, for innovation in smes and for transeuropean networks and represents a strong impetus for investment. the basis for the agreement in the council in december was also the distribution - i must say this - of special discounts and christmas presents. we have, however, in the negotiations, secured additional funding for programmes with real european added value: lifelong learning, transeuropean networks, research, social policy, innovation for smes, crossborder cooperation for natura 2000, life+, health and consumer policy, culture, youth and the media. we have also made important improvements in foreign and security policy and in neighbourhood policy. this is a small sum in comparison with the overall financial planning, but it safeguards the european added value programmes which are close to the citizens and bear our signature, because the approach of parliament, unlike that of the council, was not from the outset fixed on a mere 1% debate. the aim was to define a comprehensive negotiating position, based on an in-depth analysis of the political and economic challenges of an enlarged union, as documented in the june resolution: internal and external political priorities, modernisation of budgetary structures and improvement of the quality of budgetary management. we're not even close to being done. but we have negotiated a large package and have broken up the council's concrete structures. the implementation of reforms in particular has a high monetary value for the union, for the member states and for those who have to implement community programmes. we have been able to secure better the rights of parliament in all the instruments of foreign policy. parliament was promised an appropriate role in the forthcoming 2008/2009 revision, and the commission's statement on the evaluation of these agreements in 2009 can guarantee the newly elected parliament its powers of design. but there are still some shortcomings. the galileo satellite programme is still underfunded. the decisions on rural development and voluntary modulation in agricultural policy are more than questionable. natura 2000 has been undermined. these and other construction sites remain unfinished. but, ladies and gentlemen, the council and the commission are watching. the resolution of 8 june 2005 continues to describe for us the optimal funding and reforms to achieve the ambitious objectives of the union of citizens and states, and we will return to this again and again. we will be very careful to ensure that the substance and spirit of all agreements are strictly adhered to. i thank the austrian presidency. we had constructive and fair negotiations. the council and the permanent representatives committee have been so opposed to reform that the presidency's work has certainly not been easy. i would like to thank the commissioner for her report. after a period of weakness and a more advisory stance on the part of the commission, you have returned to positive participation and have made a substantial contribution to the final result. this gives us hope for the future! all in all, a result has been achieved which, under the prevailing conditions, involves important progress in the interests of the citizens, in terms of reforms and budgetary modernisation and in respect of the rights of parliament. for these reasons, i recommend that you accept this agreement. form of a declaration on the review of the financial framework, particularly because it takes full account of parliament's responsibilities. i would like to conclude by saying that i have always been convinced that there can be only one common solution to the important question of joint finances and the interinstitutional agreement between the three institutions. disagreement on a core issue of the president of the council. i have to say, madam president, i am pleased to be able to take part in question time again under your presidency, and i shall begin with the first question from mr bernd posselt on the progress of the accession negotiations with croatia. let me begin by explaining that the accession negotiations with croatia, like all other accession negotiations, are governed by the principle that each country is judged on its own merits. in the public interest, this principle must be emphasised again and again, and the pace of the negotiations depends solely on the candidate country's - in this case croatia's - fulfilment of the conditions for membership. the european union's capacity to receive refugees is of course also taken into account, as is stated in the relevant decisions. the council cannot and should not give a date for the conclusion of the negotiations which began on 3 october. as regards the next steps, on 20 february this year the council adopted the accession partnership for croatia, which sets out the priorities to be met on the road to accession. the commission's screening reports on the negotiating chapters science and research, education and culture, public procurement and competition are available. the council examined the screening reports on the first two chapters, science, research, education and culture, and invited croatia to present its negotiating positions. i have them now and the council will now have to define a common position. it is planned that negotiations on these chapters will begin on 13 june in the context of an accession conference at foreign minister level. i repeat that it will ultimately depend on the progress of the applicant countries themselves how far and how quickly these negotiations can be continued.
