as they concern the same subject, the following questions will be dealt with together: question no 6 by mrs batzeli (h-0314/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: further harmonization of taxation rules under current legislation, tax policy is the exclusive responsibility of the individual member states and is determined by economic and social needs or conditions at national level. there is very little community legislation on taxation. however, this fragmented tax policy in the eu often creates tax problems for companies, especially smes, as they have to bear high costs of adjustment and also face problems of double taxation when operating in more than one member state. in addition, the disparity in national tax bases leads to a certain degree of tax competition, particularly between the new and the old eu member states, which in turn leads to new inequalities in the treatment of companies and often leads to the relocation of companies to member states of the community where tax rates are lower. does the council consider that the introduction of uniform and more coherent rules in the field of tax policy would result in fairer treatment of taxpayers within the eu and could at the same time give a new impetus to the eu's competitiveness? what is the state of the negotiations on the promotion of a common consolidated corporate tax base, to which the european parliament has given its consent? question no 10 by othmar karas (h-0373/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: common cost basein the informal ecofin council, the introduction of a common cost base for business taxation was discussed. once again, it has been shown that a number of member states are opposed to this idea, or at least very sceptical. what concrete results can be expected in the foreseeable future from the austrian presidency, given the principle of unanimity on taxation? will this issue be on the agenda of the next presidencies?
the president of the council. the tax harmonization of corporate taxation is, on the one hand, about simplifying the economy, so that there is no different tax base in each country, i.e. different depreciation possibilities between country a and country b or c, but that there are always the same possibilities. because that's a big problem for a company. international companies have told us about the different regulations that have to be observed in the automotive industry alone in car production and the high administrative burden that this causes. on the other hand, it is a question of fair, transparent competition. transparent competition means that the company's profits are taxed on a uniform basis, with competition taking place at different rates. we don't want to eliminate competition. this should always be done in the spirit of the lisbon process. the second point is that we are a single market and a single market requires common rules.
the president of the council. in this connection, it should be noted that the ecofin council adopted the directive on taxation of interest-bearing income on 3 june 2003. this directive aims to ensure that cross-border interest income received by eu residents in the form of interest payments is taxed in the member state where they are resident or subject to withholding tax in the member state which is considered to be the source of the income. in order to ensure competitive neutrality vis-à-vis major financial centres outside the eu, the directive also provides for the same or equivalent measures to be applied by a number of territories and third countries, including 10 dependent and associated territories such as the isle of man and five european countries, namely andorra, liechtenstein, monaco, san marino and switzerland. the measures laid down in the directive and the agreements concluded with third countries and territories have been applied by all 40 contracting parties concerned since 1 july 2005. the territorial scope of the directive may in principle be extended to other relevant financial centres. on 1 december 1997 the council adopted a resolution on a code of conduct for business taxation, which deals with potentially harmful tax measures which significantly affect or may affect the location of economic activities in the community. 66 tax measures in the old member states and 30 in the new member states were identified as harmful by the code of conduct group and largely phased out. the code of conduct group is now focusing on its future work. a report on this is expected to be sent to the council in june.
the president of the council. i agree with the honourable member that it is of course ideal to establish tax rules in a single market covering almost all of europe. but it is also necessary that they become effective, that the same rules are applied in neighbouring countries or, if possible, beyond the continent, otherwise eu citizens will be given the opportunity to invest their money abroad, where such rules do not apply. it was therefore important - and i visited some of these countries myself during the negotiations - to overcome any resistance. in any case, liechtenstein, san marino and the countries i mentioned earlier have signed this treaty. this at least ensures that the taxation rules in these territories are uniform. it would be desirable, of course, if other countries followed suit. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
the president of the council. i shall come back to that question. one question relates to money laundering. it is of course important - and the fadf is an important institution - that uniform guidelines on money laundering are applied in all these countries of the enlarged economic area, and there are discussions on this from the commission.

council, the commission has put forward proposals to amend regulations (ec) no 1466/97 and (ec) no 1467/97, which form the legislative component of the stability and growth pact. the amending regulations in question were adopted on 27 june 2005 following a lengthy process of discussion in the course of which it had already been said that the old stability pact was dead , these regulations being adopted in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 252 of the treaty and regulation 1056/2005 after parliament's opinion. on 11 october 2005, the ecofin council also adopted a revised code of conduct on the implementation of the stability and growth pact and guidelines on the content and form of the stability and convergence programmes. all these rules are publicly available, as is information on the council's past actions under the revised stability and growth pact. the latter comprise the following acts: decisions under article 104 (6) tec on the existence of an excessive deficit in italy, portugal and the united kingdom, and recommendations on measures to correct it on the basis of article 104 (7) tec, a decision under article 104 (8) tec finding that the measures taken by hungary following the council recommendations on the correction of the excessive deficit have proved insufficient, and a council decision under article 104 (9) tec replacing germany, with a provision on the measures necessary to reduce the excessive deficit. the council also delivered opinions on the updated stability and convergence programmes of all member states, which were first drawn up in the context of the new regulatory framework of the revised economic and stability pact. in short, despite the criticism that the stability pact is practically dead, it has just been shown that the new economic and stability pact works and that it is alive. this is also reflected in the fact that deficits in 2005 were significantly lower than in 2004.

and floods, not least in the summer of 2005 the call for european solidarity is growing. the solidarity fund, set up after the devastating floods of 2002 and designed to run until 2006, is intended to give the european union greater capacity to respond to major disasters or crises. the fund is intended to make a significant contribution to the union's ability to act more effectively and more effectively in areas where citizens expect action from the european union. with the instruments in place, it has been extremely difficult, if not impossible, to respond adequately at eu level to major crises, some of which are not of natural origin. examples of this are industrial accidents such as the prestige tanker accident or the madrid bombing in march 2004. in addition, the current threshold for mobilising the solidarity fund is extremely high, so that exceptional conditions and derogations prevailed. the new regulation on the solidarity fund rightly provides for a broader scope of application, i.e. to extend the scope of major crises beyond natural disasters to industrial and technological disasters, provided that the polluter principle is not applicable and that the damage is not insurable. it also covers emergency response to public health crises and acts of terrorism, but that's the crux of the matter, with the same budget. the concept of a major disaster is also being redefined. accordingly, a disaster is considered to be a disaster which causes direct damage estimated at more than eur 1 billion or more than 0.5% of the gdp of the state concerned. this is damage in the public sector, not private or insurable damage. the threshold has so far been set at eur 3 billion, or 0.6% of gdp. these thresholds were proposed by the commission and parliament at the time but were not accepted by the council. finally, a new policy criterion is to be introduced, according to which the commission may, in exceptional and duly justified circumstances, declare a disaster situation to be a major disaster in a particular part of the territory of an eligible state, even if the quantitative criteria are not met. this is likely to be the case, above all, in the case of terrorist acts. it should be noted that the european union solidarity fund is not a preventive measure but a response to disaster situations. this excludes, for example, the use of the fund as a preventive measure for protection against pandemics or other preventive measures. the solidarity fund is not and cannot be a health-care fund. health policy remains a matter for the nation states. the only areas covered are the use of vaccines and medicines in emergency first aid, emergency medical and psychological care and measures to deal with the risk of disease, for example following floods. the financial resources of the fund are as before limited to a virtual annual budget of dm 1 000 million. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the budgetary resources available for the programme are used to finance the necessary measures. the funds are therefore non-transferable. i would like to conclude by thanking all those who have contributed to this report, the secretariat, my staff and colleagues across all political groups. i would also like to thank the commission for the good cooperation it has shown.

the next item is the recommendation for second reading by the committee on women's rights and gender equality on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of employment and occupation (recast) [15623/7/2005 - c6-0089/2006 - 2004/0084 ((cod)) ] (rapporteur: angelika niebler) (a6-0165/2006)
the rapporteur. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. we are voting today on the common position on the so-called recast directive, which the council has been negotiating with parliament for a very long time. this brings an important legislative procedure to a close. before i go into the content of the directive, i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs for their collegial and constructive cooperation. i would also like to thank the luxembourg, british and austrian presidencies for having made it possible, together with parliament, to reach a consensual solution. i also thank the commission, whose officials have always provided us with competent technical assistance. thank you very much. what is the directive about? the european regulations on equal treatment for men and women in working life are at issue. we have seven directives dealing with this subject, and there is forty years of case law on these seven directives. we have finally achieved a bit of better legislation with this recast directive, which will be voted on this afternoon, by summing up, compressing, simplifying and de-lacerating the law. this recast directive defines for the first time terms such as discrimination and harassment on grounds of sex. it will harmonise and improve legal protection for victims of discrimination in working life. the commission has also worked with the council to achieve improvements in certain areas in the field of equal opportunities. this includes cooperation with the gender institute to be set up or the continuation of awareness-raising campaigns in the member states. so much for the letter of the law, if i may put it that way. what's it like in real life? in all the euphoria about the simplification of the law and this new directive, we must not forget that in practice there are still significant shortcomings in the treatment of men and women, especially in working life. the current figures in all 25 member states show that further action is still needed in this area of equal treatment. the gender gap in the labour market has not diminished, but rather increased. for example, the wage gap: it is astonishing that after many years of case law and legislation in this area, we still have a wage gap of more than 15% in all member states, that is, women earn on average 15% less than men for the same type of work. this can't be happening. similarly, the situation with the segregation of the sexes. certain occupations, unfortunately mainly low-paid ones, are still disproportionately occupied by women, and there are still significantly more women than men working part-time. i think that is still unacceptable and we must act against it. do we need new regulations in this area? i mean, no. we have this body of law now, we have jurisdiction in this area. the important thing is not to adopt new, stricter regulations, but to put into practice effectively what we have created in terms of regulations. the revised directive can make an important contribution to this. as i said, we have brought together existing legislation and the case law of the court of justice under the umbrella of the revised directive. we have thus taken a concrete step towards greater clarity, transparency and, therefore, greater legal certainty. but we have to think of new ways. we must, for example, look more closely at the causes of the high gender segregation in the labour market and raise awareness among citizens outside the local area. the social partners are also called upon to take even more decisive action against the wage gap and against discrimination on the labour market, especially against women. it is also a general challenge in terms of social policy to ensure equal opportunities in working life, and it is not addressed to a particular group only. and this is becoming more and more important when you look at demographics, and we're getting older, thank god. we have low birth rates in all european countries and the result is that women will continue to go into the labour force even more in the coming years and decades. it is against this background that it is important that we ensure equal opportunities and conditions for women in particular. i would like to take this last minute to make a brief reference to the subject of parental leave, which has also been the subject of a very lively debate in our parliament. for systematic reasons, the provisions on parental leave are not now provided for in this recast directive, but we want this item to be at the top of the political agenda because it is crucial to the issue of reconciliation of family and work. there may be an impulse from europe to do more in terms of reconciling family and work. i am glad that the commission may be making some further comments on this today and that the european council, at its spring meeting, has also made the reconciliation of family and work a priority and adopted a european pact for gender equality. we are on the right track and we are not at the end. but if we work together to take further steps towards equal opportunities in working life, we hope to reach our goal in time.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is necessary today to recall in this house the initiatives on which the commission and i have been working over the question. i hope that in the course of 2006 a project will be drawn up to assess, as some members of the european parliament have asked me to do, the impact of the demand for prostitution on the volume of human trafficking for sexual exploitation. i am personally convinced that the more the demand from the customers increases, the more the trafficking for sexual exploitation is indirectly encouraged in some way. we do not have precise figures, but we are ready to launch a project which we will of course report to this parliament. i would like to give you some information on the list of concrete initiatives relating to the world cup in germany. firstly, together with the commission and president barroso, i have supported all the information campaigns aimed at raising awareness of the serious danger of an increase in trafficking for sexual exploitation linked to the world cup. in this connection, i had the pleasure of meeting a delegation led by mr gurmai in brussels a few days had requested a few days ago. the report, published on 2 june, analyses the risk of increased trafficking for sexual exploitation in relation to the world cup. this report is of course available to parliament. as you know, we also asked europol to draw up a report on this matter. europol has produced an analysis document, intended for police and investigative authorities, to strengthen concrete measures of coordination between police authorities. i can tell you - without going into detail for time reasons - that this document confirms the hypothesis of an increase in forced prostitution and trafficking precisely at the same time as the football world cup. the incidence of a high number of young girls trafficked during the world cup season, as some feared, is thus confirmed. i would like to refer to the question put before the start of this debate, and i do not therefore agree with the analysis of a leading german newspaper that this sporting event is irrelevant in terms of the increase in cases of sexual exploitation. this increase is foreseeable and is actually planned, so the question is not irrelevant. the german authorities, in particular the federal ministry of the interior and the ministries of the länder, have responded to our requests. we have discussed this twice in the council of ministers of the interior and arrangements have been made for more thorough checks at the borders. we have been informed that trafficking groups have organized a network of trafficking of young girls, mainly from countries on the eastern borders of the european union. i would like to stress that border controls must be tightened up. we have also asked for and received instructions on the need to protect victims of exploitation in the implementation of special assistance programmes. these are not people to be treated as illegal immigrants, but victims of a modern form of slavery who must be protected. we have also supported the setting up of two multilingual telephone lines, which are already in operation and have been entrusted to two german non-governmental organizations, well known in the country. we are aware of the problem of the absence of a single telephone number at european level, a project which, however, requires the agreement of all the telephone companies in all the member states. this is an initiative which we can implement in the medium term, just as we are implementing a european emergency number for children. we have also supported an information campaign with the german authorities, which was organized by the german women's council, which you will be very familiar with. we have decided together to organise a workshop to be held by the european commission and the german authorities immediately after the world cup, in order to prepare a document containing all the positive and negative experiences of this period and to draw up a kind of manual to be used at all international sporting events. i should also like to say a few words about the role of europol and eurojust. we have encouraged member states to cooperate more closely with these two organisations. as you know, europol has done a very good job in recent weeks, as it reported at the last meeting of the council of ministers of the interior in luxembourg last week, and the director of europol confirmed that the police cooperation network has benefited greatly from the boost given to national police forces by the member states. in conclusion, i should like to say that we have sent a request, formulated in accordance with the action plan, to the network of consulates of the member states of the european union in the countries of origin. we have asked for regular meetings to be held in the countries of origin at consular level to strengthen the preventive identification of potential victims of trafficking and thus to help them not to fall victim to such trafficking. we will prepare a report on this request by the end of 2006. this is, in summary, the list of initiatives that have been taken so far.

the nitrate regulations are extremely important. amendments nos 12, 18 and 23 propose provisions to maintain the status quo as regards groundwater quality. at the same time, it seeks to prohibit any adverse changes in the concentrations of pollutants in groundwater. i share the rapporteur's point that vigilance is needed to avoid the deterioration of groundwater quality. however, the concern that the new directive may leave room for additional pollution is addressed by the requirement in article 5 to identify and reverse any significant upward trend in pollutant concentrations. moreover, maintaining the status quo is not in line with the requirements of the water framework directive, according to which the management of groundwater quality must be carried out in such a way as to prevent any degradation of groundwater. the amendments cannot therefore be accepted. as regards the nitrates regulation, the commission can accept amendment no 36 which proposes to delete the reference to the nitrates directive. the commission considers that this reference is not necessary, taking into account the relevant provisions of the water framework directive. as regards the programmes of measures to reverse the trend of nitrate concentrations of agricultural origin, it is noted that the relevant provisions of the nitrates directive still cover these programmes and therefore do not need to be included in this directive, therefore the commission can accept amendment no 43. i would like to reiterate here that the nitrate directive, the water framework directive and this directive all have the same objectives in terms of preventing and reducing nitrate pollution. there are also no substantive differences as regards their legally binding nature and the and will have long-term effects on prosperity, the labour market and social peace. we must concentrate the limited resources on a few priorities. we have formulated strategic objectives to which member of the commission. mr president, i should like to answer succinctly as many as possible of the concerns and issues raised. firstly, on behalf of the commission and personally, i should like to thank all the members for their cooperation and support, for which i am very grateful. the number of speeches made this morning clearly proves that much attention has been devoted to the issues concerned and sends a clear signal as to the importance of european research to the future of europe and to our lives and economies. i shall start with the budget and budgetary structure. the difference between the budgets that parliament and the council are proposing is now 2%, which is a very minor difference. i believe that we have a common understanding and that agreement on this point should be relatively easy. i would like to point out that one must be careful when comparing the sixth and seventh framework programmes, as these are structured differently and are sometimes difficult to compare. for example, in current prices, there is a 60% increase for actions under fp7, against one of 30% for the old continuity actions. therefore, an increase of over 30% for certain continuity actions means that we are actually making these clear priorities. twenty-five per cent of the actions are new, and approximately 75% of the actions are continuity actions. as regards thematic priorities, we must understand that these will also be addressed by the european research council, either now or in the future, but of course we do not know in advance what the structure of those thematic areas will be. turning to small and medium-sized enterprises, i honestly have nothing against 15%, but believe that this must come about through political change. that is why i advocate simplification and why i believe that the 15% or 25% additional funding we are offering to small and medium-sized enterprises should result in changes. that is why we must pay attention to their needs, particularly in the work programmes. concerning energy, it is clear – as a number of you quite rightly pointed out – that this is one of the major challenges we must address in the future. we all agree on this. however, the commission’s opinion is that the challenge is simply too serious for us to leave any potential area out of the research – from renewables to hydrogen fuel cells, clean coal, nuclear energy, smart networks and more efficient use of energy, etc. this a truly important issue, and on the subject of environmental challenges such as climate change, i would say that these are more serious than we are sometimes ready to admit. practically all our efforts in the field of research should move in a direction that makes our lives easier in the future. if we continue in the current direction we will be faced with some very serious challenges. i would like to make a few remarks regarding embryonic stem cell research and the european research council, which i talked about in my introduction. as regards embryonic stem cell research, if you ask any top scientist about this – as i have done recently – they will tell you that the right approach to addressing major health issues is through a combination of efforts from different sources and origins. that is their clear answer. i was asked a question on the eurobarometer on biotechnology. as you know, the commission regularly conducts eurobarometer public opinion surveys on issues relating to biotechnology. the 2006 version is currently being finalised and should be available in the next ten days. however, since the question put was a clear one, i can tell you that, as regards the views on embryonic stem cell research across europe, 55% of the population surveyed approved of this provided there was the usual government regulation or tighter regulation. seventeen percent did not approve, except under very special circumstances. only 9% did not approve under any circumstances, and 15% did not know. so, if one were to draw a line, 50% would approve this with tighter regulation, 25% would oppose it, some would allow it under very special circumstances, and 15% do not know. by the way, this is in line with the study published last year on social values as regards science and technology. this study found that over 90% of european citizens believe that medicines and new medical technologies will have a positive effect on our way of life over the next 20 years. i should say that we are aware of the differences that exist between different countries as regards what we are discussing today. this is not really a discussion about moral issues, but on whether we can establish a system at european level that strikes a balance between the very different national practices, bearing in mind ethical considerations. i truly believe that the commission’s proposal is going in the right direction. the european research council represents a major change of mindset in europe. that is why we should all be proud of what we are delivering. i want to try to convey to you how seriously i am taking this. last weekend professor kafatos and i were in the united states and met the presidents of the national science foundation and the national institute of health. i wanted him to be clearly visible on stage and for him to be seen as someone with whom they should correspond and cooperate in the future. i fully agree that the cohesion fund and the framework programme on competitiveness and innovation should be used hand in hand. therefore, i fully agree with the inclusion of the concerns of the less-developed regions. we have to improve capacities there. we have to do everything in terms of infrastructure so that they can compete as regards excellence, and we need this excellence because we are in a global race. it is crucial that we understand that. fisheries will be a cross-cutting issue on which special attention should be focused, and the commission has clearly underlined that. women are genuinely under-represented and we are trying to do our best to change that. technology platforms have vast potential. they have developed from research actions but have already outgrown that purpose and have a role to play as regards lead markets and the european institute of technology, etc. they will be a crucial factor. as regards simplification, this was one of the most difficult tasks i have ever undertaken, but we are pushing ahead as hard as possible on this. in reply to the question from mr van nistelrooij about the mid-term review of the structural funds, i cannot commit myself because this is not in my area. however, it is a proposal in which i have an interest and i see it as a logical proposal which is going in the right direction. as regards the point on education, we are trying to pay special attention to universities because we believe that they could do more than they are doing now and that sometimes we are not too benevolent towards them. in conclusion, time truly matters, as some of you have underlined. it is crucial that we deliver the programme on time, so that the implementation rates in 2007 are as high as in the past. that is very important because it is a political affirmation of research and development that would strengthen our hand in future debates, which also link into budgetary issues. we want to go beyond the framework programme and into the european research area. there has been a switch of direction in europe since the second world war to a knowledge-based economy. also, the rules for participation should be addressed very carefully because they are part of this timing issue and we should consider them carefully. the commission is willing to be flexible and constructive in this trialogue, and wants to make a success of our common endeavours. finally, i agree with those of you who feel that the budget should be higher, but at this moment the best thing is to focus on the delivery. if we focus on delivery we can prove that we need more financing in the future and that we can change european reality. (applause)

a preparatory meeting with human rights non-governmental organisations, which we deemed particularly useful. i want to inform you that we will be holding the next meeting of these consultations in november in moscow and will be pursuing the idea of closer involvement of ngos. we want to make these consultations more results-oriented in the future. i can assure you that the commission will keep human rights at centre-stage in our relations with russia, not least as we are talking about the country which currently holds the presidency of the council of europe. on energy, mr kelam referred to the interdependence between the eu and russia. we can also say that we not only have interdependence but also import dependence, since by 2020 the eu will have to import around 70% of the gas it consumes. according to current forecasts, russian production and export capacity will fall short of eu needs unless massive investment takes place in russia. we are therefore working to ensure that sufficient additional quantities of gas can come into the eu and we will have to look at all possible sources and routes, including turkey, incidentally. this requires strengthened cooperation and increased imports from russia, as well as from other countries. at the same time, let us keep the big picture in mind. one of europe’s greatest challenges will be to reduce dependence on energy imports and on fossil fuels. therefore, it is very important that our energy policy and the external aspects of europe’s common energy policy are very high on the agenda of the finnish presidency and, i trust, of all the future presidencies. reference was made to gazprom and its ambitions to purchase eu assets. in this regard the main concern within the eu is the apparent lack of a level playing field. eu companies which may invest in upstream assets in russia do not have the right to independently access the russian gas transportation infrastructure. within the eu, the right to access gas transportation infrastructure is enshrined in eu legislation. in this context, the rules applicable to gazprom, notably eu competition rules, would be no different to those applied to any other company. the fact that gazprom is the exclusive supplier of gas from russia to the eu would have to be taken into account in any objective analysis. reference was also made to free trade and the pca. i want to finish with this, because this is a very important strategic issue in eu-russia relations. the objective of a free trade agreement was already included in the pca when it was concluded in 1994. for a free trade agreement, russian accession to the wto is a prerequisite. in this regard, it is important to note that the wto accession process is now coming to its final phase and we expect that this condition will soon be met by russia. reference to a free trade agreement was made at the sochi summit for further exploration. our point of departure is that trade and economic integration will be core elements for the post-pca agreement and our intention is to set up a broader and deeper free trade agreement, some kind of ‘fda-plus’ achieving deeper free trade than normal, simple free trade agreements. let me conclude now, because i know that many colleagues have more important things to do. allez les bleus!

member of the commission. the commission is aware of the problems experienced by consumers in connection with car hire and we have legislation that could help to a certain extent. one such piece of consumer directives. some of them could be relevant to car hire. one which is very important is the one on distance selling. unfortunately, based on a ruling of the court of justice, this does not member of the commission. as i am sure that the honourable member is aware, the lateral timetable set by the mauritania transition authorities is as follows: referendum on 25 june, municipal and legislative elections on 19 november, senatorial elections on 21 january 2007 and presidential elections on 11 march 2007 (first round) and 25 march 2007 (second round). this 19-month schedule is tighter than the 24-month period initially planned by the military council for justice and democracy. its aim is a return to constitutional and democratic rule by the end of may 2007 at the latest. when consultations were opened under article 96 of the cotonou agreement, mauritania gave undertakings in the areas of respect for democratic principles, fundamental rights and freedoms, the rule of law and good governance. the european union declared its willingness to provide support for the implementation of these undertakings and decided to support the transition process in mauritania during the consultation period itself by means of institutional support projects. in particular, a eur 6 million technical support project for the electoral processes was drawn up by the commission and approved in april 2006. the european community’s financial contribution of approximately 75% of total donor contributions will be implemented by the un development programme. the project’s specific objective is to strengthen the capacities and resources of the national independent electoral commission, the ministry of justice and civil society. it is also aimed at helping to ensure that the elections are free, fair and transparent, are conducted efficiently and lead to results that are nationally and internationally recognised and legitimate. regarding observation of the electoral processes, the commission plans to send a team of electoral experts in early june 2006 - around now - to help with the constitutional referendum and, in july, a fact-finding mission to assess the advisability, usefulness and feasibility of future observation missions as well as, if necessary, electoral observation missions to observe the general and municipal elections in november 2006 and the presidential elections in march 2007. as you know, mauritania is not a member of either ecowas, which it left in 2000 or uemoa, but it is member of the arab-magreb union. the country takes part in the barcelona euro-mediterranean dialogue as an observer, and formally applied for membership at the end of may 2005. no response to that request can be given before the country returns to constitutional and democratic rule.
member of the commission. the commission attaches great importance to the rights of freedom of religion, belief and expression in its dialogues with third countries. freedom of thought, conscience, religion and belief is one of the fundamental human rights and, as such, is enshrined in a number of international instruments, including the universal declaration of human rights, the international covenant on civil and political rights and the european convention on human rights. in addition, the eu charter of fundamental rights makes clear that everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and that cultural, religious and linguistic diversity should be respected. respect for human rights, democratic principles and the rule of law underpins the cotonou partnership signed by the acp states and the community and its member states. article 8 of the agreement indicates the topics on which regular political dialogues should focus, referring specifically to ethnic, religious and racial discrimination. there is no state religion in nigeria. in 1999, the constitution provided for freedom of thought, conscience and religion and the federal government generally respects those freedoms. the constitution also prohibits state and local government from adopting an official religion. however, state governors have great autonomy and it is alleged that islam has been adopted de facto as a state religion in several northern states. the return of nigeria to democracy in 1999 has seen an improvement in the human rights situation, but it has also seen an increase in tensions and violent conflicts, which currently provide the most threatening challenges to the new democratic nigeria. in this complex and unstable situation, the commission has been trying to identify the most common causes of conflicts with the objective of helping to address and prevent them. conflicts and violence have historically marked relationships between muslims and christians, particularly in the central states, where communities of different religions are numerically equivalent. it is generally not possible to cast muslims or christians systematically in the role of aggressor or victim, as they have historically been both. it is apparent, however, that conflicts always involve extremely poor people and that conflicts presented as religiously motivated are often triggered by other causes, including conflicts between traditional rulers, land and resource struggles amongst communities, political in-fighting, and tensions between state and federal governments. the significance of the tension between indigenes and non-indigenes is crucial to understanding the frequent cause of conflicts in nigeria. a recent report by human rights watch, 'they do not own this place', blames the federal government policies that discriminate amongst non-indigenes, defined as people who, no matter how long they have lived in an area, cannot trace their origins to the ethnic and genealogical roots of the original inhabitants of that area. in a country with more than 250 ethnic groups, these discriminatory practices spreading at state and local government level have relegated millions of nigerians to the status of second-class citizens, increased poverty and created the conditions for intercommunal violence. according to father george ehusani, secretary-general of the catholic secretariat of nigeria, interviewed by human rights watch, 'poverty in nigeria has assumed the moral character of war and that is what you see reflected in much of the ethnic violence in this country'. the commission and the eu member states are engaged in regular dialogue in nigeria to promote respect for human rights, basic freedoms and the rule of law among communities, religious and ethnic groups, state and federal authorities. since the first niger delta crisis in november 2004, regular visits of the eu heads of mission have been organised to various areas: the niger delta, some northern states and some middle-belt states. while one of the focal sectors of eu development cooperation with nigeria is supporting and promoting good governance at federal and state level, the commission is also engaged in financing community projects in the niger delta and is about to approve a project to support non-state actors. moreover, the ec budget lines have for years been financing projects to promote democracy and human rights.

on behalf of the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. first of all, i must apologise to mr gargani, who is ill and therefore unable to be here today. i have been asked by the group of the european people's party to represent him here today as rapporteur and to explain the content of this report. let me start by saying that this decision of the european court of justice at least for me was not a surprise. there were many who thought that this would not happen, but for me it was only logical, because we have had very different approaches in the way the european commission has made legislative proposals in the criminal justice area in the past. i would simply point out from my practical experience in the field of economic law that in the past, for example, in the directives on money laundering or also in the directives on market abuse or in the provisions on insider trading, directives proposed on the basis of legal bases of the first pillar have often contained at least elements of criminal law. it is indeed quite correct that the court has in the past very often - even if the cases were different - followed the principle that, in determining which legal basis is decisive, the objective pursued by the whole proposal is always decisive. it was therefore quite natural that the court should now, in this context, have held, on the basis of a concrete example from environmental law, that it was not possible, here too, to split up acts which were in fact interrelated in such a way that certain aspects were allocated to a field of the treaties other than the actual objective originally pursued by them, in so far as that objective was to be attributed to the first pillar. so the result is not surprising to me. but what are the consequences now? first of all, this does not change the fact that criminal law remains primarily the responsibility of the member states, at national level, and that europe has only exceptional competence in this area. in this context, i also believe that it is wise for the european legislator, who may now use this instrument but does not necessarily have to, to exercise restraint in the matter of criminal law. we must decide on a case-by-case basis in each specific situation: do we need criminal law provisions to achieve this objective, or do we not need them, or is it better to leave it to the member states to decide and regulate these matters? so, from the point of view of the legislator, whether it is the parliament or the council, restraint is in order. and this is mainly because i simply believe - and this is why the treaties have basically left the competence in the field of criminal law in the competence of the member states - that the system of national criminal law in europe is very, very different. it starts with the rules of sentencing, but also with the rules of enforcement. there are member states where the sentence is enforced, there are member states which, as a rule, have only a 50% penalty, there are those which have a penalty of two thirds, there are those which additionally have secondary consequences which are punitive in nature and which do not exist in this form in other member states. i think that if europe starts to introduce uniform penalties beyond what is necessary on all sorts of issues, then the consequence would be that we would have unsystematic interference in the criminal law of the member states. it's doubtful that makes sense. we should exercise a certain restraint for this reason in particular. i think that is what is being done in the report which mr gargani has presented and which has been accepted by the committee, and that is essentially what it is about. we also support the commission's attempt to analyse in detail the proposals which need to be revised because they no longer comply with the case law of the court of justice, where we have had the separation into two different acts, and then to make concrete proposals on how this can be adapted. as regards the amendments tabled after the decision in the legal affairs committee, i can state for my group that some of these amendments, in particular those tabled by the socialists and liberals, are acceptable, others are not. i am not going to go into details, as i have already discussed this with the rapporteur, but on the whole i find that there are no fundamental differences in the assessment of these questions in the legal affairs committee. the problems are more in the nuances, perhaps in the question of how far one can go in each individual case. but otherwise there was a great deal of agreement in the committee on this question. i thank you very much for your attention.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. the commission is not prepared to accept this. i would like to thank mrs roure for this report, which has already been appreciated by some of my colleagues. i think we have produced a really excellent inter-group paper, also in view of the fact that long before i was elected to this parliament, colleagues had already made efforts and repeatedly stressed the need for such a report. the report is much more urgent than ever, especially in the face of the modern information age. if you think about it, the amount of data stored by european authorities is not hundreds of thousands, it is not millions, it is billions of data sets that interfere with the individual personality of each individual by storing information that, if maliciously intended, which i will not submit to any state, can be linked together, with which i can create profiles that i can use to identify the behaviour of unloving citizens. the report is all the more urgent because these data volumes are still growing. we have not only existing systems such as eurodac or apis which are yet to come into force. we have the visa information system, which is being redeveloped. we have sis, the second generation schengen information system, and we may soon have the third pillar, the storage and transmission of passenger data. so these billions of records are going to grow. in addition, the commission's communication on interoperability and synergy and efficiency of european databases also aims to link these databases to each other, so that the the commission is also responsible for the implementation of the budget. mr president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, one year after the start of the reflection period, it is time to take stock. where are we? what can we do to move europe forward? what can we expect from the european council? i will begin by saying that europe is haunted by a spectre: the spectre of european pessimism. if we had the traditional euroscepticism of those who never wanted europe as a political project, we now have the pessimism of those who consider themselves convinced europeans and who very often sink into a state of "chrisophilia", each one wanting to show today that he knows better than the other the causes of the deep crisis europe is going through. what is the cause of this euroscepticism? to a large extent, this is the shadow of the negative referendums in two of our member states. this shadow cast doubt on europe and on europe's ability to define a common life project. that is one of the reasons why we must find a solution to the constitutional question. i want to say this without any ambiguity. we in the european commission are in favour of the principles, values and substance of the constitutional treaty. the question is, first of all, why do we need this constitutional text? what do we lose if we don't have a constitutional treaty? we are losing a clarification of competences between the different levels, we are losing the extension of co-decision and the extension of qualified majority voting, we are losing the legally binding charter of fundamental rights, we are losing a union minister for foreign affairs who would at the same time be the vice-president of the commission, we are losing more effective action in areas such as public health, food security and even energy, because the constitution extended competences in this area. we also lose an extra layer of coherence on the outside. and on this point i would like to say to you - the experience of a year and a half as president of the commission confirms this - that we in europe absolutely need what the constitutional treaty brought to the external sphere: more efficiency, more democracy, more coherence. the current treaties do not allow us to achieve all these objectives fully. let's be clear, nice is not enough. (applause) the question is how do we get past this? can we solve this problem by talking about the constitution every day? can we solve this problem by simply taking a pragmatic approach? i say no, i say we must avoid two traps. firstly, the trap of saying, as some would like, that the constitution is dead, let us do something purely concrete: that would be dangerous for europe. i would also like to say that it would be dangerous for europe if we were to allow ourselves to be locked into a purely institutional or constitutional debate, if we were to pretend that we are now stuck waiting for a constitutional solution. that is why we must proceed on two levels, as we said in our document of 10 may on the double track approach. at the first level, a europe of results, a europe of concrete projects, but - and this is the second level - a europe of results which is not opposed to, or an alternative to, political europe, but which is, on the contrary, a condition for citizens to accept europe as a major political project. so it is not a question of choosing between the europe of results and the institutional europe, it is a question of choosing both. we need a europe of projects, of results, to have a great project for europe. what is the europe of results that we are proposing? we have already achieved some results. that is why i cannot agree with all those who say that europe is completely broken. i think they are unwittingly reinforcing this crisis. i understand that analysts have to say this, but as political leaders, we have a responsibility. do you really think that we will restore the citizens' trust simply with negative messages? no, you can't! to move europe forward, we must be renewed with hope, with confidence and show progress. the truth is that even after the two negative referendums, we were able to settle the budgetary question for the next seven years, and that for 27 countries. we have nevertheless been able, thanks to the collaboration of the european parliament, to find a political solution to the very controversial problem of the services directive. we have nevertheless been able to relaunch the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. we have launched - something unthinkable two years ago - a common energy strategy for europe. so let us continue to make progress on the basis of concrete projects. let us achieve results to create the right moment to deal with the institutional question. in our document of 10 may we made some concrete proposals. i do not want to go into the details of these proposals again, but i will mention a few. see what's wrong with the single market to defend consumers in europe. the european council in brussels in december 1995 called for the creation of a european market for the sale of goods and services. taking stock of our social sphere: what are the obstacles to a more united europe? at the same time as we are making progress on the market question, we must also make progress on the social question. on the basis of existing treaties, make progress in the areas of justice, cooperation, the fight against terrorism and crime. it is possible, on the basis of the current treaties, to do more in the area of immigration, to combat illegal immigration, while at the same time dealing with the issues of legal migration. it's a major issue. if the member states want to do more, they can do so on the basis of the treaties themselves. so it is not just a question of institutional matters, it is also a question of political will. let us therefore make progress in the area of justice and security. these are areas where european citizens are asking member states to do more, because it is clear today that we cannot fight terrorism, that we cannot face the challenges of illegal migration on our own: we must work together. much more can be done in the field of the external dimension. the right solution is the one in the constitution: a minister for foreign affairs, vice-president of the commission. we must pool our capacities and resources in external relations, but since we do not yet have a constitution, the commission presented a document a few days ago containing concrete proposals to strengthen the efficiency, coherence and external visibility of the european union. we have also made important proposals on subsidiarity, transparency and better regulation for europe. deliver, and we will have to do that on the basis of the current treaties. we cannot afford to wait for what will shortly be 27 member states to reach a consensus on the constitutional issue. at the same time, the commission remains fully committed to debating and engaging in dialogue with citizens at european, national and regional levels. the methods we will use are set out in plan d – as in debate, dialogue and democracy. we should use that to explain the added value of the european project. we should use that to argue why we need a new constitutional treaty. we should use it to discuss the political priorities with citizens. our two institutions may not always agree on every detail, but there is one fundamental belief that we share: our commitment to becoming a more democratic, transparent and effective union. and that goes beyond any period of reflection. i also believe that european affairs suffer from a participatory deficit. still, citizens have high expectations on delivery and policy content, and this places important demands on the member states and on our institutions. we must involve citizens more in the policy process at all levels, particularly young people and women. such initiatives should be concrete and seen as a permanent function of developing european affairs, and they should ensure that the feedback process is taken seriously – what do we do with what we hear in dialogue and engagement with citizens? – and that listening is followed up by concrete actions. i have said it before and i will say it again: plan d is not a rescue operation for the constitution. it is not limited to the reflection period – be it one year, two years or even more. it is a starting point for a long-term democratic reform process. we want to create a citizens’ ownership of eu policies to make them understandable and relevant, and to make eu institutions accountable to and reliable for those they serve. i see and hear of lot of nostalgic harking back to the good old days of the european union, but nowadays it is no good having a few men shut themselves away in a castle somewhere trying to solve the problems of the european union. today we need to engage citizens; we need the support and trust of citizens and the confidence of citizens to be able to build a future for the european union. we need to engage and create the participatory functioning of the eu institutions. as you pointed out in your motion for a resolution, we need a special focus in plan d for the coming year, until the june 2007 summit. i have already promised the commission to come back after this summit with a kind of mid-term review. i will pay close attention to the summit’s conclusions in that review, and also to the resolution of this house. delivering concrete results and reconnecting with european citizens will create the favourable climate that is necessary for successful institutional reforms; that is the way we motivate it. so far, plan d has been a successful exercise in terms of setting off a wide range of activities, and i believe we have started to think and reason somewhat differently. we focus on what is our reality of today and for the future, how we need to interact with today’s and tomorrow’s citizens. over 660 activities have been taking place in member states; hundreds of thousands of citizens have visited the europe debate website. for the future, i also think, as mr leinen does, that we need more of a citizen-to-citizen approach to allow citizens to meet across borders to discuss the european agenda. we should focus particularly on young people, the europeans of tomorrow, and mobilise more women in the decision-making process. we need the whole of the european project to be more participatory, more transparent and more effective, and this ambition goes beyond any period of reflection. that is the only way we will be able to take the european union into the future. in writing. once again, the court of justice found that the council had infringed the ec treaty. the council has tried to do away with the involvement of parliament in the legislative process by choosing a legal basis other than that provided for in the treaty. therefore, his conviction by the luxembourg judges is not a surprise. it was predictable and it is welcome in every respect. of course, all institutions are called upon to analyse the judgment and draw conclusions for the future. i do not understand, however, the consequences which the commission is proposing. although the ecj acted very cautiously and reiterated the principle that the ec has no original criminal jurisdiction and therefore expressly excluded from the ec treaty a complementary criminal jurisdiction only for very specific situations, the commission seems to want to draw from the ecj judgment the conclusion of a general criminal jurisdiction of the ec. the council now believes that the commission is also seeking to derive from the european treaties its own powers which the member states have not delegated to it. the commission's approach is not only largely unlawful. it is also unacceptable from the point of view of integration policy. the commission's proposal is therefore rightly called to a halt by parliament in the gargani report.

member of the commission. mr president, i wish to thank everyone for this very interesting debate. the debate shows that this subject is a central issue for europe and that it is a priority which the commission believes can contribute towards improving the quality of life and preserving resources, especially for the benefit of future generations. it goes towards improving the economic, social and environmental dimensions of our way of life. the commission’s proposal has emphasised and given added relevance to the underpinning principles of our sustainable development policy. moreover, we have given ourselves clear objectives with correlative actions to reach these targets. concerning the need to be more ambitious, and the call for new targets, i need to underline that the essential thing is to produce results. investing in new targets may not be too difficult. however, it is much harder to get people to make and accept the changes needed to achieve those targets. we are meeting our existing targets, but the real challenge is to ensure that we do so. we are therefore proposing a new approach aimed at making the difficult changes across society that are needed for sustainable development. having said that, i agree that setting new targets is also important. however, any new targets need to be established through a proper process involving impact assessments and full stakeholder consultation, so that we have the acceptance and the commitment of those who need to work in order to achieve those targets. i would also like to say something about the integrated approach frequently mentioned during the course of this debate. sustainable development is about a coherent approach to policy-making. it requires an integrated approach, and in practice this means the lisbon strategy working hand-in-hand with the sustainable development strategy – two strategies working in parallel and in coordination towards the overarching objective of sustainable development. the commission disagrees with the idea of merging the two strategies, but agrees they should be used in parallel towards achieving the overall goal of sustainable development and that they should be complementary, both in scope and in terms of governance. the commission agrees that they can go hand-in-hand, though this does not mean that they have to be integrated. this can be achieved through sound and effective complementarity between the two, and that is what the commission’s communication seeks to achieve. concerning governance and monitoring, improving the governance of the european union’s sustainable development strategy is key to pushing forward progress. that is why the proposal for the review of the strategy proposes a new improved governance process. the commission will report on progress every two years. let me assure you that in doing so it will draw on the full range of sustainable development indicators. eurostat has made good progress in developing indicators and this work will continue. the aim is not to name and shame, but to assess where we are, how much more we need to do, and in which areas, in order to enable us to determine where we need to act and to allow clear communication to electors and stakeholders on where we need to change and on our approach to this. concerning the international dimension, sustainable development requires a global approach. the european union should maintain its position as a world leader in sustainable development through its action at home and by addressing the effect of this. it must also engage with others to achieve the commitments made at johannesburg and the millennium development goals in order, as has been said, to allow developing economies to leapfrog, to avoid old-fashioned unsustainable patterns of development and to use clean and innovative technologies. this is essential, for example, in the drive to limit climate change. it is also why the global dimension is an integral part of the reviewed european union’s sustainable development strategy and why that strategy advocates an integrated approach to development and external policies. in conclusion, the commission hopes that the interaction between us in this area can continue and intensify in the months ahead.

president of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin with an apology as, contrary to all principles, i cannot stay until the end of the debate, because i have a long-standing commitment to be present in the belgian parliament, where i shall meet both chambers – the senate and the chamber of deputies. the commission will be represented, as usual, until the end of the debate and we are always ready to answer any of your questions. let me start by telling you that i think this last european council confirmed that we are really moving forward in europe. last week here in the european parliament we discussed how this european council offered a real opportunity. it gave us all a chance to confront the sense of pessimism sparked by the ‘no’ votes on the constitution and to challenge again the mistaken perception that europe is at some kind of standstill. yes, it is true that we have problems and we have important problems to solve, but it is not true that we have been paralysed. so this european council was important to show the way forward to a solution to the institutional issues we still face; to give our citizens a clearer idea of how to move ahead to a more democratic and more effective europe. the european council confirmed that we are now moving from a period of reflection to a period of engagement. it set out a series of key actions which add up to a major programme of action and it agreed how and why we should take the next steps towards an institutional settlement. i should like to pay a very sincere tribute to chancellor schüssel for steering the european council so effectively. i should like to congratulate him, all his colleagues, the members of his government, the permanent representative – all his team – for a very successful presidency. i think, with the great austrian sense of composition, the austrian presidency made a very important contribution to our common project. i think – and i have said it before – that it was a presidency full of substance and style, and i thank you very much for that, chancellor schüssel. i am also proud that the commission was able to contribute so much to this european council, feeding the debate with ideas and pointing the way forward. the european union is now pursuing the twin-track approach that was set out by the commission in our document of 10 may: first, pressing ahead with delivery of concrete action in strategic policies; and second, drawing on the lessons of the past year, moving ahead on a step-by-step approach towards an institutional settlement. it paved the way for action across a wide range of policies. to pick just a few of the points, security, freedom and justice for our citizens constitute a real priority for the european union. member states agree that more needs to be done at european level addressing problems such as illegal immigration, trafficking of human beings, terrorism and organised crime, while guaranteeing respect for fundamental freedoms and rights. as chancellor schüssel said, there was a first orientation debate – which was very useful – regarding the issues of migration and integration. unanimity is holding up moves to make security and justice more effective and fairer across europe. i should have liked the european council to agree without delay the use of article 42 in the existing treaty. that was not yet possible and i regret that. however, it was possible to leave the door open to use the bridging clauses for freedom, security and justice. of course, we shall have to look at this on a case-by-case basis. i have no problem with that, because the argument for change is compelling and i am convinced that change must also include moves to codecision to allow proper democratic scrutiny. the momentum was stepped up still further on our economic, social and environmental agenda. there will be much more to come on this between now and the end of the year on innovation, energy, emissions trading, the european institute for technology and on very important projects for a europe of results. for instance, as chancellor schüssel has already said, some of those projects will be followed by a group made up of the forthcoming presidencies. for instance, our european response for civil protection will be based, hopefully, on the very good report presented at my request and at the request of chancellor schüssel by michel barnier. in particular, the european council endorsed the commission’s proposal for a fundamental review of the single market and the programme on sustainable development. the council rightly stressed the social dimension of the union’s actions and welcomed the commission’s intention to take stock of social realities in the european union. this work is already under way and during the first half of next year we expect to present, together, our fundamental review of the obstacles still remaining to the internal market and our assessment of the social situation in europe, which, of course, also includes an analysis of the demographic challenges that europe faces. we are, as you know, already working hard in that area. enlargement is a profoundly important issue for our union. i welcome the fact that the european council reaffirmed the common objective to welcome bulgaria and romania in january 2007 as members of the union if they comply with all the conditions that were clearly set. the council also restates that the future of the western balkans lies in the european union. as i said to you last week, we must ensure that the european union does not simply enlarge by default. we must ensure that the union is able to function politically, financially and institutionally. the european council faced this issue head-on and later this year we will have a detailed debate to clear the air and to leave no doubt about how we can build a strong europe with enlargement. we took a first step towards enlargement of the eurozone as well. slovenian membership of the euro is a real sign that the dynamism of european integration remains strong. it is, of course, very important for slovenia, but it is also important for the european union as a whole. the enlargement of the eurozone to include one of the new member states is an extremely important and positive step in the european union’s economic and monetary integration. there was also a commitment to get the most out of our external policies through more efficiency, coherence and visibility. this is not just political correctness: the commission’s proposals in its ‘europe in the world’ document can play a real part in helping to realise europe’s global potential. i also warmly welcome the fact that the european council agreed on a programme of transparency, including legislating in public on all legislative acts to be adopted by codecision. the council also endorsed the commission’s policies on better regulation and the role of national parliaments, important measures to improve the way we do our work and to make the union function better. all these areas – transparency, better regulation, subsidiarity – are crucially important to show that the european union is not, and should not be, the bureaucratic thing that our opponents sometimes present and that we are not remote and we really wish to engage with citizens. because, as i have often said, we have to understand that today the only way to build europe is not in a bureaucratic or technocratic way, but in a really democratic way. by any reckoning, this is a europe of results, a europe making a real difference on issues facing europeans every day. but where the european council took a new direction was in showing that the institutional issue is not dead, dormant, asleep, or whatever word the euro-pessimists might use. there is no question of abandoning our conviction that institutional reform is essential. everyone around the table in the european council recognised that the case for institutional change has not changed; it is just as pressing as when national leaders put their signatures to the constitutional treaty. the european council confirmed, as i have said very often, that the nice treaty is not enough, that we need an institutional settlement for our enlarged european union. (applause) as the commission set out last month, we should take a step-by-step approach. after all, that was always the method in the european community since it was founded almost 50 years ago. the european council has asked the forthcoming german presidency to present a report to the june 2007 council, which will contain an assessment of the state of discussions and explore possible future developments with a view to concluding the process by the second half of 2008. i welcome the endorsement by the european council of the commission’s idea of a political declaration to be adopted in berlin on 25 march 2007. when i speak about the institutional rules, i have to be very clear. what we need is not just a change of the rules to be more efficient, but also a confirmation of our values, and this is, of course, the substance of the constitutional treaty. the berlin declaration of march 2007 must be more than a commemoration of past achievements. it must be a restatement of and a recommitment to our values and ambitions, looking to the future for an enlarged europe. it must include a commitment to deliver. we do not need a long text – that is why i have always spoken about a messina-type declaration, because it was a very short, well-written text – but we need a deep reflection and a real debate about the priorities of europe. europe has moved on hugely in recent years and we need to set out the highly political nature of european integration today. i believe that it is critical that we will sign this together as a collective act of will, and that the european parliament will sign that declaration, alongside the member states and the commission, as proof that the european union and its institutions are working together towards the same goals. we have to build this europe in a spirit of true partnership. (applause) we cannot be complacent. if we are to use these opportunities and to take the steps needed, we must be more active, we must look for creative solutions to the institutional questions, we must continue and intensify dialogue with our citizens about where europe is going next. we must press ahead with a vigorous policy agenda: a europe of results delivering the policies our citizens need. last week’s european council gave us renewed confidence that solutions are forthcoming. i should like once again to thank the austrian presidency, because it is true that europe is about an internal market; it is true that europe is also about a political project; but the austrian presidency reminds all of us that europe is not only about the market, or about regulations: europe is also about values, music, literature, culture and our european way of life. as i said at the start of the austrian presidency – when our austrian friends chose that beautiful logo with so many colours – it was crucially important to change from the dark grey of most of the discourse in europe to a more confident colour, not because we are irresponsible optimists, but because if we want to lead we have to lead with confidence. we cannot lead if we are pessimistic, and that is why we need to show europe a new way of defending our values in a more globalised world. i believe that is the right way for europe to move forward.
