member of the commission. mr president, in the few minutes i have this evening, i am going to follow current financial trends and consolidate my opening remarks in covering both mr muscat’s report and the oral question by mrs berès on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs. as i emphasised during the hearing organised by the committee on economic and monetary affairs in january, the real debate cannot be on more or less cross-border consolidation. that is for the market players to decide, not the politicians. rather, the core of the debate is on how to create the optimal regulatory and prudential framework for the european financial sector to thrive, delivering concrete and substantial benefits to the consumers and boosting economic growth and job creation. that is why i would like to warmly congratulate the rapporteur, as well as the shadow rapporteurs, and members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs for their work. with such complex issues, it is not always easy to identify the real questions, to take into account all the different points of view and strike the right balance to set the way forward. thanks to the rapporteur’s open, transparent and inclusive approach, the report does just that. it brings a substantial contribution to the debate. i believe that there is a broad consensus on the main obstacles identified, shared by the council conclusions adopted by the ecofin council in may. we must improve the cost efficiency of the supervision of cross-border activities. in that respect, as noted in the report, further convergence of supervisory practices and standards is essential. to achieve this objective, we do not need a supervisory ‘big bang’, but rather to optimise the functioning of the lamfalussy structure. there are concrete projects that can be implemented rather soon. the role of the level 3 committees is essential, for instance to implement common reporting standards and thus avoid costly and unnecessary duplicative requirements. a number of such concrete improvements have been identified and were endorsed by the ecofin council last may. i would like to give a push to accelerating work in this area. we cannot have an internal market if companies are going to have to keep under-utilised capital tied up because we do not have in place sufficient cooperation between supervisors. i intend to come back to that in the time ahead. there is a regulatory and supervisory cost that should be evaluated. the report rightly underlines the implications of increasing integration for supervision. some complex questions, such as deposit guarantee schemes or the issue of lender of last resort, must be re-examined in that context. the commission’s white paper on financial services policy has identified those questions. this will surely be one of the most interesting policy debates for the coming months and years. besides supervision, the fragmentation of retail markets must also be addressed. the current difficulties in selling similar retail products in different countries is a major stumbling block in exploiting scale synergies. i fully agree with the report that further integration, notably in the retail market segments, should not occur to the detriment of consumers. we have means to prevent that from happening and we will use them. the ongoing sectoral inquiries, under the supervision of my colleague commissioner kroes, are a good example. a third area calling for our attention is the one related to impediments to corporate reorganisation on a pan-european basis. we are currently consulting on future priorities for company law and corporate governance to identify how we could make further progress. i would like to thank the rapporteur again for his work. we now have a shared analysis of what the main obstacles are. our challenge for the coming years will be to remove them. turning to the oral question by mrs berès, let me be clear: the commission believes strongly that market forces and shareholder choices should determine the optimal shape of exchange consolidation – not bureaucrats, not politicians. we should not be in the business of ‘picking winners’ or trying to shape markets according to a bureaucratic vision of what is best for european shareholders, investors and issuers. in the long run, european investors and european corporations seeking to raise capital will be best served by world-class institutions doing business in a world-class regulatory framework deploying cutting-edge technology and able to provide the breadth and range of services they want. those services might include the ability to trade in a multitude of currencies, time-zones and instruments. there are strong commercial pressures driving consolidation. if a deal makes commercial sense, and if the competition law and regulatory aspects can be adequately dealt with, then we will not stand in the way. however – and this is the key point – the commission considers that it is essential that financial market business in the jurisdiction of the european union is regulated by european and member state rules, and by our regulators. of course we will be very vigilant to ensure that current levels of investor protection and market integrity will be maintained. we believe in strong and effective regulation of european marketplaces. otherwise, we would not all have put so much effort into getting the mifid right, as well as the other aspects of the financial services action plan that we have laboured on for so long together. we note the preliminary assessment from some regulators in europe and the united states that the mergers being discussed will not mean significant changes of regulatory responsibility. but if there are any spillovers, regulators should work out constructively together what the rules are going to be and how to cooperate. i will be maintaining close contact with the college of euronext supervisors in the time ahead so as to ensure there is a full understanding about how all these issues will evolve. so there is no question of imposing new, extra-territorial burdens on european businesses that would put us at a disadvantage and jeopardise our internationally successful and developing financial markets. we know european users and shareholders do not favour that either. on competition issues, the commission’s competences in merger assessment are laid down in the ec merger regulation no 139/2004. within this framework, it is up to the parties in the first instance to inform the commission as to whether, in their view, the relevant turnover thresholds are met for community competence. the new york stock exchange and euronext have informed us that this transaction would not meet these thresholds. on clearing and settlement issues, in the course of our work we have been trying to determine the best range of measures – legislative or not – that will deliver improved competitiveness in these areas. as regards the steps needed to deliver those benefits, the commission has not yet taken a decision. all options remain on the table; a decision will probably be taken shortly.

regulation’ principles. respondents praised the consultation exercise. they supported the commitment to the strict application of the subsidiarity and proportionality principles. they also welcomed the commission’s commitment to undertake systematic regulatory impact assessments before any potential legislative initiative. a majority of respondents supported the objective of simplification. however, most stakeholders considered a recasting exercise inappropriate. stakeholders do not want us to take the risk of opening a pandora’s box. a codification or consolidation exercise would seem to be the most appropriate. secondly, as regards the continued relevance of the action plan, and in particular the measures proposed, respondents generally supported the work done since 2003. however, opinions were split on the details of the measures proposed for the medium and long term. a number of respondents expressed ‘regulatory fatigue’. however the general opinion was that work should continue on enabling legislation that would enhance the mobility of companies in the european union or facilitate company restructuring. the vast majority of respondents called for the adoption of a fourteenth company law directive on the transfer of registered offices. a large number of respondents also called on the commission to table a proposal for a european private company statute. in addition, a large number of stakeholders wanted to see more focus on small firms. thirdly, when it came to the detail of the measures proposed in the action plan in the field of corporate governance, views were split. there was general support for exploring certain issues at eu level, for example the issue of ‘one share, one vote’, at least by carrying out a fact-finding study, or the rights of shareholders. views were more qualified on the disclosure of institutional investors’ voting policies. there was clear opposition to the adoption of an eu wrongful trading rule, as well as to potential harmonisation of the legislation on directors’ disqualification. parliament’s report provides the commission with very useful input for the development of a strategic perspective for further action. you underscore the trends observed during the consultation exercise on the need to have more regard to the needs of small firms, the call for a fourteenth company law directive on the transfer of registered offices and the opposition to the adoption of a european initiative in the field of wrongful trading rules. it is too early at this stage for us to respond in detail to all the issues raised in this exercise. i have heard the views expressed. on the basis of the outcome of the consultation and of the report discussed today, we intend soon to publish a statement in which we will indicate our priorities for the near future. our views are mostly convergent. i welcome that. the commission and parliament must work hand in hand if we want to develop a regulatory framework that makes a difference in strengthening the competitiveness of the european economy.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to congratulate mrs lucas and thank her for her report. i would also like to thank the environment committee of the european parliament for the inclusion of aviation in the european union's greenhouse gas trading system. aviation is the sector that contributes about 3% of the carbon dioxide produced in the european union, but this rate is increasing rapidly. as mrs lucas said earlier, in a few years, by 2012, it will have increased by 150% compared to 1990, which is about a little less than 5% a year. this rate of increase in carbon dioxide is of course contributing to the further increase in the greenhouse effect, and it should be noted that it is not only carbon dioxide emitted by aircraft: there are other side effects, such as emissions that contribute to the creation of other greenhouse gases, and therefore the contribution of aviation to the greenhouse effect is much higher than the 3% contribution of carbon dioxide. as mrs lucas said, the kyoto protocol does not cover the limitation of carbon dioxide emissions from aviation. there is of course article 2 (2), to which reference is made. the european union will therefore continue and intensify its efforts to include air transport as well as maritime transport in any post-2012 regime. but that period is certainly several years away and therefore they should be included in the gas trading system now, after the co-decision procedure by the european parliament and the council, in order to achieve a limitation of the contribution of aviation to the limitation of the greenhouse effect and not to put this sector in an advantageous position compared to other sectors which contribute to the limitation of the greenhouse effect. in other words, we must not let other sectors suffer worse than aviation. it is therefore particularly encouraging that not only have there been the relevant reports from parliament's committees but also that both the council of environment ministers of the european union and the heads of state and government of the european union adopted at the european council last december the inclusion of air transport in the trading system and called on the european commission to bring the relevant legislation into the codecision procedure. i would like to make three comments on the remarks made by the committee on the environment and on the points made earlier by mrs lucas: first of all, whether a closed or an open system is better for aviation: the european parliament's committee recommendation wants the system to be closed, a separate system for aviation, either as a permanent system or at a pilot stage by 2012. the commission has taken a different approach: considers that the wider the scope covered by the trading system, the less costly it is to reduce carbon dioxide emissions and therefore the lower the cost to aviation without reducing the environmental benefit. i would also like to follow up mrs lucas's thought on the taxation of kerosene, jet fuel. it is a fact, as you said earlier, that there are bilateral agreements which essentially exempt air transport from paying taxes. and, of course, the european commission has since 2003 passed community legislation allowing member states to tax fuel on their domestic flights and also, after an agreement with another country, allowing taxes on flights between these two countries. the commission is continuing, and will continue, as you said earlier, its efforts also towards third countries to remove this system of non-taxation of kerosene, which is clearly not having any positive environmental effects. i would also like to make a comment on the geographical scope of the marketing system: the commission has proposed to include all flights from european union airports, and the parliament's committee proposes to include all flights to or from european union airports as well as flights passing through european union airspace. we believe that the commission's approach is simpler, more effective and will facilitate the extension of the system to other countries. but no doubt, because parliament is proposing it and because the airlines themselves and non-governmental organisations have proposed that all flights to and from european union airports should be included, the commission will consider this approach in the context of the detailed impact study it will have before submitting its proposal to the co-decision procedure which we hope to have before the end of this year. finally, i would like to say that, beyond the inclusion of aviation in the marketing system, there are undoubtedly other measures such as those you have mentioned: improving air traffic, investing in research to develop, improve and use technologies that are more environmentally friendly, possibly using biofuels in airlines - although this is still being researched - and a number of other measures that can also be implemented in parallel to reduce the impact of aviation on climate change.

emissions is steadily growing. our policy must aim to reduce the climate impact without cutting the growth of this key sector. the growth and competitiveness of our airlines must not be at odds with the reduction of greenhouse gases. the choice of instruments is crucial to achieving this objective. the introduction of a kerosene tax, the levying of departure charges or the taxation of tickets the question of how to restructure the european economy is therefore a question which determines the social cohesion of europe. the idea of the european union, the idea of the single market in which we live today, was in the second half of the 20th century that economic and technical progress was coupled with social progress. we are now in a phase where profit increases are coupled with a reduction in social security. if we do not stop this and return to what we have been doing successfully in the second half of the 20th century, which is to combine economic growth with social security, then we will lose the social stability of societies in europe. and social instability is always the basic precondition for political instability. the latter leads to a security breakdown. the restructuring of enterprises in europe is therefore a challenge which we must face socially. question no 34 by mr claude moraes (h-0544/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: footballis the commission aware of the problems which have arisen for many citizens in the author's constituency in connection with the commission's recent rules on broadcasting rights for football matches in the united kingdom? in some cases, it is very expensive to watch a football match, as viewers have to pay for multiple channels from different providers in order to watch certain matches. in this context, is it a fair system if television viewers are no longer able to enjoy a particular sport for economic reasons? how can people on low incomes watch their team's games if they have to pay for more than one channel?
member of the commission. i should like to underline once again that, when considering the application of ec law in the context of sport, it is important to draw a distinction between sport insofar as it generates economic activity and sporting rules as such. insofar as sport generates economic activity, it is subject to ec law, including the internal market and competition rules in the same way as other economic activities. so far so good! of course, as reflected in the nice declaration, the community takes account of the inherent social, educational and cultural aspects of sport when taking action under the treaty. the commission has followed this line in applying ec competition rules in individual cases and this approach has been confirmed by the european courts. when engaged in economic activity, sport governing bodies should, like any undertaking, ensure compliance with ec competition rules. i said that not all competition problems have been resolved, nor would i want a decision to be used against national authorities or courts should they wish to intervene further. it is clear that competition in itself creates economic activity; this makes competitors more alert and that is beneficial for the consumer and, in most cases, results in more diversity, more quality and a better price.

question no 36 by mr andrás gyürk (h-0577/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: energy market surveys in the past month and their results last month, the commission carried out on-the-spot inspections of several major energy suppliers to determine how competition is being achieved in the european natural gas and energy markets. the establishment of free competition in the energy market is crucial for healthy european economies. since we are discussing the introduction of a possible common european energy policy in parallel with these measures and the results of the inspections will have to be used in the design of the strategy, i recommend that we make the inspection process known at the appropriate level and provide evidence of the results. what is the state of the investigation of this sector and what are the important results of the measures taken so far? when can we expect a final result? does the commission intend to take further steps towards completing the internal energy market?
member of the commission. as the commission confirmed on 17 may 2006, it has indeed recently carried out on-the-spot inspections of a number of major energy companies in europe. it is not possible to comment further on these ongoing investigations. as you are aware, inspections are carried out under articles 20 and 21 of the ec regulation and form a normal part of the commission’s enforcement activities in the competition field. in general, inspections are carried out because the commission has reason to believe that the companies concerned may have violated the anti-trust rules established in articles 82 and 81 of the treaty. article 28 of the regulation prohibits the commission from disclosing information acquired during an inspection, except in limited circumstances. however, as required by regulation (ec) no 1/2003, the commission publishes all its decisions in due course. the commission is also carrying out a sectoral inquiry into competition conditions in the eu gas and electricity markets. this is a distinct exercise from the individual investigations and inspections to which the honourable member refers, but the extensive information about the functioning of the energy markets that is gathered during the sectoral inquiry will of course help to inform any enforcement action taken by the commission in individual cases. the main preliminary findings of the sectoral inquiry were published in february 2006 and identified a number of existing barriers to competition. for example, national wholesale energy markets are still highly concentrated, with few new competitors entering the sector. there is also far too little integration between the national markets. infrastructure and supply functions are so closely connected that it is difficult for new suppliers to enter the market, which means that consumers are denied choice. there is a lack of transparency, so new competitors also cannot get hold of the information. they need to get a foot in the door. finally, prices do not appear to respond to changes in supply and demand. tackling these problems will require a combination of regulatory and structural reform and robust enforcement of competition rules. the commission is committed to taking any necessary enforcement action if that proves justified. the sectoral inquiry will be completed by the end of the year. the commission will then decide whether any further measures are required in order to improve competition conditions in the gas and electricity markets. the information gathered through the sectoral inquiry will also play an important role in the ongoing formulation of a common european energy policy, as agreed by the spring european council. the commission is also conducting a review on implementation of the european regulatory measures in the energy sector. this work is being led by the commissioner in charge of energy, mr piebalgs, and the commission will report to parliament and to the council at the turn of the year. that report will also reflect on any further action that is needed to complete the integration of europe’s energy markets. all the information gathered during the sectoral inquiry and the review of implementation of the liberalisation directives, together with other information received through consultation with the stakeholders, will of course play a key part in the formulation of a common european energy policy.
member of the commission. the honourable member rightly touched upon the question of whether this is enough. i have explained to the honourable member that the commission has already initiated a number of investigations where it appears that anti-competitive behaviour contributes to the problems identified by the energy sector inquiry. however, competition law cannot open markets by itself, as the member will be aware. we need to complement our enforcement through an improved legal framework, increasing transparency, improving cross-border coordination, etc. regulatory changes may be needed for us to reap the full benefits of our energy markets. once we have the full report of the inquiry into competition conditions in the energy sector, we will reflect further on what changes may be required. my colleague, mr piebalgs, is looking at the level of current implementation of the existing liberalisation directives in the energy sector. depending on the results of that review, further measures to liberalise the markets will be considered. full structural unbundling is one option to consider. the member will certainly conclude that we will take measures when we can see that there is something rotten in the state.
member of the commission. as the honourable member rightly mentioned, there has been quite some change to the whole energy market scene. europe needs stable relationships with the main producers outside the eu too. however, this does not and must not prevent us from ensuring that there is an integrated, competitive market within the eu. an open and competitive, flexible and interconnected single eu market will guarantee a secure energy position for the future as it will make the european market attractive to external suppliers; so that is all part of the game. such a market will also be open to embracing new energy mixes. it will be able to muster the internal strength needed to master the international challenges in this field.

vice-president of the commission. madam president, the commission considers that the expression 'right of permanent residence' does not necessarily imply a contradiction, since the concept of residence, understood as the period during which one resides in a place, can be long-term, or even permanent. moreover, this is a concept which has not been the subject of any comments in the sense suggested by the honourable member, either during the preparation of the text by the commission, or during the discussions on the directive in the council, or here in the european parliament. as regards the second observation, the commission notes, as a preliminary point, that as established in article 18 of the treaty, and confirmed by the case law of the court of justice, the right of residence derives directly from the treaty for the union citizen whose residence documents serve only to establish that right. in line with this idea, one of the major objectives of directive 2004/38/ec has been to simplify the administrative formalities attached to the right of residence. according to this text, citizens of the union do not have to obtain a residence card in their member state of residence, since a simple registration with the competent authorities is sufficient, which is required only if the host member state deems it necessary. in this case, a registration certificate shall be issued immediately to union citizens on presentation of their identity card or passport and proof that they fulfil the conditions attached to the right of residence. after five years of continuous legal residence, citizens of the union obtain a right of permanent residence without any conditions and, if they apply for it, the host member state must issue them with a document attesting to this right. in conclusion, as also provided for in the same directive 2004/38/ec, member states, acting in accordance with their national legislation, issue or renew to their nationals an identity card or a passport indicating their nationality. it follows that a host member state cannot issue an identity card, in the strict sense, to a non-national citizen of the union. (e) an identity card or passport issued by the state of his nationality, stating, as provided for, his identity and nationality and, if required by the host member state, a certificate issued by the latter, attesting his right of residence.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today we are on the verge of obtaining agreement with the council on a second reading on such a sensitive proposal. we owe this above all to the excellent work of your rapporteur, mr ulrich stockmann, and i would like to congratulate him in particular. let me remind you of the approach behind the proposal for a regulation. the main objective is to maintain a high level of safety while ensuring fair competition between air carriers. the amended 2004 proposal introduced provisions on flight time and crew rest, commonly known as flight time limitation, in response to a request from the european parliament concerned about the national disparities in this area. professional pilot associations and several airlines have long been strongly critical of these disparities, which are detrimental to safety and normal competition. indeed, many accident investigations have pointed to crew fatigue as one of the factors in these accidents. the regulations on flight time are sometimes too flexible and allow airlines to make staff work for excessively long hours, to the detriment of safety and companies subject to stricter legislation. the amendment, dated 2004, also implies the certification of cabin crew on the basis of minimum requirements, as is the case in the united states and as was requested by the staff concerned and by part of the industry. these minimum requirements should improve aviation safety by raising the quality level of personnel. they must also bring about a convergence of the conditions of competition between airlines and facilitate the mobility of staff within a fully liberalised air transport market. it is true that the council had great difficulty in reaching agreement because of the very different views of the member states. but the council finally managed to reach a compromise on a common position at the end of february 2006. in its common position, the council notes that member of the commission. mr president, the proposal that is the subject of mr seppänen’s report aims at modifying and replacing directive 92/3/euratom, which lays down a community uniform administrative procedure applicable to the shipment of radioactive waste. i would first like to recall the aims of this proposal, which are: to ensure consistency with other community legislation on radiation protection; to ensure consistency with international conventions; to clarify the procedures; to simplify the structure and wording of the existing directive; and to enhance certainty, firstly by explicitly including transfers of spent fuel for re-processing – the same control procedure is now applied to all shipments of spent fuel, independently of the intended use – and secondly by generalising the automatic consent procedure. the consent of member state of transit and of destination is assumed after a reasonable deadline. this proposal takes into consideration the experience of application of the existing directive. it further takes fully into account the opinion given by the european economic and social committee on 9 june 2005, as well as the informal discussions held at the council and in parliament during 2005. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr seppänen, for the excellent report he prepared, which has received the strong support of the committee on industry, research and energy. the amendments mainly seek to clarify the commission’s proposal, and are therefore welcome. i am therefore confident that the council will take duly into consideration the content of parliament’s opinion, insofar as it might contribute to improving the directive. the commission will present positively the inclusion in the directive of the amendments in the seppänen report. i would like to encourage you to adopt the recommendation submitted by the itre committee, as this represents the best way to promote our common objectives. it enhances certainty with regard to the community uniform procedure which is applicable to the control of shipments of radioactive waste and nuclear spent fuel. i look forward to the forthcoming debate.

president of the council. i would like to thank you, mr president, members of parliament and political groups, the president and vice-president of the commission and the honourable members for the opportunity to discuss with the european parliament the priorities and the main objectives of the finnish presidency. the presidency of the european union is a demanding task, but at the same time a great honour and a privilege which finland is happy to assume. our cooperation with the european parliament as the presidency has started well. i would like to thank the president of parliament and all the other members of the european parliament who took part in the meeting between the finnish government and parliament in helsinki. several committees and political groups of the european parliament have also visited finland and had useful discussions on the objectives of our presidency. throughout its membership, finland has supported efforts to improve the efficiency of the union's institutions and to improve close cooperation between them. as president, we will work in close and good cooperation with the european parliament. i am not referring here to the role of the parliament as a co-legislator on an equal footing with the council in the co-decision procedure, but to the wider role of the parliament in promoting the union's core objectives. finland's own national parliament, the parliament, is celebrating a festive year. this year marks the 100th anniversary of the establishment of the unicameral parliament and of universal and equal suffrage. all, both women and men, were granted the right to vote and to stand for election at the same time. we are proud of this landmark of our democracy. in finland, the parliament is closely involved in eu affairs and has a great deal of influence. perhaps this experience of fruitful cooperation with parliament has in part made it so natural for us finns to cooperate closely with the european parliament too. the work of the european parliament and national parliaments is not overlapping; each has its own role in union affairs. but they share the same fundamental objective: to strengthen democracy in the union. finland's presidency will aim to turn the union's gaze outwards and forward. we must think about the kind of union we want in 10 to 20 years' time and how we will achieve it. we must, as europeans, recognize the historic forces of change in our time, respond to them and make them our partners. the eu is facing a major challenge in dealing with globalisation. the world around the union is changing and if we do not take precautions we will fall further behind. it would be devastating, above all, for the future of our children, for future generations. for their sake, europe must stop looking inward and consider its place in the global world in the longer term. the world around us is not waiting. our future requires us to take concrete action now, even if the effects of that action are not seen until later. in recent years, there has been a certain amount of hope in the union's decisionmaking capacity, and citizens are increasingly critical of it. however, i do not share the pessimism about the crisis of the union, but believe that its current problems can be overcome. the agreement on the financial framework and the progress made on the services directive are examples of the union's ability to take important decisions when there is political will. i believe that it is to be found in all the institutions of the union. the european union is a community of values which exists for its citizens. the decline in the union's legitimacy, legitimacy and credibility in the eyes of the citizens must therefore be taken seriously. part of this feeling of a weakening of the union's legitimacy is that citizens do not know what the union is doing for them. many issues that have a tangible impact on the lives of many citizens such as the right to live, work and study anywhere in the union are taken for granted. it is not to be remembered that they are made possible by the union itself. but the lack of information does not explain everything, and the union must also be able to improve its performance. the union must be able to deliver results that citizens can see in their own lives. the union's fundamental premise of safeguarding peace and stability in europe remains relevant. i was reminded of this personally on my visit to croatia a few weeks ago. they want to be part of the union so that they and their children will never have to see war again. many others, however, who have lived in peace all their lives, tend to take peace and stability for granted. it is therefore no longer enough to give the union its legitimacy. as many of you have said on many occasions, the union must be able to demonstrate its usefulness to its citizens in other ways, in more concrete ways. the union's need is best demonstrated by the effective performance of its fundamental tasks, in particular its legislative work. we can and must do so on the basis of the treaties in force today. europe cannot wait for new rules of decision-making, but must start to improve its performance immediately. the union must show that it is capable of achieving results that affect people's lives and not just of arguing about institutional issues. making it work requires bold decisions by europe's leaders and decision-makers. we cannot just think about this moment and the next election, but we must keep in mind the interests of future generations. that's why we have to make decisions that may be painful now but that will help shape the future. the willingness to challenge national positions and to take care of the european whole is also needed. the union must focus on what is essential and be effective in what is essential. it means activities where the union's action brings added value compared to the member states' actions alone. this added value can be achieved in the areas of welfare, security and freedom. achieving our goals starts with the way we work. transparency is essential citizens need to know how decisions affecting them are made. the increase in political debate in europe is in everyone's interest. your role is also very important. i am pleased that the european council decided to increase the transparency of council meetings. finland will, as the presidency, fully implement the principles adopted by the european council in order to increase the transparency of the council's work. finland also strives to contribute to openness in other ways, in all practical work and activities. we will endeavour to make all relevant information available as soon as possible on our presidency website. sometimes such practical means have a greater impact on actual access to information than political declarations. during its presidency, finland will work towards better regulation, i.e. the quality of legislation and the respect president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is a very important matter in many respects, but unfortunately the council cannot confirm or comment on the recent reports in the legislation applicable in this case. such an investigation is the responsibility of the national authorities. in the case of actions contrary to community law, the national authorities and the commission are responsible, subject to the supervision of the national and community courts. the council assumes that the current cooperation between private companies such as swift and the us authorities will be conducted in accordance with the applicable law and respect for fundamental rights. the council, like parliament, is a legislator and as such wishes to draw parliament's attention to the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the provision of information on the payer in connection with transfers of funds. this regulation is to be examined by both parliament and the council. once that regulation has been adopted, it shall apply to transfers of funds in any currency sent or received by a payment service provider established in the territory of the community. article 14 of the proposed regulation provides that payment service providers are to respond promptly and thoroughly to requests from the authorities responsible for combating money laundering or terrorist financing in the member state in which they are located concerning the information to be provided on the payer in connection with a transfer of funds and the retention of that information. the council considers that this community instrument, which is based on fundamental rights, strengthens the legislative framework to combat the flows of dirty money through transfers of funds, which can damage the stability and reputation of the financial sector. at the same time, it prevents all types of illegal activities against the community's financial system. the objectives of this regulation cannot be sufficiently achieved by the member states and can therefore, by reason of their scale or effects, be better achieved at community level. the adoption of the regulation is therefore urgent. that regulation shall be adopted by means of the co-decision procedure. on 6 december 2005, the council agreed on a general approach to the proposal. following informal meetings between parliament, council and commission representatives, the presidency hopes that a mediation solution for the whole regulation can be adopted soon. we are closely monitoring legislative action to prevent, among other things, illegal and unjustified actions against the community financial system. the council is also examining the commission proposal for a council framework decision on the protection of personal data processed in police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters. the commission adopted the proposal on 4 october 2005. the objective of this framework decision is to ensure a high level of protection of personal data of european citizens. it requires common provisions to determine the legality and quality of the data processed by the competent authorities of the member states. although the proposal does not directly concern the financial system, it does provide for the protection of personal data and may also be relevant to the subject matter under consideration. the proposal will be examined by the competent council bodies. i believe that we all share the desire to protect the citizens of europe, not only from terrorism but also from all kinds of illegal activities against the european financial system, also by means of community measures and legislation.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, hostage situations are increasingly targeting citizens of the european union and sometimes these kidnappings are also linked to terrorist acts. the european union and the united nations have repeatedly condemned the taking of hostages. the demands for ransom from the hostage-takers should be rejected as a matter of principle. ransom payments to hijackers encourage more hijackings and may thus lead to an increase in terrorism. international cooperation, especially within the eu, is very useful in dealing with such cases. the eu member states' actions in hostage crises are guided by the un international convention against the taking of hostages. the convention entered into force on 3 june 1983 and has been ratified by all eu member states. the eu council has dealt with hostage-taking issues, as well as directly between member states. practical responses to hostage situations include, inter alia, joint eu political support and action in a hostage situation, preparation for hostage situations through joint pilot projects and crisis exercises, strengthening of national crisis teams with experts from other member states, and a checklist to identify opportunities for cooperation between member states. in some specific cases, ad hoc cooperation has already been put into practice, but it would be useful to further clarify the basis for such cooperation. in order to be as effective as possible, this cooperation should be informal, voluntary and highly practical. all information must also be treated with the utmost confidentiality and the autonomy of the third country concerned must be respected.

member of the commission. madam president, between 29 june and 1 july, mariann fischer boel and i attended ministerial meetings in geneva on the doha round of trade talks. we also met and remained in contact with the meps who were present in geneva during those days. i would like to thank the honourable members of this house for their effort and for their commitment. it is much appreciated by the commission. the ministerial meetings did not find agreement on the main parameters for reductions in tariffs and subsidies, in agriculture and industrial goods, the so-called modalities of the agreement which are necessary to move to the final stage in the talks. we met several times with the ministers from the group of six, that is ourselves in europe, the united states, brazil, india, japan and australia. we also met in the green room format of 30 ministers and in the trade negotiations committee, which brings together the entire wto membership. there was no shortage of ministerial meetings and encounters, but the encounters were frankly better than the quality of the negotiations that took place within those encounters. we went into the discussions stressing the eu’s agreement with a principle expressed by pascal lamy beforehand, that the landing zone for an agreement would require effective real cuts in farm subsidies by all and real cuts in both agricultural and non-agricultural market access – real cuts in tariffs. we then specified that to capture such a basis for agreement we would on our side be prepared to move towards and close to the level of average cuts in farm tariffs proposed for developed countries by the g20, provided that others moved in concert, with a similar level of ambition in other areas of the negotiation. we made it clear to our partners that we would not be prepared to meet every g20 demand, in particular on the structure of the cuts. we pushed hard to establish a clear correspondence between the effort that we would make in agricultural market access and the effort that the united states in turn would have to make in the reduction of domestic subsidies close to the g20 levels of average cut by us, to be matched by close to g20 reductions of trade-distorting subsidies by the us. the united states was the only major player to refuse to consider moving on this basis and declined to signal any room for further movement within this landing zone. indeed, they demanded further significant moves by others in order only to sustain their present offer, which all others regard as insufficient. we also made it clear that, if a negotiating landing zone was to be identified in agriculture, we would only take our position in this pillar to the limit of our flexibility if we got a fair result in non-agricultural market access, requiring real cuts in developed and advanced developing countries’ tariffs. that is economically doable and, i would argue, desirable for these developing countries and politically essential for us and for other developed countries. the united states’ unreadiness to engage stopped developing countries from making any move or showing any flexibility of their own. the conclusions of the meeting therefore focused on the political handling of our failure to reach a breakthrough. all members reaffirmed a willingness to reach agreement by this summer. in this context g6 members first, subsequently backed by the broader membership in the trade negotiations committee, asked the director-general, pascal lamy, to intensify consultations and act as a catalyst for generating the basis for an agreement in the coming few weeks. he has not been asked to author a final agreement or provide a dunkel-type text, like the previous director-general at the end of the uruguay round, but instead to use his good offices to act as a go-between for a final agreement to emerge. that will require very active engagement by us with him and with the main players in the next ten days to two weeks. depending on progress made, it is likely that ministers will need to meet in a similar format towards or at the end of july to take the key decisions on modalities as well as to confirm progress made in the other key areas of the round, i.e. services, rules and the development package. the possibility of a meeting of heads of state and government in some formation or another to take forward the negotiations around the time of the g8 meeting in ten days is not ruled out. there is a lot at stake here and we shall have to work very hard and very fast in the coming days and weeks. failure of the dda would have severe consequences, not least for the developing countries. this is an opportunity that will not repeat itself to open markets further, to reduce subsidies, to strengthen world trade rules and to make a real contribution to growth in the poorest countries in the world. this is why these multilateral negotiations continue to be the eu’s top trade priority. no number of bilateral deals would have the same widespread effects or benefits. this being said, our trade agenda goes beyond achieving a successful doha deal. in the months ahead, the commission will define its commitment to boosting our competitive performance at home and abroad and this will be set out after the summer in an overarching commission communication on the external aspects of europe’s competitiveness. this will examine how future trade policy can contribute to our internal competitiveness policies and what the priority tasks are for us to build new and secure global markets for our investment and trade. this will include a new strategic approach to market access, including non-tariff barriers, the consideration of new bilateral and regional policy approaches and the examination of our political and economic ties with china. this is not, however, an alternative to the dda: it is an extension of a successfully concluded end to this round. our immediate priority remains, therefore, to bring about the necessary political engagement by all governments to negotiate a balanced and ambitious end to the dda. we will, of course, take a closer look at the social dimension of globalisation. modern social systems and a better quality of life are not optional extras: they are an integral part of a formula to deliver a lasting political response to globalisation and it is this goal, above all, that remains at the heart of my mandate.

the next item is the report by mrs karin riis-jørgensen, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on the taxation of motor vehicles (com (2005) 0261 - c6-0272/2005 - 2005/0130 - cns)) (a6-0240/2006).
member of the commission. madam president, honourable members of parliament, i am pleased to have the opportunity to present to you, on behalf of the european commission, the proposal on passenger car related taxes. once adopted it will have a direct impact on about 15 million new passenger cars presented for registration in the eu each year and, to a certain extent, on more than 200 million used passenger cars circulating on the roads of the community. the proposal is designed to benefit the internal market, the citizens, the car industry and the environment. first of all, the proposal contains a number of measures needing to be taken at community level in order to improve the functioning of the internal market, mainly by abolishing registration taxes – which currently involve unnecessary cost and administrative burdens, the lack of transparency and legal uncertainty for citizens. the proposed community measures are furthermore aimed at avoiding double payment of car-related taxes, when a car registered in a member state is exported or permanently moved for registration to another member state. registration taxes also involve high costs and reduced competitiveness for the car industry and result in the fragmentation of the car market. the proposal also promotes sustainability by implementing fiscal measures to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from passenger cars, as it establishes a more direct relationship between taxation levels and carbon dioxide emissions. it is important to mention that the application of the proposed measure is budget neutral: the gradual abolition of registration tax and its replacement by an annual circulation tax does not involve revenue losses for the national budgets, nor does it increase the total tax burden for citizens. the proposal takes a minimalist approach to car taxation and addresses only those issues that can best be dealt with at community level. it only seeks to establish the principle and structure of passenger car related taxes; it does not seek to harmonise tax rates, which will continue to remain the responsibility of the member states. it does not introduce new car taxes, but instead provides for the gradual abolition of registration taxes in the 16 member states currently applying such taxes, as well as for their gradual replacement by an annual circulation tax. the proposal has been discussed only once in the council so far, and the reaction of the member states has been mixed. strong support from the european parliament can maintain the momentum and help the council reach a unanimous decision. i want to emphasise that the proposed measures would make passenger car taxation citizen-friendly, car-industry-friendly and environment-friendly.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission is not prepared to accept this. i was going to thank the rapporteur, but she is not here yet, so we will catch up. she has presented a good draft report. we voted on it controversially on certain points. the report adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs contains a contradiction in one point, namely article 4. we have adopted two different, mutually exclusive approaches, and our group therefore wishes to make it clear once again that we want to base the assessment of future motor vehicle taxes strictly on co2 emissions. as mr wiersma said earlier, energy efficiency is of course also an issue. but if you try to regulate all the things that are possible with tax policy, you will fail in the end. our line is quite clear: we want a strict approach to co2 emissions, regardless of the technology used, the consumption and the size of the car, so that it is purely environmentally friendly. if we were to use this instrument to start an action against, say, larger cars, we would be wrong, because it is the larger models, the more expensive cars, that bring about the technological progress in car manufacture, where important safety and environmental measures are first enforced, because in these more expensive cars a new technology can be better developed. so instead of defaming the larger cars, we should be strictly guided by our common objective of reaching 120 mg/km by 2010. the project is difficult enough; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union's transport policy. we need a certain degree of flexibility so that the common objective of renewing the car fleet does not lead to discrimination in the european internal market. we therefore also believe - and this has been documented in a decision of the committee - that the commission should also present a study by 31 december 2006 on the weighting of possible factors other than co2 that might be appropriate to compensate for this. but we don't want to reduce co2 by including all the pollutants that are already there. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we have tabled an amendment, namely amendment no 40, which would give member states the possibility of treating vintage cars with a minimum registration period of 20 years separately. these vintage cars tend to have relatively high emissions because they are based on old technology. however, their share of the total market is so small that we can handle it in the way that is already done in several member states. as for the registration tax, i believe that it should be abolished after a certain transitional period, because it is an obstacle to the european internal market. we should therefore agree to let this registration tax run out in such a way that both the fiscal interests of the individual member states are taken into account and that an orderly transition is possible. in conclusion, i wish you every success, commissioner. i know how difficult european tax policy is. the harmonization process is facing problems from all sides. we are making little progress on many issues, and as long as unanimity is the rule, it will be difficult to make any really useful progress. we are therefore supporting the report and your difficult work as tax commissioner.
i have to say, madam president, i too would like to thank the rapporteur for drawing up the report. i have followed the opinion on behalf of my group in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety and have therefore also dealt with the dossier and i would now like to concentrate on two main points: first of all, i should like to say that i very much welcome the abolition of the registration tax proposed by the commission. i therefore support the report on this point too, in so far as it also maintains the gradual abolition of the registration tax. there are major differences between the member states which have a registration tax, both in the basis of assessment and in the level of registration tax. the registration tax has the widest variation of all taxes on cars in europe. these differences affect the smooth functioning of the internal market and therefore the registration tax should also be abolished as proposed. i am also in favour of a direct proportional relationship between taxation and co2 emissions, as are my colleagues, and mr langen in particular. every gram of co2 emitted has the same effect on the climate and should therefore be taxed at the same rate. the taxation must also be technology neutral. proportional taxation ensures that vehicles with higher co2 emissions are taxed at a higher rate than those with lower co2 emissions. this is crucial for climate protection. i also think that pollutants such as nox and particulate matter should be included in the tax base for motor vehicle taxation. this promotes environmentally friendly motor vehicles. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the amendments are adopted and i shall vote in favour of amendments nos 10 and 19 and the report as a whole in the plenary tomorrow.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to thank the rapporteur. i'm grateful to the commissioner for allowing her to be here today and for the preparation of the report. the report on the taxation of motor vehicles is a step in the right direction for two reasons. firstly, from an environmental point of view, it makes sense to include all emissions as a basis for taxing passenger cars. both co2 emissions, which are responsible for climate change, and emissions of nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, which are responsible for ozone formation and lung diseases, should be included in the taxation. it makes sense and it's the right thing to do. secondly, from the consumer and environmental point of view, the abolition of the registration tax is still welcome. the registration tax is responsible for the fact that motor vehicles produced in one eu member state are exported to another eu member state with registration taxes before being reimported by re-importers from the country of manufacture. this leads to redundant motor vehicle traffic and higher purchase prices. perhaps the abolition of registration tax in europe will stop this re-import trade and reduce the average age of the motor vehicle fleet, which will ultimately benefit the environment.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur on her report. i think you look very fit without makeup. the unification of the 25 different systems of taxation of cars in the eu will make it possible for the internal market to function better. we know that, and we have to admit it, ladies and gentlemen, to those who deny it: the proposal aims to eliminate double taxation in the case of crossborder movements of vehicles, and to eliminate distortions and inefficiencies. the partial registration taxes - we have heard this enough - naturally lead to the fact that citizens have to face considerable financial and administrative obstacles when they want to transfer a vehicle from one member state to another. so let us finally slaughter this sacred cow of admission taxes - also and perhaps especially because of the environmental aspect! tax measures are one of the three pillars of the community strategy to reduce co2 emissions from cars. this approach is good, but in my opinion it is too short-sighted. the tax should not be linked to co2 emissions only, but to pollutant emissions in general. because in addition to co2 - and this has been said many times already - there are also nitrogen oxides and, of course, particulate emissions. for this reason, these elements should also be taken into account in the tax. the abolition of the registration tax - i am convinced of this - will have positive environmental effects, because of course it will lead to a faster renewal of the vehicle fleet. the aim of reducing the cost of ownership is to encourage consumers to replace their old vehicles as quickly as possible with fuel-saving and less polluting vehicles. the tax base for motor vehicle taxes should therefore generally be emissions. and in order to ensure fair and neutral taxation, the tax rates must be defined in direct proportion to the emissions of pollutants. the annual emission-related control load must increase linearly with increasing emissions.
member of the commission. mr president, firstly i should like to thank the rapporteur and those meps who supported the abolition of registration taxes, the establishment of refund systems for car taxes and the application of fiscal measures to reduce co2 emissions from passenger cars and improve fuel economy. the latter implements the third-pillar measures provided for by the community 13 and 22 ask for a one-stop online solution in order to calculate registration taxes. amendments 34 and 37 ask for the scope to be extended to cover light duty vehicles. the commission, although sympathetic, considers that those measures would be difficult to adopt, mainly for reasons of subsidiarity of an economic or technical nature, or because they are beyond the scope of the proposed commission cannot support amendments 33, 35, 38, 39 or 40, either. i should like to express my thanks to the rapporteur and to parliament for the support and efforts to conciliate and strike a balance, taking into account the complexity of the issue of passenger car taxation.

been traded via market intermediaries, valued at more than eur 6 million. so, no one can say that the emissions trading system has failed. in 2006, the monthly trading volume has increased steadily, with volumes of 80 to 100 allowances in a busy month. a number of organised exchanges across europe are offering platforms for trading allowances and a number of other market intermediaries, such as brokers, are also active in the market. i would like to say a few words about the so-called ‘over-allocation’ of allowances to installations that are covered by the emissions trading system. it is a fact that we had about 3% more allowances allocated than actual emissions. that could be for various reasons, one of which could be that companies’ installations reacted to the emissions saving system and the obligations arising from the system, and they have made the most obvious and easiest reductions in emissions by improving energy efficiency, for example, or through other easy-to-take measures. it was the case in germany that we had a real reduction in emissions of carbon dioxide from installations. another reason could be the very mild winter that we had in 2005, which reduced the cost of heating, and – perhaps the main reason – the companies participating in the system were over-optimistic about their business growth and over-estimated their emissions, while the member states were complacent in accepting their figures. but, during the second trading period, we have made it quite clear to all member states that the 12 criteria of the directive should be kept, especially for those countries that did not contract to achieve their individual quota target, which will contribute to the overall target for the european union. also, the actual emissions that we have now should be taken into full account. i am going to be tough but fair with member states regarding the national allocation plans and am very glad for the support for this approach that has been obvious from your contributions today. the onus is firstly on governments to propose plans to the commission which ensure that the european union emissions trading system delivers its contribution to achieving our quota targets. at the same time, all stakeholders should engage in the process of improving and expanding the european union scheme, so as to secure a global carbon market that can deliver the emissions reductions necessary to tackle climate change. i would like to thank you for the rich debate with encouraging and important contributions and for your continued support for the fight against global warming and the threat posed to future generations.

question no 40 by mr van hecke (h-0613/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: american crude oil stocks us crude oil stocks rose by 1.4 million barrels to 347.1 million barrels in the week ending 16 june. american oil reserves are now at their highest level since may 1998. was this issue of the conspicuously high us oil reserves discussed at the annual eu-us summit in vienna? could it be that the us is hoarding the large reserves in order to keep the price of oil artificially high, with all the negative consequences for the european economy? what is the volume of us crude oil imports into the eu?
member of the commission. it is true that the united states’ reserves of crude oil and petroleum products have recently reached record levels. however, growing reserves of crude oil or petroleum products in any consumer country should normally not put upward pressure on the world oil price. it is a well-documented statistical belief among experts that prices of oil and oil products increasingly relax with growing levels of reserves in major consumer countries. that is because risk premium is an important element in the price of oil in the world markets and is priced in by market operators on the basis of evaluations of various risk factors. besides due political considerations, the probability of supply disruptions caused by insufficient spare capacities and reserve levels is a primary risk factor. hence comfortable or even record levels of crude oil or petroleum product reserves in important consumer countries such as the united states tend to reduce the perception of risk by a vast majority of operators in global oil markets. against this background, there was no need to discuss the question of levels of us crude oil and petroleum product reserves at the annual eu-us summit. as for the crude oil imports from the us to the european union, in the past three years the united states has supplied negligible quantities to the eu – less than one million tonnes per annum. that is less than 0.2% of eu’s total crude oil imports. in fact, the us itself is highly and increasingly dependent on crude oil imports.
member of the commission. it is true that given the situation of oil prices, a number of initiatives have been studied and included in the five-point plan presented by commissioner piebalgs since september 2005. these were further developed in the green paper on a european strategy for sustainable, competitive and secure energy. the commission aims gradually to reduce the eu’s dependency on imported oil by creating energy efficiency, on the one hand, and by replacing it, on the other hand, with other energy sources, including biomass and other renewables. it also aims at strengthening the producer-consumer dialogue with oil-producing countries in order to promote new exploration and development to meet rising global demand; promoting transparency and predictability of the oil market and being well prepared for emergencies, especially by ensuring that member states maintain the stocks as set out in the relevant eu legislation. it is important to know that all these policies – the ones on the use of fuel for cars, biomass and all the other measures just mentioned – will have a beneficial impact mainly in the medium to long term and not for the immediate future.
member of the commission. there is a number in the plan of commissioner piebalgs in this respect, so i would not, at this point, list which are priorities or otherwise. the issue of biofuel is one of the priorities in the european union. it has been discussed in the college of commissioners and in the council, as have other areas such as the use of wind and solar energy. what i can do, given that i am not an expert on this issue, is to make sure that there will be a written reply from my colleague with more detail on this issue.

product. we have two approaches. on the one hand, in the consultation document we are to bring forward on the smoke-free environment, we shall ensure that we refer to the classification of ets as a workplace, and perhaps we should consider including that as well. that would apply to the workplace, but it would be a first step. in conclusion, we will present every possible aspect in the paper which will be published soon – before the end of the year. however, in the meantime we will look at how to improve our existing legislation to ensure that we also have the legal competence to classify ets as such as a carcinogen.

know that pollution, poor nutrition, food allergies affect our physical and mental well-being. the effects of toxic chemicals on hormonal balance are evident. the nervous system disorders caused by environmental toxins and pesticides, and the relationship between attention deficit disorder and food intolerance, are finally in need of urgent analysis. we also know, for example, that gifted children and adolescents are mistakenly admitted to psychiatric hospitals because they are not recognized as gifted. this is another issue we need to address more. this is why i am concerned about the risk that the pharmaceutical industry will jump on this bandwagon and simply market drugs as the only solution. we need to face the problem that instead of further medicalisation and pathologisation of life cycles, a comprehensive approach to analysis and treatment is needed. it's not possible that children who are healthy, who are vibrant, who were once considered perfectly healthy, are now diagnosed with attention deficit disorder or zappel-philipp syndrome and are being treated with medication, it's not possible that adolescents are exposed to high levels of violence in the media and then labeled as mentally ill and treated with medication. we also have to ask ourselves if in our consumer society, there is a guarantee of happiness, and if it is not a false signal that every mood, every grief process that we have to go through naturally, must be treated with antidepressants. so my concern is that with this green paper, and also a white paper, we may be taking the wrong course here. we must analyse the causes and not rely on medication alone. the demand by parliament that medicines be used as a last resort when the causes of mental illness have been sufficiently elucidated must be at the very centre of attention, and we must not become mere handlers for the pharmaceutical industry and for the further pathologisation and medicalisation of life cycles and processes.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. our greatest asset is undoubtedly our health, both physical and mental. the focus of health policy has been and is all too often physical health. it is tangible, often visible, and often better to treat. moreover, maintaining physical health is costly, and many of the options available today are unaffordable. our health care system, from prevention to aftercare, is blowing up the public purse. it is not the intention of this report, for which i congratulate john bowis, that the european union should become active in the field of health. that is a matter for the member states and should remain so. but we support the commission's green paper, which is a discussion on the importance of mental health in the european union, a discussion on the need for a strategy and on possible priorities. we now know that good mental health is a prerequisite for good economic performance. but we must ask questions and seek answers. the question is, who is mentally ill? why do 13% of europeans seek professional help in this area? why do so many people in the european union commit suicide? the figures have been given; the hearing said 58,000 a year. why is society so sick? what are the causes? is our society in general too demanding? and then the big question: where do the disadvantaged people go? the discussion must be held to create awareness. one thing is certain: we also need to bring about social change to prevent these diseases. we know that it is difficult to deal with the harshness and competition of professional life. but it is much better to endure when one has a resting-place and a place to retreat. i see the family above all, offering the opportunity to rest and refuel. but families need help and support to fulfill all the important roles they are supposed to play in society. one thing is certain: humanity cannot be decreed by law, but it can and must be created so that humanity and health can grow in body and soul. so let us support our families, and if that is the intention of the report, then we have thought a lot of good.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i'll join john bowis in his best wishes. he is proving once again that health policy is a passion for him and not a duty. successful politics and successful psychotherapy have one thing in common. both require a great deal of openness, honesty, patience and commitment. we are debating an interesting, little-noticed and widespread issue in our european community: mental health. according to the who definition, health is a state of physical, mental and social well-being. in this order, the three objectives mentioned above are also realistic to achieve. when we look at mental health, we have to say that we have a dramatic increase in mental illness in the union. both pathogenetically and molecularly, we have a very colorful picture of disease patterns, causes, diagnoses and treatments. to name just a few: depression, schizophrenia, borderline psychosis, bulimia, anorexia, phobias, neuroses and mania. i do not want to go into toxicological and environmental causes here, that would be a separate dossier. i want to show how we as the european union can help in the context of prevention, how we can reduce the suffering of the sick, how we can detect the precursors of the disease in time and thus prevent the outbreak. just a few numbers: one in four will get sick; there are 58,000 suicides out of ten times that number of attempts, and suicide has something difficult, something demonic, something elusive about it, because we feel obligated to prevent it. mental disorder means stigma, mental illness is often associated with feelings of inferiority, mental institutions have often been abused for political purposes in the history of europe. we have the opportunity to call on our national governments to do more than they have done before. with this call we are not interfering with subsidiarity, but we want to give direction and to show a pan-european approach to more human dignity and less discrimination, e.g. healthy families as the basis for the upbringing of children, equal opportunities throughout the union, both within europe and within national borders. a strategy must include nationwide and local treatment options. a holistic treatment is required, i.e. body, soul and social environment. forced treatment can only be considered as ultima ratio, and alcohol, drug and medication abuse must be included and validated in an overall approach. the emphasis here is on prevention. today we are opening a new chapter in this report, which we hope will be followed up in a white paper shortly.

traders, where small claims are involved, it is practically impossible for lawyers and judges to apply 25 different legal systems in the european union in parallel, and if you count scotland, 26 this house. this is also the opinion of the main lawyers and one of the reasons why the ccbe, the association of european lawyers, has planned a conference in rome to be held in the autumn of this year and which will support the project ex post facto. it is therefore crucial for us to have not just a framework of reference that is exclusively concerned with consumer contract law issues, but a
