member of the commission. mr president, intellectual property rights (ipr) are at the heart of a knowledge-based economy. innovation is the key to europe’s prospects of becoming more competitive on a global level. protection of intellectual property is of crucial importance, because ipr not only rewards investment in new products and services but also ensures the transfer of technology stimulating further innovation. the recent consultation on the future of the patent system in europe delivered one simple message: the legal framework should offer an affordable patent protection for all businesses, small and big, ensure legal certainty and be applied for the benefit of all players. a solid legal framework is therefore essential. i must repeat that we need to keep up. compared to our major trading partners, europe is losing ground. the community patent remains blocked in the council, but recognising the economic importance of patents, i felt that it was not a good thing to leave the entire patent agenda in limbo. so, earlier this year, as you know, i launched a broad consultation of all interested parties on future patent policy in europe. the consultation has shown that industry favours the commission’s effort to simplify the patent system in europe and to make it more cost-effective. there are two major issues here: languages, or translation costs, on the one hand and the jurisdictional system on the other. there is strong support for the introduction of a community patent. however, industry is not enamoured of the political compromise reached in the council in 2003 on the community patent. it rejects the proposed solutions on both language and the jurisdictional system because they do not achieve the cost reductions and simplification of the patent system that industry is calling for. at the same time, there is also a strong call for the improvement of the existing european patent system, established by the munich convention, by the successful conclusion of a european patent litigation agreement (epla) on jurisdiction, and by the ratification and entry into force of the london agreement on language arrangements. it is interesting to note that no single initiative for the improvement of the eu patent system has received unanimous support from stakeholders. different stakeholders highlight different aspects, and many suggest that a package of different measures is needed, which should be implemented in parallel. i am therefore convinced that we need to take a multi-faceted approach. in order to succeed, we should tackle all the patent issues in one package. that package will have to respond to stakeholders’ criticism and needs. we will only succeed if we can demonstrate that what we propose will have added value compared to the status quo, in particular, regarding costs of patenting (translation costs) and legal certainty (jurisdictional system). we are currently working on the options for the way forward and will present them in a communication and action plan, which the commission should adopt before the end of this year. a key component of this work concerns the jurisdictional issue. at present, although business has a one-stop shop where it can acquire a patent (the epo), it may find itself defending the patent on several fronts at once. that is because the patents granted by the european patent office are in fact a bundle of national patents and can only be enforced by national courts. the possibility of multi-forum litigation concerning the same invention naturally adds cost, but even more importantly it creates uncertainty, as different courts in different countries can deliver diverging interpretations on the same patented invention. we need to tackle that issue as a matter of urgency. the current ‘patchwork’ may prevent patent holders from being able to enforce their rights and it discourages candidates, in particular smes looking for efficient and affordable patent protection, from using the european patent. europe is, at present, unable to offer innovative businesses an optimal solution when it comes to protecting their intellectual property. we cannot aspire to be the most competitive economy in the world if we do not find workable solutions for patent application and protection. the community patent and the initiatives to improve the european patent, that is, the london agreement on translations and the epla, are not mutually exclusive. they both aim for the same goal: a better, cheaper, more reliable patent system. that is why i want to pursue both. we face similar challenges in designing the jurisdictional arrangements for the community patent: we need to find a unified system that provides judicial independence and gives clarity and reliability to patent users while avoiding both over-centralisation and fragmentation. in order to achieve that objective, the community needs to get involved in the epla, which addresses shared responsibilities between member states and the community. it goes without saying that parliament will have to contribute when the community proceeds with the required proposals, in order to take this issue forward in the near future. i am aware of some critical voices against the epla. let me just say that i see the epla as a practical initiative to bring greater unity to the case law on patents in europe. and legal certainty is what our industry, big and small alike, need. there are hundreds of thousands of patents granted by the epo. even if we had a community patent, there would be a need to streamline the jurisdiction process for epo-granted patents. it is up to us to get involved in this initiative to ensure that it serves the competitiveness of our economy. i recognise that there are legitimate doubts and concerns: the cost of litigation under the epla, the impact of the rules of procedure, which we have yet to see, and the independence of the epla judges from the epo. but i am convinced that the best way to confront these problems is by engaging actively with the process and by securing an outcome that is satisfactory and fair to all concerned and in full conformity with eu law. of course, neither the community patent nor the epla are a panacea. there will always be businesses – the smaller ones – that prefer to deal with their national patent offices, or to use business models that do not rely on patents. we need to look at ways in which we can help and support them. and, of course, we need to ensure that large companies do not abuse their position, either by unfairly exploiting their own patents or by unfairly ignoring the patent rights of others. the consultation threw up many such issues, for example, the possible mediation mechanisms that could precede litigation, the need to create technology markets that would enable businesses to trade their ipr more successfully, and the idea of exchanging best practice between national patent offices, especially in terms of the special needs of smes. i will be responding to all these issues, in cooperation with my colleagues in the commission, and therefore intend to propose a comprehensive strategy. faced with a 21st-century global and knowledge-based economy, we urgently need to find a solution to the patent issue. i count upon parliament’s support in finding a comprehensive solution to these rather complex issues.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i have been one of the two rapporteurs in the european parliament's steering group for the lisbon process for two years. you know that we started the lisbon process together in 2000. since then, we have not tired of pointing out in statements by heads of state or government and in resolutions of parliament that the further development of the european patent system is one of the crucial conditions for achieving the objectives defined by lisbon. commissioner mccreevy has made a very strong point about the importance of this issue. the aim must be to obtain a simple, inexpensive, and if possible pan-european patent, which will give the opportunity to protect innovations in the internal market not only to large industry but also to smes in particular. smes are in fact the ones holding the most innovative patents. it is crucial that we bring about a change in the current fragmented patent landscape in europe with the aim of drastically reducing the costs of advice, litigation and translation, which are again particularly burdensome for smes. that is the crucial objective we must achieve. of course, you can already protect your inventions anywhere in the eu, but you have to do so in practically all the member states either directly through the national patent offices or indirectly through the european patent office, with the bundled patents that have been discussed here. in the event of a dispute or infringement, you are theoretically liable to sue in all these countries, pay legal costs, etc. this needs to be addressed and made sustainable and practical, especially for smes. this is where the single market must develop. under your predecessor, commissioner bolkestein, a laudable proposal for a uniform european patent regulation to create a community patent was launched. but if article 308 is the legal basis and unanimity in the council is required, then agreement is difficult. in this case, the agreement fails because of the language dispute. at present, there are 20 official languages required in the council. after the next round of expansion, it will be 22. the industry rightly says that no one needs such a patent. it's so exorbitantly expensive that you can't do anything with it and it has virtually no economic value. the competitiveness of the european patent would also leave us far behind in world standards and would not provide the necessary quality. such a patent would be interesting, if at all, at most to very large, rich companies that can afford it. it would be completely useless for the medium-sized enterprises. the regulation is therefore binding. the council is not moving. the idea i put forward of continuing with the harmonization, which you, commissioner, kindly included in the consultations, is also rejected by all the parties, especially after the experience we have had in the second reading of the directive on computer-implemented inventions, which showed that there was a danger that legislation would have been introduced which might not improve the current patent system but would have significantly worsened it. so we are not getting anywhere with harmonization either. what's left then? the only thing left to do is to go ahead and develop the existing patent system. there are, however, institutional problems, on the one hand, the european union's perfectly legitimate claim that the member states should not regulate areas which are, at any rate, partly within their sphere of jurisdiction and the internal market, but on the other hand, the member states' efforts to make progress. i am of the opinion that we must try to link and solve these two problems. i think one conceivable option is that the european union should be involved in some way - which must be negotiated - in the european patent convention and in return the european union should address the institutional concerns about the epla, the convention on the establishment of a dispute settlement system for european patents. this could be a possible way of improving the situation as long as it is not possible to reach agreement in the council on a community patent. as regards the public criticism of the lobby, i think that the claim that the introduction of a common european court, as defined by the epla, would make it easier to patent software is nonsense, to say the least. this is a mere conjecture, for which there is no evidence. in one case it is a question of procedural law, in the other of substantive law. epla is not more expensive either. you have to see that apples are being compared to pears. the epla does not have to be litigated in all the countries involved. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i would like to thank commissioner mccreevy very much for the way in which the consultation was conducted. i have heard from the commissioner's public comments that he seems to be drawing the right conclusions from the outcome of the consultation. i would like to say on my own behalf and on behalf of the great majority of my group that we support this line. there is no alternative. otherwise the great project of developing the european patent system is doomed to failure.
member of the commission. mr president, i have listened carefully to the debate this afternoon. we all agree that the situation is not perfect and we all know that there are different views as to the right solutions. i am convinced that in an ideal world the community patent is the solution, but in the real world there is no prospect of agreement on the community patent in the near future. so should i sit around doing nothing, just waiting for something to turn up? well, that would certainly be an easy way out, but it would also be grossly irresponsible, because nothing will happen unless we take the initiative. the consultation delivered some clear and important messages. there is an overwhelming desire for a patent system that is simpler and more cost-effective and maintains the highest standards in the quality of its examination and grant procedures. all the stakeholders went to great lengths to convey their views to us. now, quite rightly, they expect action. and i agree. i believe the time has come to make a concerted push to improve the patent system in europe. as policymakers and regulators, it is our duty. currently, we are at a standstill. we have to take the first most difficult step in one direction or another. there is no perfect solution. no single element will provide all the answers. we need to combine different instruments to meet the different needs of different stakeholders. as i said in my introductory remarks, the community patent and the epla are not mutually exclusive initiatives; indeed, our aim should be to ensure that they converge. in both cases our goal is the same: a better, cheaper, more reliable patent system. i am not blind to the potential drawbacks and dangers of the epla. but we have a better chance of getting the right outcome for europe’s business if we actively engage in the negotiation of the agreement. the patent strategy now contains more than just our future plans for a community patent and epla. there is a whole range of framing and supporting measures that we need to consider, most of them directed at smaller companies. our objective is to produce a system that meets the needs of all stakeholders at all levels – national, european and community –and provides a fair balance between the diverse interests involved. i would like to make one final point. as a politician for 30 years now, i am not easily surprised. but this week i have been mildly surprised. i was mildly surprised that the outline for our future strategy, which i set out in a speech in helsinki some weeks ago, has been used by some to make assertions that the commission wishes to bring the computer-implemented inventions question back on to the agenda. now i am used to hearing strong arguments and to links being made, but this one leaves me quite perplexed. i have stated before this house on various occasions that as long as i am commissioner for the single market and services the commission will not present any initiative and will not carry out any work on this. some might like that, others might disapprove. but this parliament rejected the common position last year. i respect and accept that decision and will do absolutely nothing to turn it around. let me reassure you that i am a man of my word. when drawing conclusions from the consultation exercise, computer-implemented inventions were not in any way on my mind. that will remain so for the rest of my mandate. president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, negotiations on the transfer of passenger data to the united states were concluded last week. the negotiating result avoided a no-deal situation between the eu and the us, which is very important. the presidency has received yesterday's letter from sophia in 't veld, rapporteur for the european parliament's pnr report, and we will return to the questions raised in it in more detail in writing as soon as possible. the negotiations resulted in the conclusion of a new interim pnr agreement. it is intended to replace the previous agreement of 2004, which was annulled by the ec court of justice in a judgment delivered last may. the negotiations were difficult, as the repeal of the previous agreement threatened to drive the eu and the us into a no-deal situation altogether. despite the difficulties, the negotiating mandate given by the council in june 2006 was upheld. the new contractual arrangement ensures both a level of protection of personal data equivalent to that of the previous agreement and the continuity of transatlantic air traffic. the arrangement therefore allows for the continued transfer of passenger data to the us authorities while ensuring an adequate level of data protection in the processing of the data, in line with the commitments previously made by the us customs and border protection. the committee of permanent representatives closely followed the progress of the negotiations and discussed the outcome and content of the negotiations as early as 6 october. coreper expressed its support for the initialling of the negotiating text. the outcome of the consultations was reported to the ministers of justice at the justice and home affairs council, which began immediately after coreper. the provisional agreement resulting from the negotiations shall apply from the date of its signature. the eu's signature of the agreement will be discussed by coreper tomorrow and the aim is for the council to give the signature powers as soon as possible. the interim agreement will run until july 2007. during this period, the parties are to agree on a more permanent arrangement for the transfer of pnr data. the aim is to start these negotiations as soon as possible. the agreement was reached after tough negotiations. the us wish in the negotiations was to change the previous arrangement to better reflect the changed operating environment. the main challenge of the negotiations was to respond to the changes in us legislation and the organisation of government since 2004, while maintaining the principles of european data protection standards. in addition to the actual text of the agreement, the negotiations also covered a letter from the us negotiators to the commission and the presidency on the interpretation of the commitments on the use of pnr data. the eu will take note of the letter, but it will not become part of the agreement. the outcome of the negotiations has been a success for a number of reasons. first, the purpose of the tfa is to ensure the safety of air passengers. this is of the utmost importance. secondly, i would like to emphasize that the commitments previously made by the us administration regarding the use of pnr data will continue to apply. the aim is to guarantee the same level of protection for citizens' pnr data as under the previous system. the agreement includes a provision that the us department of homeland security (dhs) is considered to provide adequate protection for pnr data transferred from the eu. this is based on the fact that dhs continues to comply with the commitments made in 2004. the new agreement increases the number of authorities with electronic access to pnr data, due to the reorganisation of the us administration. however, these authorities are defined in the contract. thirdly, i am pleased that the new agreement will also include the same 34 fields of pnr data as in the previous arrangement. fourthly, the new agreement will ensure legal certainty for citizens and the continuation of transatlantic flights. the new agreement will also ensure the operational conditions for airlines. we have other good news for the airlines. in the context of these negotiations, the united states has committed to allowing the testing of systems whereby airlines can themselves store pnr data in us authorities' databases to begin as early as the middle of this year. this has been a very important goal for us. negotiations on a new, more permanent pnr system to replace the interim agreement reached in july 2007 will be launched in the near future. we have also agreed that the question of the retention and destruction of data will be settled only in the context of these negotiations on the pnr system. so we'll get back to that very soon. i am sorry, mr president, that i cannot be present for this debate because i have to leave parliament at 6.20 p.m. as previously agreed and unfortunately the plane will not wait more than a minute.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, first of all i can fully agree with the positive assessment made by the presidency of the validity of this agreement, which has a limited duration until july 2007 but which has the advantage of ensuring legal continuity in a highly sensitive area and allows airlines to ensure proper processing of personal data of citizens travelling to and from the united states of america without interruption of air traffic. this agreement is part of a larger commitment. i can say without any doubt that during the extremely complex negotiations that have taken place, both the european institutions, the presidency and the commission, and the united states have confirmed their willingness to start joint work immediately, which has a wider scope and therefore includes the reaffirmation of a common will, of the european union and the united states, to work together towards a definitive agreement - the agreement that will replace this temporary agreement, that is to say the one that will come into force after august 2007 - and to tackle together the wider field of common cooperation against terrorism, together with the protection of the individual rights of individuals. it is a much broader political perspective in which, as i have said on many other occasions, i believe that the involvement of the european parliament is politically necessary, even if the procedures will necessarily fall within the so-called 'third pillar' following the decision of the court of justice. it is clear that the content of this agreement must be studied in depth: i know that many honourable members have studied it carefully. i should like to make a few brief remarks: firstly, this agreement does not allow for the exchange of more data. it allows for the transmission of data to additional agencies, in addition to the border protection authority and the customs authority, in full compliance with comparable rules on the protection of personal data. this is not the result of a change in the agreement because, as you know very well, we have clarified the meaning of the undertakings. after 2004, there was a change in the structure of the agencies as a result of domestic us legislation. before that, at the beginning of 2004, there were only the customs agency and the border protection agency. today, for example, we have a new interlocutor, namely the department of homeland security, which we could not, at least in the interpretation of the undertakings, disregard. it also includes the agencies mentioned above, so it was impossible not to mention them. what is the characteristic of this interpretation? on the one hand, the existence of different agencies is acknowledged, on the other hand, it is established that the customs and border protection agency retains the same function as before, being the direct recipient of the data transfer. the other agencies can obtain from this first agency, on a case-by-case basis, the data they need. so there is no direct access to data by other agencies in the first place but a transmission to other agencies on the basis of a request. what is the request that justifies the transmission? as has already been said, this is a case-by-case request. we have specified that the concept of 'case by case' means either the indication of a concrete threat or the indication of a flight or a specific flight or a flight route, for which there is an indication justifying the request for data. this request for data is justified only, as it was before again nothing has changed for reasons of anti-terrorist investigation. we have therefore specified that us agencies with investigative tasks other than counter-terrorism investigations cannot have access, even on the basis of an indirect request. the other important element in my view is the impossibility of direct access and the change in the way data is accessed. many honourable members have often pointed out in the past the malfunctioning or the lack of guarantees of the so-called 'pull' system, that is to say the system which allows information to be extracted directly from databases. as a result, we have asked for and obtained that the system be changed and replaced, as has been expressly requested on numerous occasions by authoritative members of parliament, by the 'push' system. push means, as the word clearly says, that data is not extracted but is provided on demand. it was agreed that the new mechanism, as we wrote in the accompanying letter from the united states, will be operational no later than december this year, that is to say, within a month and a half at the latest. the mechanism will first be tested to see if it works, but in any case it will be operational - i repeat - at the end of this year. a specific obligation was also reiterated, namely to respect - recalling in this connection article 6 (2) of the treaty on european union - the fundamental right of individuals to the processing of personal data. we have inserted a reference to article 6 of the treaty on european union itself, replacing the reference to a data protection directive, because the court of justice had ruled that, in matters of security, that directive is not directly applicable. an important european legislative reference would therefore have been lost. we have replaced it with a more general - and in my view even more binding - reference to article 6 of the eu treaty, which refers to the fundamental rights of individuals. in conclusion, the commitment of the american authorities is to continue to guarantee, also by the department of homeland security, an adequate level of protection of the data processed and therefore, of course, the possibility of reviewing the application of this agreement, as, moreover, already established in the agreement previously in force. the last aspect concerns the confirmation of the data retention period, a subject which has not been touched upon. it's true. there was a request to retain data for a longer period than the agreement in force provided for or was in force. the request was not granted, firstly because the agreement expires in july 2007 and secondly because we considered that a subject as sensitive as the retention period could be the subject of subsequent negotiations. i can assure you that the commission intends to start these negotiations in january 2007 so that by the end of july 2007 they will be sufficiently mature to reach a final agreement.

the commission has done a good job of systematising a debate which has been very - i would say - wild. in essence, the commission has made the following economic consideration: it first examines six occupational groups: lawyers, notaries, engineers, architects, pharmacists and accountants. it defines five restrictions on competition: fixed prices, price recommendations, competition rules, advertising rules and the whole range of conditions for access, forms of company or merger possibilities. it has compared this with four major groups of consumers - public budgets, large enterprises, small and medium-sized enterprises and private consumers - and has then admitted that there are certain special arrangements here due to asymmetries: in the field of market transparency, as regards external effects, or in the question of the extent to which a public good is provided here. we welcome this systematization, it is necessary for the course of the discussions, it makes sense that parliament should take a position on this debate at this time. we have tried to give some support, but also to contribute to the differentiation of this debate. first of all, there is a broad consensus on the issue of subsidiarity. the european community will have the difficult task of coordinating its action with the member states. secondly, we have called for - and i think this is very important, also as a consequence of the debate on the services directive - that the objectives of liberalisation be clearly stated and also empirically substantiated. what growth can be expected from what liberalisations? what employment effects are expected? it is also important to have a clear statement of the figures, otherwise the member states will not be able to accept it. we have stated that we see a parity of self-government compared to state regulation. we said we think we need to differentiate the systematics. for example, public budgets must be differentiated in our view, because it is a difference whether a small municipality issues a call for tenders or whether a national government issues a call for tenders for professional services. we have said that while we recognize the geographical and traditional features, we see them as special arrangements which must not be allowed to continue, that the possibilities for liberalization and growth in these areas must not be constantly questioned. we have made it quite clear that we regard special arrangements for mergers and promotions as a matter of concern. we have said that we want to differentiate clearly certain restrictions of competition according to consumer groups. and we have said recently that, in the field of voluntary work in particular, we very much welcome the voluntary code of conduct for the voluntary service sector. the point is that we want to tell the commission that we welcome these considerations. but we also want to make it clear that we need to systematize and further differentiate in these areas. only then will we achieve the necessary acceptance in the nation states.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs mccarthy, warmly for her work and her efforts to bring this project, which is very important for our citizens, to a satisfactory conclusion. like the rapporteur, i would also like to thank the former united kingdom presidency, particularly baroness ashton, for the work done in moving ahead with this important project. as you know, this regulation on the european order for payment procedure aims at facilitating the mass recovery of uncontested claims in europe. it is thus very important, as it will allow all creditors in europe to recover their claims in a uniform way and more rapidly and cheaply than in ordinary court proceedings. it will also alleviate the burden on the courts by removing from ordinary proceedings those claims where the debtor does not contest the debt. the proposal potentially concerns all citizens and economic operators in europe. a european order for payment can circulate freely in europe and will be enforced automatically. there will be therefore no need to request a declaration of enforcement – the ‘exequatur’ – in the member state of enforcement. concerning the amendments, i can accept the third amendment as proposed. on the second amendment, i can accept the compromise amendment on the comitology procedure, which is in line with the council decision taken in july 2006. on the first amendment, while i understand the reason and the concern expressed by the committee, i think that we should not at this stage reopen the question of the definition of a cross-border case, adopted at first reading by the council and the european parliament. at the same time, i can confirm that the commission is available and willing to look more closely into the effects of the regulation for parties domiciled in third countries and, in particular, states of the european economic area. i am ready to give very careful consideration to any proposals.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission is not the rapporteur, mrs mccarthy, has essentially discussed the economic significance. this european order for payment procedure represents a significant advance in the field of cross-border enforcement, in particular for the business sector, which has a particular interest in the rapid determination of the existence of claims, the rapid issuance of a title and the enforceability of that right in the debtor's country without any further costly steps. but - and this is my main point - crossborder legal relationships will also become increasingly important for private individuals. it is particularly difficult for private individuals to assert claims across borders, whether or not they are contested. we are dealing with unchallenged claims today. that's why this first step is important. in particular, private individuals, for whom the legal enforcement of claims is already complicated, have great problems with cross-border claims. the present instrument will be a relief to them. a form which can be filled in by a private individual will make it possible to make claims without great expense and with relative ease. another aspect: there is always talk of the economy, of creditors, but too little of debtors. we have introduced systems in the member states of the european union - including my own country - which make the securitisation of such claims extremely cost-effective for the debtor. the debtor who is willing but may not be able to pay can agree with the creditor who has an interest in having the limitation period overruled by the title to a reasonable installment payment, and thus less costs will be incurred because no contentious proceedings have taken place. it is therefore in the interest of all concerned that we establish a fast, efficient and cost-effective crossborder procedure.

member of the commission. sweden is currently one of the 11 member states with a derogation from the adoption of the single currency. member states with a derogation are obliged to adopt the euro as their currency and to do so they must endeavour to meet the convergence criteria laid down in the treaty. however, the treaty does not set explicit deadlines for member states to comply with this obligation. in its 2004 convergence report, the commission concluded that sweden fulfilled the criteria on price stability, the government budgetary position and the criterion on long-term interest rate convergence. however, the commission concluded in the same convergence report that sweden did not fulfil the exchange rate criterion, which requires that the country concerned has observed, without severe tensions and for at least two years prior to the examination, the normal fluctuation margins established by the exchange rate mechanism of the european monetary system. furthermore, the commission noted in the 2004 convergence report that the swedish legislation was not fully compatible with articles 108 and 109 of the treaty. in the light of this assessment, the commission concluded that sweden's status as a member state with a derogation in this area should not be changed. in accordance with the treaty, the commission and the european central bank will publish the next convergence report before the end of this year. the new member states have committed themselves to adopting the euro as soon as they meet the criteria laid down in the treaty. slovenia will join the euro area on 1 january 2007, cyprus and malta want to join on 1 january 2008, slovakia on 1 january 2009 and other member states, which had previously defined target figures, are in the process of revising them. in any event, as i said at the beginning of my reply, with the exception of the two states with a derogation clause, namely the united kingdom and denmark, the other members of the european union which have not yet adopted the single currency, and which are in that situation of derogation, have the obligation to adopt it and to prepare to meet those criteria, but there is no mandatory date for them to do so.

on this proposal, which has enabled us to reach agreement with the council at first reading. this is an important directive. the aim is to restrict the placing on the market and use of perfluorinated octansulfonates (pfos) and related substances. these substances are persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic. they have the potential to lead to unacceptable risks to human health and the state of the environment. the proposed directive is based on targeted risk assessments and impact assessments of possible measures. extensive consultation with all concerned parties was included. the directive prohibits in principle the placing on the market and use of pfos and related substances, with very limited exceptions. derogations are provided for essential uses in small quantities which, according to the opinion of the scientific committee on health and environmental risks of the commission, do not pose unacceptable risks. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the use of biofuels in the production of biofuels is not restricted to the production of biofuels. the proposed directive not only protects human health and the environment but will also strengthen the internal market by introducing harmonised rules for the marketing and use of pfos and related substances throughout the community. with regard to the derogations contained in the proposal, i agree that the use of pfos and related substances in photoresists, photographic materials, hexavalent chromium and other metal galvanisation and hydraulic fluids should continue to be allowed because the risks associated with these uses are acceptable, because there are no equivalent alternatives and because it is not certain that the toxicological profiles of possible alternatives are more favourable. as regards fire-fighting foams, i can agree that the placing on the market and use of new fire-fighting foams should be prohibited and that a period of 54 months should be allowed for the continued use of existing stocks. on the other hand, i do not want to support at this stage an extension of the proposed restrictions to other perfluorinated alkyl compounds such as pfoa, as this is premature in the absence of a completed risk assessment and sufficient knowledge of current uses and alternatives, but we can return to this subject. in conclusion, i would like to say that the process of change has benefited greatly from the close cooperation between parliament, the council and the commission. the commission can therefore agree to all the compromise proposals proposed by the rapporteur, mr schlyter.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. first of all, i should like to thank mr schlyter for his very thoughtful report. pfos, a halogenated hydrocarbon, is a toxic substance to humans that is both carcinogenic and herbicide-damaging. there are no scientific limit values for this category of substances, only empirical threshold values. these substances are not biodegradable, they are fat soluble and they last, once produced, practically forever. man, too, can hardly excrete them once they have been ingested. pfoa is very likely to have a very similar or identical effect from a medical and toxicological point of view, although the scientific data are not yet conclusive. i think that is where reach will come in, and the substitution principle will play a crucial role, although i personally have always had reservations. i am not going to go into the details of the commission's proposals, but i would like to say that the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. i am appalled by the results of measurements of these chemicals in both marine and river fish. we are now going beyond the original proposal of the commission and the council with good reason and good conscience. the threshold is being lowered massively by almost two tenths. the exemptions for chromium plating have been significantly reduced. the exception for fire extinguishers has been deleted in a sensible way, since unlimited quantities can be released into the environment. the exception for closed systems has been deleted, as it is difficult to prove leakage. i would like to thank you for the good cooperation and, above all, for the speed with which we worked out a workable compromise within three months.
member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs muscardini, and the committee on international trade for the excellent work that they have done on this important issue. the european union is a major exporter worldwide and this leaves us exposed to trade defence actions by third countries. when such actions are taken in compliance with wto rules, we cannot and should not complain, and we do not. however, that is not always the case and these actions can easily become a serious and unjustified impediment to our legitimate market access opportunities. therefore, we must closely monitor third-country actions against our exports and intervene to minimise the negative impact of such actions on our companies. and we should certainly be vigilant. whenever possible we favour the diplomatic route, which is the quicker and the most efficient way to solve those issues when we have partners who wish to solve them. but when diplomacy fails, we do not hesitate to resort to wto panels, as it is our right to do. both the diplomatic and the litigation approaches have met with notable successes. take, for example, the indian cases mentioned in the report. diplomacy has resulted in the removal of no fewer than 12 measures. we also hope for significant success on the agricultural products cases that you have identified. it is well known that the united states is a recurrent problem for us in this context. it is pro-free trade, but its use of the trade defence instrument is seen by many as unreasonable on certain issues. this has been particularly marked in the steel sector, where we have been arguing against certain practices for years on a large number of their dumping and subsidy measures. we have had a considerable success in geneva but, frankly, it is a long hard slog even getting them to implement the remedies to the disputes which they have lost. we cannot solve everything through diplomacy or litigation. this is why we welcome your support for the proposals we have tabled in the doha round to strengthen the rules and the disciplines governing the use of anti-dumping and countervailing measures. the round is suspended, something i deeply deplore and regret, but we are fighting hard to get it restarted. for trade defence this would allow us to seek improved disciplines along the lines of the eu practice in this field, making it more difficult for countries to abuse the system, which i am afraid some are only too prepared to do. we need tightened disciplines in the anti-dumping system. we need greater transparency in the operation of trade defence instruments. we need less arbitrariness on the part of governments. such behaviour simply discredits the rules. it brings the system into disrepute and it does not reflect credit on the multilateral trade system and its principal institution, the wto. we agree with you that the dispute settlement mechanism is an essential feature of the wto system, which needs protecting, but we are working hard to improve it so that faster remedies can be achieved. we will take the opportunity of any bilateral trade agreement with third countries to ensure that our partner countries take on specific obligations on the fair use of trade defence instruments. this is not an alternative to strengthening and improving the rules at the wto. on the contrary, it underpins that. it is a way of getting insurance in place, so that we can use all available methods to bring reason and discipline to the operation of these instruments. this would particularly apply for those countries that abuse them the most. good practices are as important as good rules. that is why the commission’s departments devote a great deal of time and resources to providing technical assistance to third countries that become new users of trade defence instruments. our aim is that they should apply them in a fair and balanced manner and in accordance with our own high standards. these efforts seem to bear fruit. the end of 2005 saw a welcome change from the trend of previous years, with a significant fall in the number of trade defence cases initiated against community exporters, from 33 in 2004 to 19 in 2005. market access, including a fair and proper implementation of wto trade defence instruments by our trading partners, features high on our priority list and we will continue to take any steps required to ensure that our exports are not unduly penalised. of course it is difficult to follow each and every case with our current resources and i would certainly like to do more for our exporters, in particular small and medium-sized companies, which often have little experience in this area. the eu must remain an example that others can follow. as the report recalls, we are viewed as a moderate user of trade defence instruments. that reputation is deserved and that must remain so. it is in that spirit that i recently launched a reflection process on how europe’s trade defence instruments such as the anti-dumping instrument operate in the modern global economy. a broad public consultation will take place early in 2007, based on a green paper expected in the coming months. this consultation will allow the commission to draw on a wide range of views and identify whether there is scope to improve our rules and practices further. our trade defence instruments can make an important contribution to ensuring both free and fair trade, thereby stimulating our competitiveness. this will involve strong and close cooperation with all stakeholders, including member states and industry, and, i would add, the support and involvement of the european parliament.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the council is very concerned about the recent environmental disaster in côte d'ivoire involving the probo koala. as the president of the council, finland considers it very important that this regrettable case be thoroughly investigated. it once again brought the world's attention to the serious threats posed by waste shipments to developing countries. this is a problem that must be addressed with decisive action. the european union has indicated its readiness to assist, together with the united nations, in protecting human health and the environment where the impact of the case has been particularly severe. recent events in west africa have also reminded us of the importance of effectively implementing the agreements on the control of transboundary movements and treatment of hazardous waste. these include the basel convention and its 1995 amendment, the marpol convention on the prevention of marine pollution by ships and regional maritime protection agreements. the basel convention amendment prohibited the export of hazardous waste from eu and oecd countries and liechtenstein to other countries. of course, it is equally important to ensure that agreements are also respected. the 8th conference of the parties to the basel convention on the control of transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal will be held in nairobi at the end of november. the positions of the european union for this conference are currently being prepared by the council on all the issues on the agenda. these include illegal waste shipments, ship dismantling, contract financing, synergy between the waste and chemicals cluster and monitoring of the strategic plan for the implementation of the convention. as part of this preparatory work, the environment council held a thorough debate on 23 october, the day after, at the end of which the president drew conclusions on the eu's preparations for the basel cop. the conclusions stress the importance of taking decisive and effective action to tackle illegal transboundary movements of hazardous waste. it is important that as many other countries as possible, in addition to the current ratifiers, ratify the amendment to the ban on the export of hazardous waste so that it can enter into force worldwide as soon as possible. as you know, the ban is already in force in all eu member states, as it has been fully implemented by the waste shipment regulation. almost all eu countries have also ratified the amendment. the revised eu waste shipment regulation, which will come into force next july, also contains provisions to improve cooperation on its implementation at both member state and eu level. there is also a directive on port reception facilities for ship-generated waste and cargo residues, compliance with which may also be a matter of concern in the probo koala case. in a debate held the other day, the environment ministers also stressed that effective enforcement of existing legislation is a priority for the eu. the key to preventing illegal waste shipments is to increase the harmonisation of environmental and maritime legislation, particularly at international level, and to improve cooperation between public authorities. the most important thing is that all types of waste are treated in an environmentally acceptable way, no matter where it occurs. this must also be the primary objective when scrapping ships. the conclusions of the chair also stress the need for external assistance to help developing countries implement the basel convention and manage waste in an environmentally sound manner. developing countries should also integrate waste management into their poverty reduction and sustainable development strategies. the presidency also met the cote d'ivoire delegation in the context of the environment council, from which it received up-to-date information on the case. the scale of the environmental disaster is enormous: in addition to the loss of many lives, the acute health effects are extensive. disasters also have significant ecological impacts, on livelihoods, on human living conditions and on the functioning of communities. the main priority is to clean up contaminated areas and sewage systems and to mitigate the damage caused to citizens and businesses. in côte d'ivoire, both international and national investigations, including criminal investigations, are ongoing. in some member states, too, such as the netherlands and estonia, criminal investigations have been launched to fully investigate the circumstances surrounding the probo koala case. i now turn to the oral question by mr florenz, chairman of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety: the member states of the european union have attached importance to the development of eu-wide legislation and cooperation in the prevention, investigation and prosecution of environmental crime. environmental crimes are typically international in nature, as the effects of illegal emissions extend far beyond national borders. however, as the honourable member states in his question, the council framework decision of 27 january 2003 on the protection of the environment by criminal law was annulled by the court of justice of the european communities on 13 september 2005. on 25 november 2005, the commission sent a communication to the european parliament and the council on the consequences of the judgment of the court of justice of the european communities. the court's judgment and the commission's communication were discussed at the informal meeting of justice and home affairs ministers in vienna in january 2006 and were discussed by the council in brussels on 21 february last spring. in those discussions, the commission indicated that it wished to continue to consider the procedure to be followed in respect of previous framework decisions adopted by the council, which might need to be reviewed in the light of the court's decision. that consideration also applies to the framework decision which the court of justice annulled. the council is therefore awaiting the commission's reaction: it may submit an amended version of the proposal for a directive it adopted in 2001 and amended in 2002, or it may submit a completely new proposal.
member of the commission. mr president, the recent incident of toxic waste dumping in côte d'ivoire has dramatic consequences. at least 10 people are dead, while thousands have been poisoned and hospitalized. although the actual circumstances surrounding this heinous environmental crime have yet to be clarified, the need to strictly enforce the ban on the export of hazardous waste to africa has become much more urgent. the commission, in cooperation with the member states, the united nations and the ivorian authorities, is seeking in various ways to make good the damage caused, as well as to take appropriate action to deal with any illegal activities that may have taken place. when the incident occurred, commission representatives - and in particular teams from the member states - were on the scene to help the victims and to help protect the natural environment. the commission is closely following developments in côte d'ivoire and is in constant contact with the authorities in the country. on monday i also met with the presidency and the delegation from the ivory coast, which included three ministers. the institutions and the member states of the european union must consider all possible means of supporting the victims in côte d'ivoire and contribute as much as possible to the elimination of pollution. criminal investigations are currently under way in several member states with which we are in contact. i myself after his return . the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if we look beyond the ivory coast incident, we find that there is a serious gap in the member states' compliance with the european union regulation on shipments of waste. this regulation contains clear rules prohibiting the export of hazardous waste to developing countries. these rules are to be tightened up and, from july next year, will impose on member states the obligation to carry out on-the-spot checks and inspections and to cooperate in cases of illegal shipments of waste. however, the mere existence of rules means nothing if they are not properly applied in practice. the gaps in the legislation must be filled by strict complementary measures to ensure its proper application. environmental crime is one of the most serious problems facing the community. the environmental damage it can cause is enormous. often they are even part of international organized crime, making their suppression difficult but imperative. the provision of effective penalties, including criminal penalties, is essential for the proper application of community environmental legislation. this is precisely why action at community level is urgently needed. in 2001 the commission put forward a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment through criminal law. the proposal was to establish a minimum number of criminal offences relating to the environment throughout the community and to provide for effective criminal penalties in all member states for such offences. it is regrettable that the council did not adopt the commission's proposal at that time. the proposal was based on article 175 of the treaty and was to be adopted by the co-decision procedure. the council did not agree with the legal basis and decided to adopt a framework decision on the basis of the third pillar instead of the directive we had proposed. in the european commission's view, this choice of instrument was not legally correct and would have made it impossible to monitor the transposition of the framework decision into national law and its implementation by the member states. in clear contrast to the council, the european parliament fully supported the commission's proposal and also supported the commission in the case when it was referred to the court of justice of the european communities. i would like to stress the particular importance of this good cooperation between our institutions and i hope that we will continue to do so in the further development of the matter. the european court of justice has now clarified that criminal measures necessary to ensure the effective implementation of environmental policy can be adopted under the first pillar. the council framework decision infringed the powers of the community under the treaty and had to be annulled. the european commission is particularly pleased with the court's decision. it is not a decision which regulates a mere technical point, it is of crucial importance for clarifying the rules of the treaty as regards the demarcation between the first and third pillars. it has a great institutional impact, because it clarifies that the measures in question must be adopted by the co-decision procedure, which means the full participation of parliament. in addition, under the first pillar, national implementing measures are subject to review by the court of justice of the european communities, whereas under the third pillar measures are not. a directive on the protection of the environment through criminal law - under the first pillar - will bring about better protection of the environment, while at the same time being a more democratic method in the legislative process. unfortunately, in the meantime, precious time has been lost. environmental crimes continue to be committed and we must put in place the necessary legal measures to deal with them. we have analysed and discussed in the commission the various options for following up the court's ruling. we considered two options in particular: either to leave the 2001 commission proposal as it is and invite the other institutions to continue the co-decision procedure, or to submit a new commission proposal. we preferred the second option, in order to take account of the court's decision. the original proposal dates back to 2001, since then there have been many changes in environmental legislation and therefore the proposal needs to be adapted accordingly. finally, new developments have taken place in the field of european cooperation in criminal matters, which must also be taken into account in the proposal. we must ensure that the proposal is consistent with other criminal legislation which has been adopted at european level. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the legal framework for the protection of the environment. the first step was, as i said, to analyse in detail the court's decision and its consequences and to make a thorough comparison of the various legislation already in force. we then carried out an impact assessment study comparing the pros and cons of the different options. after that, the proposal will be finalised and i hope it will be adopted before the end of 2006.

question no 1 by mrs panayotopoulos-cassiotou (h-0779/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: service provision and freedom of movement for families with childrenan increasing number of european families complain that they are discriminated against in the provision of services and exercise of the right to freedom of movement in the eu because they have children under 15 with them. in greek press reports it was presented as positive that children should not have access to publicly accessible commercial establishments such as hotels and restaurants. what measures will the council take to put an end to this discrimination and this form of ageism against children, young people and their families? is there any plan to harmonise the rules governing the provision of services and the guarantee of free movement in the eu in order to ensure that the rights of european minors and their families are not infringed?
president of the council. mr president, we have legislation to prevent discrimination against all groups of people and all age groups, such as the directive on racial equality and the directive on employment and occupational discrimination. they include provisions, inter alia, on the prohibition of discrimination in most everyday situations. as regards the examples of restaurant culture given by the honourable member in his question, it must be remembered that not only the council, but also the citizens of the member states as consumers and, ultimately, the people who pay for these services, have a significant influence on the way in which the culture develops from the point of view of families with children.
president of the council. mr president, there has of course been a great deal of discussion in the field of advertising to children, particularly about marketing and what kind of marketing and in what circumstances is appropriate when targeted at children. but as regards the example of hotels, which the honourable member has mentioned, i would like to return to what i said in my previous answer, namely that, of course, consumer organisations and paying customers have a say in the type of services provided.
question no 2 by mr ortega (h-0781/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: strengthening frontexthe european agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders (frontex), which was set up last year, has started its work with limited resources and obvious weaknesses. does the council intend to adopt measures to increase the effectiveness of its activities either through intergovernmental cooperation or by providing it with additional community funds?
president of the council. first of all, mr president, it is of course a positive thing to hear that frontex has done well. while acknowledging that it has also had some problems or at least challenges, it must be remembered that the agency is very young in its establishment and is at the same time in the process of building its own administration and taking care of the agency's tasks. it has also been involved in a very large number of operations both in the mediterranean and elsewhere. of course, the scale and effectiveness of this follow-up also depends on additional funding.
president of the council. mr president, one very important issue relating to this illegal immigration, or immigration as a whole, is of course our cooperation with these countries of origin and transit. the union has recently been trying to pay particular attention to the intersections between migration and development, with the idea that we must be able to intensify our cooperation with countries of origin in order to reduce the pressure on migration there too. of course, part of this cooperation with the countries of origin is to inform them of the possibilities or impossibilities that exist. the next eu-africa high level meeting will be held in tripoli in november and will focus on migration.
president of the council. mr president, the ability of frontex and the union in general to act in these situations of illegal immigration naturally depends very much on the level of commitment of the member states. this has been the subject of much discussion at various levels of the union in recent times, most recently at the eu summit in lahore last friday, but this debate is still in progress and it is therefore still difficult to give a precise answer to this question.
question no 3 by sarah ludford (h-0783/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: exchange of information on convicted paedophiles how far has the proposal for a council framework decision on the recognition and enforcement of professional bans in the european union based on convictions for sexual offences against children progressed in the council? this framework decision would allow, in cases where pedophiles or child molesters are prohibited from working with children after having been convicted of a sexual offence or of engaging in child pornography in a member state, the information to be shared so that the names of these persons can be entered in other national sex offender registers and the ban can be enforced across the eu. why has the council apparently not been able to agree on this important proposal, which the european parliament endorsed in june 2006 and which would serve as a practical example to the citizens of europe of the valuable role the eu plays in fighting crime and increasing security? has the council departed from its stated objective of giving priority to combating the sexual abuse of children?
president of the council. mr president, of course this question time is not about what i can personally approve, but about what kind of debate and decision-making is being sought in the council. but the council is now going to proceed in this respect too, in accordance with the so-called principle of assimilation, i.e. that the member state would be obliged to attach to a foreign criminal conviction the same legal effects as to a national conviction, but in the end this is linked to much wider cooperation in the field of justice and home affairs and to the way in which mutual recognition of convictions and extradition are otherwise proceeded with.

question no 7 by mr van hecke (h-0791/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: increased press censorship in china recently, the chinese government has again tightened its grip on the foreign press. she must now abide by strict internal regulations. the news disseminated by foreign press offices is first controlled and, if necessary, censored (literally) in order not to endanger the stability, national unity and sovereignty of the country. this is another violation of human rights. the european commission has already expressed its concern and has promised to raise the matter in future contacts. will the council follow suit and what measures does it propose to take against this totally unjustified censorship of the press?
president of the council. mr president, the council is concerned, as is the rapporteur, about the tightening of press censorship in china. the european union has systematically and repeatedly called on china to ratify the international covenant on civil and political rights, which contains provisions on freedom of expression, and to lift travel restrictions on foreign journalists and other requirements for interviewing citizens in china, in all the biannual eu-china human rights dialogue rounds. this issue was raised at the eu-china human rights dialogue round in beijing on 19 october.
president of the council. mr president, firstly, on the occasion of the asem summit in helsinki on 10 september, the foreign ministers of the presidency and china met. the question of freedom of the press was then recently raised in public and was at the heart of the foreign ministers' discussions. it could therefore be said that the european union's reaction is as rapid and as typical as it is in its discussions with other countries. the eu-china summit was also held in early september and human rights issues in general were also discussed.
question no 8 by brian crowley (h-0793/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: community agency for fundamental rightscan the european council make a statement on the state of play in the creation of the new community agency for fundamental rights? can the council give information on the possible powers of this agency?
president of the council. mr president, at its meeting in june 2006, the european council noted progress in the negotiations on the proposal for a council regulation establishing the european union agency for fundamental rights and the proposal for a council decision authorising the european union agency for fundamental rights to carry out activities in the fields covered by the third pillar of the treaty on european union, namely cooperation in the field of justice and home affairs, which were submitted by the commission in july last year. the european council called for the necessary steps to be taken as soon as possible to enable the agency to be set up and to be operational by 1 january 2007. in accordance with the conclusions of the european council, the finnish presidency organised a series of bilateral meetings in july, august, september and october to resolve the main remaining issue, namely the extension of the agency's activities to the areas covered by the third pillar of the treaty on european union. at the council meeting in early october, the presidency presented a report on the negotiations and asked for support for the idea of extending the agency's activities to the areas covered by the third pillar, but in a more limited form than in the commission's original proposal. the majority of the delegations that expressed their views supported this view of the chair, although some delegations questioned whether there was a proper legal basis for enlargement. the presidency will continue to examine the options and will present a proposal for mediation to the delegations in the near future. as regards the agency's remit, its objective is to provide advice and expertise on fundamental rights to the community institutions, bodies, offices and agencies and to the member states in the application of community law, and thus to assist them in ensuring respect for fundamental rights when they take action or define policies within the framework of their remit. there is a consensus that the establishment of such an agency will add value to and increase the coherence of the european union's human rights policy. the agency will also be the main contact point for fundamental rights issues in the european union. the agency will carry out its tasks in complementarity and synergy with the work of the council of europe once the decisions on its establishment have been taken.
president of the council. mr president, first of all, the agency is to be set up as an advisory body of experts. but we also believe that it would be difficult to justify, even to the citizens, the creation of a fundamental rights agency which would be deprived of such core competences as its activities in the area of the third pillar. that is why we are continuing to work on this matter.
president of the council. mr president, perhaps such an attempt is sometimes made in certain contexts. but we have tried to work as a presidency to make the administrative structures themselves as light as possible. as for the fundamental rights agency, on the other hand, as i said at the beginning, there is a strong consensus that it is necessary. it is therefore necessary to make a great effort to ensure that decisions are taken and that the agency is operational from 1 january and that it has competence in matters which are essential to its operation.
question no 9 by eoin ryan (h-0795/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: eu-iran relationscan the european council make a statement on the current state of eu-iran relations, with particular reference to the issue of the future of the nuclear industry in iran?
president of the council. mr president, the council is committed to continuing to build a long-term relationship of trust and cooperation with iran. the development of relations requires progress on all the problematic issues, including human rights, terrorism, iran's attitude to the middle east peace process and regional issues, and iran's nuclear programme. on the nuclear issue, the council has repeatedly stated its commitment to a diplomatic solution that takes account of international concerns about iran's nuclear programme, while at the same time strengthening iran's right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy in accordance with the npt. in this context, on 17 october the council noted the continued efforts made by the high representative, mr javier solana, since june to encourage iran to respond to the demands of the international atomic energy agency's governing council and the un security council and to continue discussions on long-term arrangements. the eu takes very seriously the iaea's assessment that, after almost four years of intensive verification, the agency has failed to make progress in its efforts to verify the accuracy and completeness of iran's declarations concerning the peaceful nature of its nuclear programme. the eu is also very concerned that iran has not suspended all its uranium enrichment and reprocessing activities, as requested by the iaea board of governors and the un security council. in its resolution 1696, the security council indicated its intention to take appropriate measures under article 41 if iran failed to comply with the request. accordingly, the council considers that, as iran continues to engage in uranium enrichment activities, the union has no choice but to support the negotiations on those sanctions. however, the council now stated in october that the door to the negotiating table was still open to iran and urged iran to choose the positive course proposed to it. the eu high representative presented the six countries' proposals to iran on 6 june. these far-reaching proposals would form the basis of a long-term agreement and give iran everything it needs to develop a modern civilian energy sector, taking into account international concerns. the choice of this positive approach would pave the way for new relations with iran, which could be based on mutual respect and enhanced cooperation in the political and economic fields. the council hopes that this positive path can be taken further.
president of the council. mr president, the discussion of these possible coercive measures is of course linked to the fact that un security council resolution 1696 is also a commitment of the european union. the drug trafficking is linked to the overall situation in afghanistan, which could even be the subject of a separate question. the union has a long-term commitment to afghanistan, not only to peacekeeping and crisis management but also to the development of a comprehensive approach to drug production.

president of the council. mr president, member states decide whether to apply transitional periods to the free movement of labour for the new member states. there are also member states which applied the transitional period in the previous enlargement but no longer do so in this new enlargement. the reason is that it is better for labour to move within the framework of the common european acquis than to create derogations. as i said in my answer to the previous question, equal treatment in the labour market is very well protected in the area of regulation, but there is a need to pay more attention to implementation and monitoring.
