question no 37 by sharon bowles (h-0963/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: workers from romania and bulgariathe commission's report on the application of the transitional arrangements laid down in the 2003 accession treaty shows that the overall impact of the mobility of workers from those eu member states which joined the eu-15 in 2004 has been positive. is the commission therefore disappointed that some member states, such as the united kingdom and ireland, have decided to restrict the rights of romanians and bulgarians to work in those countries once romania and bulgaria become full members of the eu on 1 january 2007? does the commission believe that this will have any negative impact on the economy in these member states and the eu as a whole, or that more people will be forced to work illegally as a result? in view of the fact that the united kingdom, ireland and sweden (which did not apply restrictions after may 2004) have experienced a decline in unemployment, rising employment and strong economic growth, does the commission consider that the concern expressed by some member states about an 'inflow' of migrant workers is a genuine concern?
member of the commission. as a matter of principle, the commission is in favour of full application of the four freedoms, including the freedom of movement of workers in the european union. one should remember that this freedom is one of the core principles of the treaty of rome. however, the accession treaty with bulgaria and romania, like those of the previous enlargement, lays down transitional provisions on the right to free movement of workers. essentially, these provisions leave it up to each current member state to determine whether, during a transitional period, to grant bulgarian and romanian nationals access to their labour markets. this is thus a prerogative of each and every member state. the commission plans to send a letter to all the member states recalling their obligations under community law and asking member states to provide the details of any national measures that might be introduced for the first two years that follow the accession of bulgaria and romania. at the same time, let me draw your attention to the commission’s report on the functioning of the transitional arrangements for the enlargement of 1 may 2004, and in particular to the finding that the arrival of workers from the accession member states has had a beneficial effect and actually helped to reduce imbalances in national labour markets, without the newcomers largely taking the place of local jobseekers. this applies, of course, to those member states that have facilitated the free movement of workers. this report also found that there have been overall positive effects on the economies of the eu 15 member states, with workers from the new member states contributing to a better functioning of the labour markets, to sustained economic growth and to better public finances. it also found that restrictions on labour market access may increase the incidence of undeclared work. the commission believes that those findings are still valid and trusts that the member states will consider them closely when deciding whether to introduce transitional measures applicable to bulgaria and romania.
member of the commission. thank you for your question. it is perfectly possible that this might happen, but only time will tell, which is why we are constantly analysing developments in the labour markets in the eu and its member states. there are two basic scenarios, which may vary from one member state to another. namely, a given member state may benefit from having the possibility of receiving workers from the new member states, owing to its demographic profile and the challenges posed by an ageing population. at the same time, it may be that another member state has labour market problems, and higher unemployment, and that the national government consequently decides that, given the circumstances, it would benefit from the transitional arrangements. that is why we have decided to leave this matter to the member states to judge, and why we have given them the option of applying the transitional measures.
member of the commission. i have taken note of the decisions of the united kingdom and ireland. it is without doubt a prerogative of those countries, as for any other member state. prior to these decisions, i used the united kingdom and ireland as a benchmark when arguing the case for opening the labour markets of the other member states to the candidate countries. i am proud of having in my previous capacity helped the prime minister of the member state i know best to draft his speech on 1 may 2004 when he declared that member state – finland – was likely to remove the restrictions on free movement of workers from the new member states. that particular member state maintains the same liberal practice for bulgaria and romania. the point is that on the basis of very reliable studies there are overall positive effects, but at the same time we want to leave it to the member states – and we have to leave it to the member states because that is the decision of the council of the european union, which is the highest decision-making body in cases of this kind in the union.
member of the commission. i am glad to note that mr stubb has made a rapid career move from the back benches to the front benches here. that is impressive and remarkable. i want to tell you that we are continuing to analyse developments in the labour markets in the european union and all the evidence shows that those countries that have applied a liberal practice of receiving workers from the new member states, such as the united kingdom and ireland, have benefited in terms of overall economic growth and better functioning of the labour market. therefore we can continue to argue the case so that we have positive benchmarks, like those two countries and other countries such as the member state you know best. after we have argued the case, then it is the prerogative of each and every member state; and of course we have to trust the judgement of each and every national government, because they should know best the circumstances in the country and what is best for the country and its citizens.

member of the commission. i thank mr martin for his question. the aim of commission regulation (ec) no 1546/2006 is to address the new threat to civil aviation that is posed by homemade liquid explosives. as such, it prohibits passengers on flights departing from community airports from taking liquids in hand luggage in individual quantities greater than 100 ml. however, an exemption has been granted for liquids sold at airport shops and on board aircraft when certain security conditions are met, including the tamper-evident bag system. given that community legislation does not apply in third countries, it is currently not possible to ensure that airports in third countries or non-community air carriers have security requirements that are equivalent to those applied within the european union and the european economic area. consequently, such airports and airlines cannot benefit from the exemption. the commission will consider whether it is possible to work with third countries to develop a means of establishing equivalence of security measures.
member of the commission. thank you for that question. i wish to begin by underlining the fact that one cannot compromise on security. the commission and the community is doing what it can to further open up the system in place with regard to the european union, although it will probably be quite difficult to achieve significant results in the very short term, and therefore before christmas, as this calls for negotiations with third countries in order to achieve similar positions to ours. regarding your point concerning the publicity campaign, the commission has been working with the international airport and airline stakeholder organisations concerned so that they can inform their members in third countries about the new eu rules. in addition, the commission has assisted those stakeholders in their campaign to inform passengers by developing standardised information posters and leaflets that their members can use as part of their own information campaigns.
member of the commission. the commission is of the view that in fact they do contribute to increased security in real terms, because, obviously, physical checks are carried out on passengers in order to determine that there are no such liquids. any liquids would be carried in transparent bags. secondly, there is also the question of perception: passengers feel that something is being done and that one would think twice before trying to take on board things which could be suspect and which would be spotted.

question no 39 by mr rack (h-1048/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: compensation for delays in air transportintra-european air transport is increasingly subject to long delays with great inconvenience to passengers. does the commission consider that it is possible to revise regulation (ec) no 261/2004 (oj l 46, 17.2.2004, p. 1) so that, as in the case of rail passengers, compensation in cash is paid to air passengers according to the length of delay?
member of the commission. according to the air passenger rights regulation (ec) no 261/2004, airlines are not obliged to offer passengers financial compensation when stranded for long delays. however, the regulation requires that passengers receive assistance from the airline, including food and drink and accommodation as necessary. in addition, the montreal convention, the updated version of the warsaw convention which was transposed into regulation (ec) no 889/2002, dealing with rules for international carrier liabilities, provides for certain rights in case of delays, from which the airline’s liability is limited to 4150 special drawing rights, which is approximately eur 5000. in this case, the passenger must demonstrate a causal link between the damages he or she has suffered and the incident provoked by the airline. according to article 17 of regulation (ec) no 261/2004, the commission will submit to parliament and the council a report on the application of this regulation in the eu member states. a call for tenders has been launched in order to contract an external consultant to give input with regard to quantitative and qualitative data. the study will deal in particular with issues related to delays and cancellations, as well as with the enforcement of the regulation concerned. the commission cannot at present prejudge whether additional measures will be proposed to improve the protection of air passengers. the commission will have to wait for the final results of the assessment made by the external consultants.
member of the commission. i would like to point out that the important difference between the previous regulation and the present one which is based on the montreal convention is that passengers are entitled to receive direct and on-the-spot information, assistance and rerouting facilities, whereas the montreal convention only covers ad hoc claims to be presented in a court, as you rightly indicated, for possible damage caused because of a delay. i will, however, pass on the remarks that you have made to vice-president barrot in order to see whether anything further can be done, although as i pointed out in my reply to the question, the commission does not envisage coming up with additional measures before the final results of the assessment – which is being carried out by an external consultant – are known.
member of the commission. as a general comment, regulation (ec) no 261/2004 does not provide for any extraordinary circumstances linked to denied boarding. if because of technical failure an airline replaces the original aircraft with a smaller type, and some of the passengers are denied boarding because not all of them can board that aircraft, and they have to stay behind at the airport, those stranded passengers have to be assisted and offered financial compensation as provided for in the regulation. it is only for reasons of health, safety or security or inadequate travel documentation that passengers can be refused embarkation on a flight. i will also refer to vice-president barrot for his attention the specific comments you have made with regard to last night’s events concerning air france.
member of the commission. you are right that security measures and additional security measures – and this links up to the previous question – have a cost. however, one needs to underline that if we really want to tackle the question of security on board aircraft then cost considerations can only be secondary. however, having said that, i will again pass your remarks on to vice-president barrot, to see whether there is scope for trying to identify possibilities of cost-sharing in this regard.
this brings us to the second part of our question time. since we have only about half an hour left, i can only allow a total of 10 minutes of question time per commissioner. i would ask all those who are asking to take a moment to reflect on this.
question no 40 by chris davies (h-0991/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: eu action to end by-catch discardswhen will the commission introduce measures to end by-catch discards by fishing vessels?
member of the commission. it is somewhat premature to give details because if one starts going into detail now before discussions with the stakeholders, it could be somewhat alarmist, as always happens in fisheries. our intention is to heavily involve the regional advisory councils and to involve the stakeholders in how to manage fisheries in a way in which we try to tackle the cod problem effectively. there is, as all of us know, a serious problem with regard to cod sustainability. in most, if not all, community waters it is in a virtually depleted state. it is possible for it to be rescued, but we need to be inventive in this regard. the general idea behind a cod by-catch fishery is that, for as long as cod is not recovered, you do not target cod. thus fishers would not target cod, but they would be allowed to land cod caught as a by-catch within certain limits. in that way you can provide an incentive for the diversification of fisheries into other fisheries so you would not thereby be targeting cod and at the same time you would reduce the unnecessary and very costly discarding of cod. these are initial ideas which we need to ponder further and which we need to discuss primarily with the stakeholders, to see whether there is a way forward, or whether, as in many other respects, we end up concluding that the system as it operates is giving better results in certain respects. but i hope that we will manage to work out a system which will give much better results than those we have at the moment with regard to cod and to cod recovery in particular.

member of the commission. the question of the age of retirement is a highly sensitive one, which cannot be answered very clearly and fixed by a decision at european level, and is therefore entirely a matter for the national states. i would like to stress that this is a legitimate question and that the commission's strategy is not to set a fixed age. the commission's strategy, which i strongly support, is to extend working life, to extend the actual time a person spends working in his lifetime. it is less important to set an administrative age, it is far more important to create the conditions for people to end their working careers later. very often you will notice that the administrative age is set at 65, whereas the average age for leaving an economic career in europe is currently 59. i would also like to emphasize that there is an extended average life expectancy in good health, which is 62 years on average in europe, but there are very substantial differences between countries. that is a question that must of course be taken into account in the debate. i would like to emphasise that the concept of an inclusive society is based on the fact that work has a character of active inclusion in society in addition to its economic character. i think that sociological research shows very well that early retirement at a time when one has not reached one's potential is perceived as a disadvantage rather than an advantage. let me return to your basic question. the commission does not intend to set and recommend any administrative, fixed retirement age. on the other hand, it is of the opinion that, in view of demographic ageing, in view of the significant increase in the age at which people are entitled to receive a pension, it is appropriate to increase the total time spent in work. to do this, a number of measures must be taken, of which the administrative extension of the retirement age is, at least from my point of view, among the less significant.

questions 48 to 53 will be answered in writing. question no 54 by mr tarabella (h-0955/06) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: failure of consumer policy in the single marketthe latest eurobarometer survey, conducted in march 2006, has once again shown the total distrust of consumers towards the single market and their complete ignorance of their rights and the possibilities of solving their problems. can the commission explain why the existing legal instruments are inadequate and/or poorly implemented to the extent that consumers are deterred from making cross-border purchases? how does it intend to protect consumers from the growing disadvantages caused by the explosive growth of online shopping? why does it not take into account the thousands of complaints it receives from its own networks concerning cross-border purchases, travel, health services, etc.?
member of the commission. madam president, the survey referred to by the honourable member does indeed confirm the commission's view that much more needs to be done to strengthen consumer confidence in the internal market. but if we think about where we started from, where we started from and where we are today, we should not adopt such a totally negative attitude. the progress is significant and can be seen in the measures we have taken and their implementation in recent years. the commission is certainly not complacent and is constantly working to strengthen consumer confidence, but the member states also have an important role to play. although low confidence is due to many factors, one of them is clearly the lack of a harmonised consumer protection system, which means that consumers do not know what to expect when they shop across their national borders. but they must recognize that much has been achieved in recent years to solve these problems. but it is clear, of course, that more needs to be done, particularly in terms of existing legislation and its implementation, in order to increase consumer confidence. both the measures taken and those planned are intended to deal with the growing number of unfair and illegal practices. what has been achieved at european union level? first of all, i would like to assure you that the commission has never ignored the complaints it has received or is receiving through its networks. on the contrary, it is precisely these complaints that have triggered action in the past, for example, to adopt legislation against unfair commercial practices. they also form an important part of the evidence base and information for future action, for example for time-sharing. with this legislation on time-sharing we will cover travel products which escape the legislation and thus do not provide an acceptable level of consumer protection. the other legislation i referred to, the unfair commercial practices directive 2005/29, prohibits aggressive practices such as pressure selling, misleading marketing and unfair advertising. consumers in the european union will have the same protection whether they buy locally, from other member states or via the internet, and the horizontal nature of this protection will allow it to also cover new practices that will emerge as the market evolves. in addition, the directive 2000/31 on electronic commerce imposed information requirements to ensure that consumers are fully informed as to the identity of the trader, the commercial nature of internet communications, the actual price, and the technical means. regulation 2006/2004 on consumer protection cooperation will enable the competent national authorities to take swift action to combat crossborder ruthless and unfair traders, wherever they are in the european union. in the proposal for a regulation on the law applicable to contracts, the so-called 'rome i regulation', the commission proposal will significantly increase consumer confidence by giving them the advantage of the legislation they are familiar with. we also have the european consumer centres networks or the financial dispute resolution network which inform consumers about their rights and help them to secure their rights through legal recourse and through out-of-court settlement of cross-border cases. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of consumers. a green paper will shortly be adopted for consultation with the general public. the aim is to find ways of modernising and improving existing legislation in order to further increase consumer and business confidence in buying and selling across the internal market's borders. the issue of consumer confidence will of course also be considered in the context of the forthcoming strategy for consumer policy. as you can see, although our investigations show that there are still significant problems, i think it is clear that the commission is not complacent, it is not passive, but is taking measures which are part of a comprehensive programme to tackle the shortcomings identified by the investigation.
member of the commission. we are going to look into how all the legislation has been transposed and we are checking it through our review of the acquis. we will make sure first of all that member states have properly transposed this legislation. if it appears that even if the transposition has been done properly there are still problems in the internal market and still trade barriers or discrepancies in consumer protection between member states, we will make sure that these are corrected through additional initiatives. so we are following this very carefully and will make sure that member states properly apply all the european legislation when it comes to consumer protection. as you know, as of 1 january my colleague mrs kuneva is going to take over consumer protection and she feels very strongly about this issue as well.
question no 55 by sarah ludford (h-0965/06) subject: the use of the euro in the european union subject: genetically modified ricewhile the commission's decision of 23 october on the mandatory testing of imports of genetically modified organisms is welcome, many aspects of this are of great concern. the competent authorities of the united states have repeatedly certified that their rice is free from the unauthorised gmo llrice 601; however, this was found in the deliveries. in view of this, how can eu consumers have confidence in the reliability of these certification schemes? genetically modified rice from the united states has been reportedly sold in uk supermarkets with the approval of the uk's official food regulator, the food standards agency (fsa). does this build trust in the fsa? how could the authority's decision be in line with eu law? the uk government has proposed to allow the joint cultivation of gmo crops and conventional and organic crops. how will the commission prevent infringements of eu legislation on contamination?
member of the commission. it is true that this is a very important issue for us and it is clear that no unauthorised product can enter the market in the european union. we have a very strict system in place to ensure that no product slips through the very high standard assessment procedure. the question of the contamination of us long grain rice, involving unauthorised gm llrice 601, proves that this is not just a statement but a fact. our reaction has shown that we intend to apply our legislation in every possible case. as soon as the commission was informed of this contamination of us rice, we took every possible measure to prevent unauthorised products from entering the market. first, we introduced a requirement for certification of every single consignment arriving in the european union. but when we became aware that shipments of us rice certified as gm-free tested positive at the port of arrival in the european union, the certification requirement was strengthened by the imposition of systematic counter-testing of each consignment originating in the us. furthermore, it is also important that this counter-testing be carried out on the basis of a harmonised and very strict sampling and testing procedure, which guarantees reliability and comparability of the results, so our consumers can be assured that every consignment of us long grain rice is tested twice, both in the us and on arrival in the european union. i have to remind you that member states bear the primary responsibility for enforcing these requirements and verifying that they are fulfilled by business operators. the commission has systematically reminded national authorities of this obligation to carry out adequate checks and withdraw contaminated products. the uk food standards agency has clarified its approach by agreeing to the conclusions of the standing committee on 11 september 2006. in that context, member states commit themselves to checking all stored bulk consignments of us rice already on the european union market. when it comes to products on the shelf, our legislation provides that member states will take all appropriate measures to ensure that these are tested and removed from the market if necessary. but the aim is to provide the legislation. it is up to the member states to ensure that measures are taken in the most effective way. on the issue of cross-pollination, it is important to remember that no gm crop can be grown in the european union unless it has been evaluated as safe for the environment and human and animal health and authorised for cultivation. member states are developing coexistence strategies to ensure that they can limit as much as possible admixtures of gm and non-gm crops and address the economic consequences. the competence for this lies with the member states, following the recommendations and guidelines of the european union. however, the special characteristics of each member state – the landscape, the environment, climate conditions – make it important for them to take the most appropriate measures. we know that many member states, including the united kingdom, have defined or are in the process of defining approaches to ensure that gm crops can coexist with conventional and organic crops. member states are obliged to notify national coexistence measures to the commission and the commission follows this very closely.
member of the commission. as long as we have gm products throughout the world that are not authorised by us, we will always have to be alert and to take all measures available. i think the fact that we identified early on that we could not rely on us certification and that we introduced our own testing system proves that we are very serious about this. on the uk issue, any product containing an unauthorised gm component has to be withdrawn because it is on the market illegally. that is an obligation for all member states including the uk; this was made clear to them and they understood that. it is true that the european food safety authority said that there was no imminent danger to human health, and the uk repeated that, but, as far as the commission is concerned, any product of this sort that has not been authorised through our procedures is on the market illegally and has to be removed. after we made it clear to the uk authorities that this was the legal position, they adjusted their position. in this respect, we make sure that member states also apply the legislation, which is very strict, and no unauthorised product can reach the consumer. after some discussions, the uk has corrected its position.

been an accepted reality in italy for years. the eu driving licence contributes to road safety by preventing driving tourism. drivers who have been caught speeding or with alcohol in their blood and have had their driving licence revoked can now go abroad and obtain a new licence. this practice poses serious risks to road safety. the road-traffic offenders often avoid the months-long driving test and the urgent medical and psychological examination by going to poland or the czech republic. with the eu driving licence, that will no longer be possible. there is no longer any chance of all-inclusive packages that allowed alcoholics, drug addicts and speedsters to obtain a new driving licence abroad. this not only saved the street roadies from the tedious waiting times, but also the costly medical and psychological examination at a cost of 1 000 euros. given the high number of accidents caused by racing and drunkenness, this is an important contribution to road safety. in fact, sample checks revealed that 75% of german drivers with foreign driving licences had previously had their licences withdrawn because of alcohol or drug problems. the eu driving licence prevents this abuse, because thorough data exchange prevents it. unfortunately, my home country, germany, was on the brakes and after 15 years of decision-making, it also imposed a transitional period of 26 years until the holders of driving licences had to change their grey patches. this is not only a social injustice at the expense of future generations new drivers already have their second license due to the renewal deadline before the old ones even have to be changed for the first time but also another state tolerance of organized crime due to the delayed exchange of data. in the interests of road safety, and especially because of the long decision-making time, parliament and the council should have refrained from any transitional period and established a uniform system of validity for old and new driving licences. member states are free to reduce the time limits, so i urge you to do so so that the eu driving licence will become a reality in 10 years.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to present to you today the amendment to the regulation on double-hull tankers. the proposal aims to bring the regulation into line with the political declaration made to the international maritime organisation in december 2003 by the presidency of the european union on behalf of the member states and the european commission. that statement was extremely clear. it was intended to inform all the contracting parties to the marpol convention that no member state of the european union would allow oil tankers flying its flag to use one of the exemptions provided for in the convention, namely the use of single-hull vessels for the transport of oil. as regards the prohibition on the carriage of heavy petroleum products in single-hull vessels, the regulation in force today applies only to vessels entering waters under community jurisdiction. this means that a member state can theoretically, and contrary to the public commitment of 2003, allow the transport of heavy petroleum products in single-hull tankers flying its flag, i.e. one of the european flags, as long as these vessels operate outside community waters. this situation, ladies and gentlemen, is unacceptable. we can only imagine the consequences in a third country if a black tide is caused by an oil tanker flying the community flag, even though europe is providing its own protection! i would add that almost all the member states have already formally informed the international maritime organisation that they would not make use of this option. our political commitments to maritime safety vis-à-vis our partners must be made concrete and legally guaranteed. that's the point of this proposal. i would like to thank mr le rachinel and the committee on transport and tourism for their support.

and i am pleased that the commission has found its role under your leadership and is doing a convincing job - we do have a common objective, namely to make this european union strong and capable of action. i would like to conclude, mr president borrell, by making a request to the political groups, to the chairmen and to parliament: let us always treat each other with respect and dignity in parliament and between the institutions. when we have respect and esteem for one another, that builds trust. and when that trust is there, europe is the beneficiary. i am sure that we will achieve our dream: a strong europe, a europe that is capable of action and democratic, a europe based on the rule of law. and this is the new thing in the 21st century. if we have that respect, that respect, that trust, then i am convinced that this european union will take a good development for our values and for our interests at home and abroad. the socialist group will be voting in favour of the report. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the president of the council has accepted the thanks of the epp group. that's nice, i want to join that. i am very grateful to mr vanhanen for the finnish presidency, which i think has done a good job. the finnish presidency has done a very good job in the circumstances in which it has had to lead the european union. i also share your view, mr vanhanen, that a summit where journalists say it is boring is not necessarily a bad summit. the european union needs less journalistic carnage than concrete results. i would therefore like to judge this summit not by the boredom or the joy of journalists, but by its results. two good things: the clear message of this summit is that europe is committed to its responsibility for enlargement! we have a responsibility in this enlargement process. the prospect of accession has been and remains peace-making, particularly in the balkans. but those who believe that enlargement can go ahead without the reforms that are essential in the constitutional process have also received a clear message over the weekend: there will be no enlargement without the necessary reforms of the eu. that is also an important message. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. so if we want enlargement to meet needs and to bring about peace, we need an effective europe. i would therefore like to make it clear that without the reforms introduced in the constitutional process, there will be no enlargement with my group. with the constitutional reforms, there is enlargement! (applause from the centre) we have heard in this debate over the weekend a second positive - and i mean very positive - series of statements which will be indicative for the coming years. it is a very positive signal that the european union is committed to migration policy, moving away from just restrictive, but acknowledging that we need migration and orderly immigration on this continent. finally, i must say, finally! but here again, one thing is clear: the necessary instruments which - you are right - would have been available even under the nice treaty, using the passerelle, are not being used. so if i describe a goal on the one hand, but deny myself the tools i need to achieve it on the other, i am not very credible. so it was not a peak of boredom, but, once again, a missed opportunity. i am therefore firmly convinced that we as parliament must continue to urge the council to finally act coherently, to act in a coherent way and to say: if we want to control migration, we must also give the eu the instruments it needs to do so. we have, as the european parliament, together with you - and this has been mentioned by all the speakers - completed two important, landmark legislative procedures. the services directive is one of the greatest achievements of the internal market in my group's view. the neoliberal concept of destruction has become socially responsible legislation. the second concerns the chemicals policy: i saw at the reception that the representatives of the chemical industry and the representatives of greenpeace were drinking champagne together. so it cannot be such a bad piece of legislation! as you can see from the interim reports, my group has worked to ensure that legislation makes possible a reasonable compromise aimed at social balance and industrial rationality and consumer rights. i would like to thank evelyn gebhardt and guido sacconi, who have been the pilots for our group, once again for this great achievement that we have made as the european parliament under the leadership of my group. (applause from the centre) mr poettering has - i will say this to conclude - referred to his outgoing term as chairman of the epp group. i do not want to address all the other group leaders either, i am only addressing him. yes, we had a very, very constructive and collegial cooperation, for which i want to thank you. i would also like to pay a great compliment to mr poettering: i must say that he is an extremely skilled politician. let me illustrate this with a small example from this morning: no one has noticed in the meantime, after two and a half years, the phrase 'i say for the epp part of my group'. the group is called the epp-ed. this formulation implies that a whole section of his group will not speak at all. the european parliament has always been a party to the european convention on human rights. in this way he has actually managed to be the chairman of two political groups without anyone noticing. this is political art, and i commend you for it, mr poettering. (applause from the centre and the right) such a man, ladies and gentlemen, is capable of greatness. we shall see! i want to thank you for your cooperation. the fact that hans-gert poettering has been a figure in the european parliament since 1979 is one thing: one can disagree with him, one can argue with him, one can be angry with him, one can rejoice with him. but one thing is always certain, you will never be fooled by hans-gert poettering. he is a man of clear words and above all a man of reliability. i think those are virtues that are rare in politics. the more you pursue a career in politics, the less you encounter these virtues. if someone has reached such a high level and maintains it so consistently, then thank him, acknowledge him and wish him well! (applause from the centre) mr president-in-office of the council, on behalf of my group i would like to expressly welcome the decision of the summit to keep the european union open to new members and to keep the commitments made to the countries in the process of enlargement. although no one can at present predict exactly when we will be able to welcome new states into the european union after bulgaria and romania, it must be clear that all european states that share our common values and that meet the conditions for admission, in particular the copenhagen criteria, have a right to apply for membership of the european union. i am personally convinced that the existing treaty of nice is not a suitable basis for future enlargements. the future of the union therefore requires strengthening the union's capacity for integration and launching a truly comprehensive and far-reaching reform of the union of 27. it is not only the candidates who have to change. first of all, the union itself must do its homework. and i believe that this means that during the german presidency of the council a solution to the constitutional crisis that is acceptable to all must be found. the crucial point is that it is not only the citizens of france and the netherlands who are finally being shown that the reflection phase, mr president-in-office, also has consequences for other policies. the prospectus is not going to help. people must reconnect with europe their very personal prospects for the future, for themselves and for their families. work and social security that is what they expect from europe. decent working conditions, effective equality of opportunity in education and employment, protection against illness, a guaranteed minimum income - all these things matter. and that, mr president of the commission, would be a europe of results. but if the union and its member states continue as they have been, if wage dumping, social dumping and crossborder competition between workers remain the everyday experience of people, then europe will continue to lose its popularity. but that's exactly what we can't have. and that is why, mr president of the council and mr president of the commission, the question of social justice must be given the highest political priority.
